bal.17.so17: I bow to Hanumān, son of the Wind, a fire to the forest of the wicked, full of wisdom.
In the house of his heart Śrī Rāma dwells, holding his bow and arrows.
ayodhya.0.shloka1: He in whose lap the daughter of the mountain shines, on whose head the river of the gods,
on whose forehead the young moon, in whose throat the poison, and on whose chest the king of serpents;
he who is adorned with ash, the foremost of the gods, the ruler of all,
Śarva, all-pervading, Śiva, fair as the moon: may that Śrī Śaṅkara protect me always.
ayodhya.0.shloka2: That which neither brightened at the coronation nor faded at the sorrow of exile in the forest,
the beauty of Śrī Rāma's lotus face: may it ever bring me lovely blessings.
ayodhya.0.shloka3: Dark and soft of limb as the blue lotus, with Sītā seated at his left side,
a mighty arrow and a lovely bow in hand: to Rāma, the lord of Raghu's line, I bow.
ayodhya.0.dou1: Making the mirror of my own mind clean with dust from my revered Guru's lotus feet,
I tell the spotless glory of Śrī Rāma, which grants the four fruits of life (dharma, wealth, desire and liberation).
ayodhya.1.cau1: Ever since Śrī Rāma came home married, there have been fresh festivities, joy and rejoicing every day.
On the fourteen worlds, as on great mountains, the clouds of merit pour down the rain of happiness.
ayodhya.1.cau2: Lovely rivers of prosperity, success and wealth swelled and came flowing into the ocean of Avadh.
The men and women of the city are clusters of gems of the finest kind, pure, priceless and beautiful in every way.
ayodhya.1.cau3: The splendour of the city cannot be told at all; it is as if Brahmā's craft had gone this far and no further.
All the people of the city are content in every way, for they behold the moon of Śrī Rāma's face.
ayodhya.1.cau4: The mothers, with all their friends and companions, are glad: they see the vine of their hopes in fruit.
Seeing and hearing of Śrī Rāma's beauty, virtues, gentleness and nature, the king is overjoyed.
ayodhya.1.do1: All have this one wish at heart, and praying to Śiva they say:
May the king, in his own lifetime, give Śrī Rāma the place of crown prince.
ayodhya.2.cau1: Once the king of the Raghus sat in state in the royal court with all his assembly.
The king, the embodiment of all merit, was full of delight at hearing of Śrī Rāma's fair fame.
ayodhya.2.cau2: All kings live in hope of his favour, and the guardians of the worlds keep to his wishes and show him love.
In the three worlds and the three times, nowhere in creation is anyone as fortunate as Daśaratha.
ayodhya.2.cau3: Whatever is said of one whose son is Śrī Rāma, the root of all blessings, falls short.
The king happened to take a mirror in hand, and as he looked at his face he put his crown level.
ayodhya.2.cau4: Near his ears the hair had turned white, as if old age were giving him this counsel:
O king, make Śrī Rāma crown prince; why not take the reward of your life and your birth?
ayodhya.2.do2: With this thought taken to heart, the king found an auspicious day and a fitting moment,
and, his body thrilling with love and his mind glad, he went and told it to his guru.
ayodhya.3.cau1: The king said: Hear me, O lord of sages. Rāma has become capable of all things in every respect.
Servants, ministers, all the citizens, and those who are our enemies, our friends or neither,
ayodhya.3.cau2: to all of them Rāma is dear, just as he is to me; he is your blessing, as it were, shining in bodily form.
Lord, every Brahmin and his household are as fond of him as you are.
ayodhya.3.cau3: Whoever bears the dust of the guru's feet on his head has, it seems, every kind of wealth at his command.
Nobody has tasted this truth as I have, for every good thing came to me from honouring that pure dust.
ayodhya.3.cau4: One longing is in my mind now; your favour, my lord, will bring it to pass.
The sage's heart warmed at the king's natural affection, and he said: Give the order, O king.
ayodhya.3.do3: O king, your name and fame alone grant every wish.
O jewel among kings, the desire of your heart only follows after its fruit.
ayodhya.4.cau1: Knowing in his heart that the guru was pleased in every way, the king spoke gently and with joy:
My lord, let Rāma be made crown prince. Be gracious and say the word, and let the preparations be made.
ayodhya.4.cau2: While I am still here, let this joyful event happen, and let every eye among the people be rewarded.
Śiva, by your favour, my lord, has carried all my affairs through; this single longing is what my heart holds.
ayodhya.4.cau3: Then it will not trouble me whether this body lasts or falls; only let nothing be left for me to regret.
The sage heard Daśaratha's pleasing words, and they, the root of blessing and joy, delighted his heart.
ayodhya.4.cau4: Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O king: he from whom those who turn away come to regret, without whose worship the burning within does not cease,
that very Lord has become your son: Śrī Rāma, who follows where love is pure.
ayodhya.4.do4: Be quick, O king, make no delay; have everything made ready.
The day is auspicious and full of blessing the moment Rāma becomes crown prince.
ayodhya.5.cau1: The king came home to the palace in joy and called his servants, his ministers and Sumantra.
Crying Victory and long life, they bowed their heads, and the king told them the auspicious news.
ayodhya.5.cau2: If this counsel seems good to you, the council, then with glad hearts mark Rāma with the tilaka of kingship.
ayodhya.5.cau3: The ministers rejoiced at the welcome words, as though water had fallen on the sapling of their wish.
With joined hands the ministers pleaded: Lord of the world, may you live for millions upon millions of years.
ayodhya.5.cau4: The plan you have made is good and will bless the world. Hurry, my lord; let there be no delay.
Hearing the ministers' fair words, the king was glad, like a growing tendril that has found a good branch.
ayodhya.5.do5: The king said: Whatever command the king of sages may give,
carry it out at once for Rāma's royal anointing.
ayodhya.6.cau1: The chief of sages spoke gently and with joy: Bring water from all the holy places.
Herbs, roots, flowers, fruit, betel leaves: he named many auspicious things one by one.
ayodhya.6.cau2: fly-whisks, hides, garments of many kinds, woollen and silken cloths of countless sorts,
gems, and many auspicious things such as are fit in this world for a king's anointing.
ayodhya.6.cau3: He explained every rite known from the Vedas, then said: Put up canopies of many kinds throughout the city.
Plant mango, areca and plantain trees laden with fruit along the lanes all round the city.
ayodhya.6.cau4: Lay out fair squares of gems, and send word to have the market decorated at once.
Worship Gaṇeśa, the guru and the family deity, and serve the Brahmins in every way.
ayodhya.6.do6: Adorn flags, banners, arches, pitchers, horses, chariots and elephants.
Taking the great sage's words on their heads, everyone set to his own task.
ayodhya.7.cau1: Whoever received a command from the chief of sages had that task done, as if he had done it beforehand.
Worshipping Brahmins, holy men and gods, the king carries out auspicious works for Śrī Rāma's good.
ayodhya.7.cau2: At the welcome news of Śrī Rāma's anointing, festive music rang out loudly through Avadh.
Śrī Rāma and Sītā felt omens in their bodies, for their fair and auspicious limbs were throbbing.
ayodhya.7.cau3: Their bodies thrilling, they lovingly tell each other: this foretells Bharata's arrival.
It has been many days and the waiting is hard; the omens make us sure that we will see our dear one.
ayodhya.7.cau4: Who in the world is as dear as Bharata? This is the omens' fruit, and no other.
Day and night his brother is on Śrī Rāma's mind, the way a tortoise's heart stays with its eggs.
ayodhya.7.do7: At this time the queens' palace heard the supremely auspicious news and rejoiced,
like the play of the ocean's waves, splendid as they see the moon wax.
ayodhya.8.cau1: Those who went first and told the news received ornaments and clothes in plenty.
Love thrilled through the queens' bodies and their hearts glowed with devotion as all of them began to adorn the auspicious pitchers.
ayodhya.8.cau2: Sumitrā filled in lovely squares of gems, of many designs and most beautiful.
Śrī Rāma's mother, lost in joy, called the Brahmins and gave them many gifts.
ayodhya.8.cau3: She worshipped the village goddesses, the gods and the Nāgas, and vowed to bring them offerings again:
Be merciful and grant the boon by which Śrī Rāma may prosper.
ayodhya.8.cau4: Women with voices like the cuckoo's, faces like the moon and eyes like a fawn's sing songs of blessing.
ayodhya.8.do8: Hearing of Śrī Rāma's royal anointing, men and women rejoiced at heart,
and, deeming fate favourable in every way, all set about the auspicious preparations.
ayodhya.9.cau1: Then the king summoned Vasiṣṭha and had him go to Śrī Rāma's home to counsel him.
Word of the guru's coming reached Śrī Rāma; he came to the doorway and touched his head to the guru's feet.
ayodhya.9.cau2: With reverence he offered water, brought him into the house, and honoured him with worship of sixteen kinds.
Then, with Sītā, he clasped his feet, and joining his lotus hands Śrī Rāma said:
ayodhya.9.cau3: When a master comes to his servant's house, it is the source of all good and puts an end to all harm.
All the same, my lord, it is proper to send for one's servant kindly and give him the errand: that is the custom.
ayodhya.9.cau4: My lord's love, which set his lordliness aside, has today made this house holy.
Give me your order, holy sir, and I will do it; to be allowed to serve his master is what a servant gains.
ayodhya.9.do9: The sage heard these love-filled words and, praising Śrī Rāma, said:
Rāma, how could you not speak so, you who are the ornament of the line of the Sun?
ayodhya.10.cau1: The king of sages first described Śrī Rāma's virtues, gentleness and nature, and then spoke, thrilling with love:
Everything for the anointing has been arranged by the king; his wish is to give you the rank of crown prince.
ayodhya.10.cau2: Rāma, observe all the rules of restraint today, that the Creator may see the work through without mishap.
Having given this counsel the guru went to the king, and this misgiving arose in Śrī Rāma's heart:
ayodhya.10.cau3: All of us brothers came into the world at one time; eating, sleeping and childhood games, we shared them all;
the ear-piercing, the sacred thread, the weddings: all these festivals we had side by side.
ayodhya.10.cau4: In this spotless line there is this one thing amiss: the eldest alone is anointed, and his brothers are passed over.
May the Lord's loving, lovely regret take away the crookedness in his devotees' hearts.
ayodhya.10.do10: Just then Lakṣmaṇa came, steeped in love and joy;
and Śrī Rāma, the moon to the lilies of Raghu's line, welcomed him with loving words.
ayodhya.11.cau1: Instruments of many kinds are playing, and the joy of the city is past telling.
Everyone prays that Bharata may come soon and that his eyes too may have their reward.
ayodhya.11.cau2: In markets and roads, in houses, lanes and meeting-places, men and women say to one another:
Tomorrow is the auspicious hour; how long is it now till then? Brahmā will fulfil our longing,
ayodhya.11.cau3: when Śrī Rāma takes his seat on the golden throne with Sītā and our heart's wish comes true.
All of them ask when tomorrow will come, but the scheming gods are praying for some obstacle.
ayodhya.11.cau4: The festive music of Ayodhyā gives them no pleasure, as a moonlit night is no joy to a thief.
The gods call Sarasvatī and plead with her, again and again clasping her feet and falling at them.
ayodhya.11.do11: Mother, look on our great distress and today bring about that very thing
by which Śrī Rāma gives up the kingdom and goes to the forest, and all the gods' purpose is served.
ayodhya.12.cau1: Hearing the gods' plea, Sarasvatī stands there full of regret: I have become a frosty night to a forest of lotuses.
Seeing her so, the gods implore her again: Mother, not the least blame is yours.
ayodhya.12.cau2: Śrī Rāma is beyond both dismay and joy; you know all the greatness of Śrī Rāma.
Each soul shares in joy and sorrow as its own karma decides. For the gods' sake, go to Ayodhyā.
ayodhya.12.cau3: Her feet clasped again and again, she could not refuse, and she set out thinking how mean the minds of the gods were:
they live on high yet act basely, and another's prosperity is more than they can bear to see.
ayodhya.12.cau4: Then, thinking of the work that lay ahead, she reflected that skilled poets would seek her out.
Glad at heart, she came to the city of Daśaratha, like an evil turn of the planets bringing unbearable sorrow.
ayodhya.12.do12: Mantharā was the name of a slow-witted maid of Kaikeyī's.
Sarasvatī, the goddess of speech, made her a casket of infamy, turned her mind and went away.
ayodhya.13.cau1: Mantharā saw the city decked out and heard the sweet music of rejoicing.
She asked the people what the festivity meant, and the news of Śrī Rāma's tilaka set her heart on fire.
ayodhya.13.cau2: The malicious maid of base nature turned over in her mind how, this very night, the work might be spoilt,
as a crafty tribal woman, spying a hive of honey hung up, bides her time and works out how to take it.
ayodhya.13.cau3: She went in tears to Bharata's mother. The queen laughed and said: Why so downcast?
She gives no answer but only draws long sighs and, putting on a woman's show, lets her tears fall.
ayodhya.13.cau4: The queen laughed and said: That is a bold tongue of yours; my mind tells me Lakṣmaṇa has corrected you.
Still the wicked maid says nothing, but breathes out like a black she-serpent hissing.
ayodhya.13.do13: Alarmed, the queen said: Why do you not speak? Are Rāma, the king, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata and Śatrughna all well?
Hearing this, the hunchbacked maid felt a pang in her heart.
ayodhya.14.cau1: Mantharā said: Who would bother to teach me, lady, and with whose backing would I boast?
Today it is Rāma alone who fares well, for the king is making him crown prince.
ayodhya.14.cau2: Today fortune smiles broadly on Kausalyā, and seeing it, she swells with more pride than her heart can hold.
Go and look at all that splendour with your own eyes; it is the sight of it that has unsettled me.
ayodhya.14.cau3: Your son is in a far country and you have no care, thinking your husband is in your power.
You care only for sleep and a soft bed, and are blind to the trickery the king is working.
ayodhya.14.cau4: Though the words were sweet, the queen knew her heart was foul and rebuked her: Enough, be quiet now.
You home-wrecker, if ever you speak like this again, I will have your tongue seized and torn out.
ayodhya.14.do14: Those who are one-eyed, lame or hunchbacked are to be known as crooked and given to mischief,
above all a woman, and a maidservant besides. So saying, Bharata's mother smiled.
ayodhya.15.cau1: You who speak so pleasingly, I was only setting you right; never, even in a dream, am I angry with you.
That will be the good and blessed day on which what you have told me comes true.
ayodhya.15.cau2: The eldest rules and the younger brothers serve; such is the lovely way of the Sun's line.
Should Rāma's anointing really be tomorrow, name the thing your heart wants, friend; it is yours.
ayodhya.15.cau3: It is Rāma's nature to love every one of his mothers as he loves Kausalyā.
For me he has a special affection; I have put his love to the test and seen it.
ayodhya.15.cau4: Whenever Brahmā in his kindness gives me birth, may I have Rāma for a son and Sītā for a daughter-in-law.
Rāma means more to me than life itself; what is there in his anointing to upset you?
ayodhya.15.do15: I bind you by an oath on Bharata: leave aside all deceit and concealment and tell me the truth.
At a time of rejoicing you are grieving; tell me the reason.
ayodhya.16.cau1: Mantharā said: One word from me, and every wish I had came true! From now on I will talk with a different tongue.
Fit to be smashed is this ill-starred head, when even saying what is good only brings you pain.
ayodhya.16.cau2: Those who dress up lies as truth are the ones you hold dear, lady, and I am the bitter one.
I too will now speak only flattery, or else hold my tongue day and night.
ayodhya.16.cau3: Brahmā shaped me ugly and left me at others' bidding; what is sown must be harvested, and what was given comes back.
Let anyone be king, it costs me nothing; am I going to give up service and turn queen?
ayodhya.16.cau4: A nature like mine is fit for the fire, for I cannot look on while harm befalls you.
That is why I let slip a word or two; pardon me, my queen, the fault is mine and it is great.
ayodhya.16.do16: Hearing those sweet words full of hidden deceit, the queen, a woman of shallow judgement,
under the spell of the gods' māyā (power of illusion), took her enemy for a well-wisher and trusted her.
ayodhya.17.cau1: The queen questions her respectfully again and again, like a doe spellbound by a huntress's song.
Her mind turned just as destiny would have it, and the maid rejoiced, as if her stroke had gone home.
ayodhya.17.cau2: Mantharā said: You ask, but I am afraid to speak, for you have named me the home-wrecker.
Shaping and polishing her words in many ways until she had won full trust, she who was Saturn's seven-and-a-half-year blight upon Ayodhyā then spoke:
ayodhya.17.cau3: My queen, you tell me you love Sītā and Rāma and that Rāma loves you in return; that much is true.
It held once, but those days are gone; when time turns about, the loved ones themselves become foes.
ayodhya.17.cau4: It is the sun that keeps lotuses alive, and the same sun, once the water is gone, scorches them to dust.
Your rival wife is out to pull up your very roots; work out some means and hedge them round with a sound fence.
ayodhya.17.do17: Secure in your married fortune, you never worry, believing the king does as you wish.
Yet the king's heart is dark while his words are sweet, and you are simple by nature.
ayodhya.18.cau1: Rāma's mother is shrewd and keeps her own counsel; she seized the moment and set her own affairs right.
That the king sent Bharata away to his mother's family, you may take to be the counsel of Rāma's mother.
ayodhya.18.cau2: In Kausalyā's eyes, every co-wife serves her well except Bharata's mother, who is proud on the strength of her husband.
That is why you are a thorn in Kausalyā's side, lady; but she is so practised in guile that none can tell.
ayodhya.18.cau3: The king loves you especially, and with a co-wife's nature she cannot bear the sight of it.
So she laid a plot, won the king to her side and had the hour fixed for Rāma's anointing.
ayodhya.18.cau4: For this family it is fitting that Rāma should receive the tilaka; everyone is glad of it, and to me it is very welcome.
But when I think of what is to follow, I am afraid. May fate turn and give her the fruit of it.
ayodhya.18.do18: Weaving together countless crooked turns, she filled the queen with false counsel,
and told her a hundred tales of co-wives in such a way that the enmity grew.
ayodhya.19.cau1: As destiny would have it, trust took hold of the queen's heart, and she questioned her again, putting her on oath.
Mantharā said: Why ask me? Do you not see it yet? A mere animal can tell what helps it and what hurts it.
ayodhya.19.cau2: The arrangements have taken fifteen days, and only now, from me, has word reached you.
Your realm feeds and clothes me; speaking the truth, then, is no fault of mine.
ayodhya.19.cau3: Let me invent one false word, and Brahmā will make me pay for it.
Once Rāma has the tilaka tomorrow, the seed of calamity for you is sown by fate.
ayodhya.19.cau4: I draw a line and say it with all my force: lady, you have become a fly in the milk.
Serve, you and your son together, and you may keep your place at home; nothing else will do.
ayodhya.19.do19: As Kadrū made Vinatā suffer, so Kausalyā will make you suffer.
Bharata will be kept in prison, and Lakṣmaṇa will serve as Rāma's deputy.
ayodhya.20.cau1: The daughter of Kekaya heard the harsh words and, cowed and drained, could not speak at all.
Sweat broke out on her and she quivered like a plantain; at that the hunchback pressed her tongue between her teeth.
ayodhya.20.cau2: With story upon story of guile, countless of them, she calmed the queen, telling her to keep her courage.
Her fate had turned; the evil path now seemed good to her, and she lauded the she-crane as though it were a swan.
ayodhya.20.cau3: Kaikeyī said: Hear me, Mantharā, your words are true; my right eye twitches constantly.
Every night I have bad dreams, and, lost in my own delusion, I kept them from you.
ayodhya.20.cau4: What am I to do, friend? I am simple by nature, and have never told right from left.
ayodhya.20.do20: Never yet, by any doing of mine, have I wronged anyone;
for what sin, then, has fate heaped this grief beyond bearing on me at a single stroke?
ayodhya.21.cau1: I would sooner go and live out my life in my parents' home, but while I live I will not serve a co-wife.
For one whom fate keeps alive in an enemy's power, death is better than such a life.
ayodhya.21.cau2: The queen spoke many piteous words; hearing them, the hunchbacked Mantharā set to work her womanly wiles.
She said: Why do you speak like this, so downcast at heart? Your happiness and your wedded fortune will grow twofold day by day.
ayodhya.21.cau3: Whoever has wished you grave harm will reap this fruit himself in the end.
Since this evil plan reached my ears, my mistress, hunger has left me by day and sleep by night.
ayodhya.21.cau4: I asked the astrologers, and they drew their lines and declared: Bharata will be king; this is certain.
My lady, if you are willing to do it, I will tell you how; your service has already made the king yours.
ayodhya.21.do21: Kaikeyī said: If you told me to, I would leap into a well; I could give up son and husband.
You speak because you see my great sorrow; why should I not do it for my own good?
ayodhya.22.cau1: Having won Kaikeyī's consent, Mantharā whetted the knife of deceit on the stone of her heart.
The queen did not see the sorrow close at hand, just as a beast kept for sacrifice goes on grazing the green grass.
ayodhya.22.cau2: Her words were soft to the ear and harsh in the end, as if she were giving poison stirred into honey.
The maid said: My mistress, do you remember or not the story you once told me?
ayodhya.22.cau3: Two boons of yours are held in trust by the king; ask for them today and cool the fire in your breast.
Give the kingdom to your son and exile in the forest to Rāma, and take for yourself all your co-wife's joy.
ayodhya.22.cau4: Ask only when the king has sworn by Rāma, so that his word cannot be withdrawn.
If tonight goes by, the plan is lost; hold my words dear with all your heart.
ayodhya.22.do22: Having laid this foul snare, the sinful woman said: Go to the sulking-chamber.
Carry the whole thing through with care, and do not be quick to believe him.
ayodhya.23.cau1: The queen held Mantharā as dear as her own life and praised her great wisdom again and again.
She said: In all the world I have no well-wisher like you; I was being swept away, and you became my support.
ayodhya.23.cau2: My friend, if the Creator fulfils my wish tomorrow, I will make you the apple of my eye.
Having honoured her maid in many ways, Kaikeyī went to the sulking-chamber.
ayodhya.23.cau3: Calamity was the seed, the maid the rainy season, and Kaikeyī's evil mind became the soil.
Watered by deceit, the seed sprouted; the two boons were its two leaves, and its fruit in the end was to be sorrow.
ayodhya.23.cau4: Arraying herself in every sign of anger, she lay down there; while she was enjoying her reign, her own evil mind brought her to ruin.
Palace and city were loud with festivity, and no one knew anything of this wicked scheme.
ayodhya.23.do23: All the men and women of the city, overjoyed, were making ready the auspicious rites.
Some went in and some came out, and the king's court was thronged.
ayodhya.24.cau1: Hearing the news, Śrī Rāma's childhood friends rejoiced at heart and went to him in little groups.
Recognising their love, the Lord received them with honour and asked after their welfare in gentle words.
ayodhya.24.cau2: With their dear friend's leave, they went home praising Śrī Rāma to one another.
They said: Who in the world is like Śrī Rāma in keeping faith with good conduct and with love?
ayodhya.24.cau3: In whatever birth our deeds may lead us to wander, may God grant us this one thing there:
that we be servants and Sītā's lord be our master, and that this bond hold to the very end.
ayodhya.24.cau4: Such was the wish of everyone in the city; but in Kaikeyī's heart there was a fierce burning.
Who is not ruined by bad company? Cleverness does not survive the counsel of the base.
ayodhya.24.do24: At evening the king went joyfully to Kaikeyī's palace;
it was as though love itself had taken a body and gone to the side of cruelty.
ayodhya.25.cau1: Hearing of the sulking-chamber, the king shrank back; fear held his feet from going forward.
he on the strength of whose arms the king of the gods has his dwelling, and on whose looks all kings wait,
ayodhya.25.cau2: that same king withered at hearing of a woman's anger. See how great is the power of Kāmadeva.
Those who can bear the blow of trident, thunderbolt and sword are struck down by the flower-arrows of Rati's lord.
ayodhya.25.cau3: In fear the king went to his beloved, and seeing her state he was sorely grieved.
She lay on the ground in a coarse old garment, and had flung off the many ornaments from her body.
ayodhya.25.cau4: How well that unseemly garb became the evil-minded queen, as if it foretold the widowhood to come.
The king went close and said in a gentle voice: Beloved as life, why are you angry?
ayodhya.25.cha1: Why are you angry, my queen? the king asked, touching her; but she pushed her husband's hand away,
and the lady glared at him with a cruel look, like an angry serpent.
Her two desires were its two tongues and the two boons its fangs, and she was looking for the vital spot to strike.
Tulasīdāsa says: in the grip of what was to be, the king took it all for the play of love.
ayodhya.25.so25: Again and again the king said: My fair-faced one, my lovely-eyed one, you whose voice is like the cuckoo's,
you who move with an elephant's grace, tell me the reason for your anger.
ayodhya.26.cau1: Beloved, who has done you wrong? Who has two heads to lose? Whom does Death wish to take?
Tell me, which beggar shall I make a king? Tell me, which king shall I drive from his land?
ayodhya.26.cau2: I could slay your enemy were he even an immortal; what then are poor men and women, mere insects?
You know my nature, my fair one: my heart is a cakora bird gazing at the moon of your face.
ayodhya.26.cau3: Beloved, my life, my sons, all that I have, my household and all my people are in your hands.
If I say anything to you in deceit, my lady, let a hundred oaths by Rāma be upon me.
ayodhya.26.cau4: Smile, ask for whatever your heart desires, and adorn your lovely limbs with jewels.
Consider in your mind whether this is a fit hour or an ill one, and quickly, my love, put off this sorry garb.
ayodhya.26.do26: At these words, turning the mighty oath over in her mind, the foolish queen got up smiling
and began to put on her jewels, as a huntress who has spotted a deer sets out her snare.
ayodhya.27.cau1: Believing her a friend at heart, the king, thrilling with love, spoke again in soft and sweet words:
My lady, what your heart wished has come about; in every house in the city there is joyful celebration.
ayodhya.27.cau2: Tomorrow I will make Rāma crown prince; my lovely-eyed one, put on your festive array.
At these words her hard heart quaked, as when a ripe boil is touched.
ayodhya.27.cau3: Even such pain she hid behind a smile, as a thief's wife does not weep openly.
The king did not see through her cunning, for she had been schooled by a teacher who was the crown jewel among countless schemers.
ayodhya.27.cau4: The king was a master of statecraft, yet the ways of women are an ocean none can sound.
Then, making more of her false affection, she turned her eyes and face aside and said with a smile:
ayodhya.27.do27: My dear lord, you keep saying, Ask, ask, but you never give and nothing is ever received.
You promised me two boons, and even of getting those I am in doubt.
ayodhya.28.cau1: The king laughed and said: Now I see the secret: you dearly love to sulk.
You left the boons in my keeping and never asked for them, and I, forgetful by nature, forgot them.
ayodhya.28.cau2: Do not blame me falsely; ask for four in place of two if you like.
This has always been the way of the Raghu line: life may go, but the given word does not.
ayodhya.28.cau3: No heap of sins equals untruth; can even millions of guñjā seeds equal a mountain?
Truth is the root of every fair virtue; the Vedas and Purāṇas make this known, and Manu has proclaimed it too.
ayodhya.28.cau4: On top of that I have sworn by Rāma, and Śrī Rāma is the utmost of my merit and my love.
Having made the matter fast, the evil-minded queen spoke with a laugh, as though she had slipped the hood from the hawk of her wicked plan.
ayodhya.28.do28: The king's hope was a lovely forest, and his joy a flock of fair birds;
and like a huntress she was about to loose on them the fearsome hawk of her words.
ayodhya.29.cau1: Listen, beloved as life, to what my heart desires: grant me one boon, that Bharata be crowned.
The second boon I ask with folded hands; fulfil my wish, my lord.
ayodhya.29.cau2: In an ascetic's dress and utterly detached, let Rāma live fourteen years in the forest.
Hearing these soft words the king was stricken with grief, as the cakravāka bird is distressed at the touch of the moon's rays.
ayodhya.29.cau3: He was struck with dread and could say nothing, like a quail in the forest when a hawk swoops.
The king lost all his colour, as a palm does when lightning strikes it.
ayodhya.29.cau4: Hand on brow and both eyes closed, he sank into thought, as though care itself had put on a body and was fretting.
He thought: The wish-granting tree of my hope had come into flower, and just as it was bearing fruit a she-elephant has destroyed it root and all.
ayodhya.29.cau5: Kaikeyī has laid Ayodhyā waste and set down the foundation of a calamity that will not pass.
ayodhya.29.do29: At what a moment what has befallen! I am undone by trusting a woman,
as ignorance destroys an ascetic at the very hour when yoga is to bear its fruit.
ayodhya.30.cau1: Thus the king lamented within himself. Seeing his wretched state, the evil-minded queen grew angry at heart.
She said: Is Bharata not your son? Or did you buy me and bring me here for a price?
ayodhya.30.cau2: If my words struck you like an arrow the moment you heard them, why do you not weigh your words before you speak?
Give me an answer: say yes or say no. You are, after all, the one true to his word in the Raghu line.
ayodhya.30.cau3: You promised me boons; now do not give them if you will: forsake the truth and take the world's disgrace.
You praised truth and promised me boons; you must have thought I would ask for no more than some parched grain.
ayodhya.30.cau4: Śibi, Dadhīci and Bali, whatever they had said, gave up body and wealth and kept their pledged word.
Such bitter words Kaikeyī spoke, like salt rubbed into a burn.
ayodhya.30.do30: The king, bearer of the burden of dharma, gathered his courage and opened his eyes;
beating his head and heaving a deep sigh, he said: She has struck me in a cruel place.
ayodhya.31.cau1: Before him he saw her burning with great anger, like the bare sword of wrath.
Its hilt was an evil mind, its edge was cruelty, and the hunchbacked Mantharā had laid it on the whetstone and sharpened it.
ayodhya.31.cau2: The king saw how fearful and hard it was: would it truly take his life?
Steeling his heart, the king spoke humbly, in words meant to please her:
ayodhya.31.cau3: My beloved, why do you speak so unkindly? Timid one, you have put aside both trust and love.
Bharata and Rāma are my two eyes; I say this truly, with Śaṅkara as my witness.
ayodhya.31.cau4: In the morning I will surely send a messenger, and the two brothers will come quickly when they hear.
Fixing an auspicious day and making every preparation, I will give the kingdom to Bharata to the beat of drums.
ayodhya.31.do31: Rāma has no greed for the kingdom, and he loves Bharata dearly.
It was I who, weighing in my mind the elder and the younger, was keeping to the custom of kings.
ayodhya.32.cau1: I swear by Rāma a hundred times and tell you plainly: Rāma's mother never said anything to me.
I did it all without asking you, and that is why my wish has come to nothing.
ayodhya.32.cau2: Now give up your anger and prepare for the festivities; in a few days Bharata will be crown prince.
One thing alone has grieved me: the second boon you asked is one that leaves me in a quandary.
ayodhya.32.cau3: My heart still burns in its heat. Was it said in anger, or in jest, or is it really true?
Put aside your wrath and tell me Rāma's offence; everyone says Rāma is truly good.
ayodhya.32.cau4: You too used to praise him and show him love; now, hearing this, I am in doubt.
How could one whose nature is kind even to an enemy act against his mother?
ayodhya.32.do32: My beloved, leave jest and anger aside, and ask with careful thought and good sense,
so that now I may see Bharata's coronation to my eyes' content.
ayodhya.33.cau1: A fish might rather live without water, and a snake live on, wretched, without its gem;
but I tell you plainly, with no deceit in my heart: without Rāma I have no life.
ayodhya.33.cau2: Think it over in your mind, my wise beloved: my life hangs on the sight of Rāma.
Hearing these gentle words the evil-minded queen burned all the more, as fire does when ghee is poured into it as an offering.
ayodhya.33.cau3: Kaikeyī said: Try a million schemes if you like; your tricks will not work here.
Either give, or say no and take the disgrace; all this elaborate pretence does not suit me.
ayodhya.33.cau4: Rāma is good, you are good and shrewd, Rāma's mother is kind: I have seen through you all.
As Kausalyā wished me well, so will I repay her, with a deed to be remembered.
ayodhya.33.do33: If at break of day Rāma does not put on a hermit's dress and go to the forest,
then, O king, understand in your mind: my death and your disgrace will follow.
ayodhya.34.cau1: With these words the crooked queen rose and stood, like a river of wrath in flood.
That river sprang from a mountain of sin, brimming with the water of anger, too fearful to look on.
ayodhya.34.cau2: The two boons were its two banks, her hard obstinacy its current, and the hunchback's urging words its whirlpools.
Felling the king like a tree from its roots, it flowed on towards the ocean of calamity.
ayodhya.34.cau3: The king saw that the thing was true in earnest: death, in the guise of a woman, was dancing on his head.
Clasping her feet, he made her sit and pleaded: Do not be the axe that fells the line of the Sun.
ayodhya.34.cau4: Ask for my head and I will give it to you this moment; but do not kill me by parting me from Rāma.
Keep Rāma here by any means at all, or your heart will burn as long as you live.
ayodhya.34.do34: Seeing the sickness was past cure, the king fell to the ground, beating his head,
crying out in utter anguish: Rāma, Rāma, O Lord of the Raghus!
ayodhya.35.cau1: The king lay distraught, every limb gone slack, like a wish-fulfilling tree struck down by a she-elephant.
His throat was parched and no word came from his mouth, like a pāṭhīna fish helpless out of water.
ayodhya.35.cau2: Then Kaikeyī spoke again, bitter and harsh, as if pouring poison into a wound:
If in the end this was what you meant to do, what strength made you keep telling me to ask?
ayodhya.35.cau3: Can two things happen at once, O king: to laugh aloud and to puff out one's cheeks?
To be called a giver and yet be a miser? Can safety and well-being go with a warrior's life?
ayodhya.35.cau4: Either give up your word or bear it bravely; do not wail like a helpless woman.
Body, wife, son, home, wealth and land are counted as mere straw by one whose vow is truth.
ayodhya.35.do35: Hearing these words that pierced him to the quick, the king said: Say what you will; the fault is not yours at all.
My doom has seized you like a ghoul, and it is my doom that makes you speak so.
ayodhya.36.cau1: Bharata would not want the throne even in error; it is by fate's will that ill counsel has come to dwell in your heart.
It all springs from my own sins, and for them fate has turned against me at so ill a moment.
ayodhya.36.cau2: Fair Ayodhyā will be settled and happy again, and Rāma, home of every virtue, will hold the lordship.
All his brothers will serve him, and Rāma's glory will fill the three worlds.
ayodhya.36.cau3: Your disgrace and my remorse will not be wiped out even by death, nor will they ever pass.
Now do whatever pleases you; hide your face and sit out of my sight.
ayodhya.36.cau4: As long as I live, say nothing more to me: this I beg of you with joined palms.
You will be sorry in the end, unhappy woman: you are killing a cow for its sinew.
ayodhya.36.do36: Why are you bringing ruin? So pleading in a myriad ways, the king lay on the ground.
But Kaikeyī, cunning in deceit, said nothing, as if keeping a sorcerer's silent vigil in a cremation ground.
ayodhya.37.cau1: The distraught king kept crying Rāma, Rāma, helpless as a bird without wings.
In his heart he prayed that dawn might not come, and that no one might go and tell Śrī Rāma.
ayodhya.37.cau2: Do not rise, O Sun, guru of the Raghu line; seeing Ayodhyā, your heart will ache.
The Creator shaped the king's love and Kaikeyī's hardness, both of them, as the furthest bounds there could be.
ayodhya.37.cau3: While the king lamented, day broke, and lute, flute and conch sounded at the gate.
Bards recited praises and singers sang of virtues; to the king, hearing them was like being struck by arrows.
ayodhya.37.cau4: None of the festive things pleased him at all, as jewels do not please a woman about to follow her husband onto the pyre.
No one slept that night, for longing and eagerness to see Śrī Rāma.
ayodhya.37.do37: At the gate a crowd of servants and ministers, seeing the sun risen, said:
The lord of Avadh has not woken even now; what can be the special reason?
ayodhya.38.cau1: Every day the king wakes in the last watch of the night; today we are greatly surprised.
Go, Sumantra, and wake him, so that the work may be done on his command.
ayodhya.38.cau2: Then Sumantra went into the palace, but finding it fearful he grew afraid as he went.
It seemed ready to spring and devour him; he could not bear to look at it; it was as though calamity and grief had made it their home.
ayodhya.38.cau3: No one answered when he asked; he went on to the chamber where the king and Kaikeyī were.
Saying Victory and long life, he bowed his head and sat; at the sight of the king's state he withered.
ayodhya.38.cau4: Racked with care and drained of colour, the king lay on the ground as if a lotus had let go of its root.
Afraid, the minister could not ask. Then Kaikeyī spoke, brimming with evil and bare of any good:
ayodhya.38.do38: The king did not sleep last night; why, the Lord of the world alone knows.
Crying Rāma, Rāma, he has passed the night till dawn, but he will not tell the secret.
ayodhya.39.cau1: Go and bring Rāma here quickly; then come and ask what has happened.
Reading the king's look, Sumantra set off; he saw that the queen had played some evil trick.
ayodhya.39.cau2: Distraught with worry, he could hardly set foot on the road: what would the king say to Śrī Rāma once he had called him?
Taking heart, he went to the gate, and all who saw him downcast questioned him.
ayodhya.39.cau3: Having set them all at ease, he went to where Śrī Rāma, the crown of the solar line, was.
Śrī Rāma saw Sumantra coming and received him with honour, as he would his father.
ayodhya.39.cau4: Gazing at his face, Sumantra gave him the king's command and led Śrī Rāma away.
Śrī Rāma went with the minister in no fitting state, and people everywhere who saw it grieved.
ayodhya.39.do39: Śrī Rāma went in and saw the king in a sorry plight indeed,
like an aged king of elephants that has caught sight of a lioness and collapsed in fear.
ayodhya.40.cau1: His lips were parched and his whole body burned, like a wretched snake robbed of its gem.
Near him Śrī Rāma saw Kaikeyī in her wrath, like Death counting out the hours.
ayodhya.40.cau2: Śrī Rāma's nature is tender and full of compassion; he now saw sorrow for the first time, never having even heard of it before.
Yet, holding himself steady and weighing the moment, he asked his mother in gentle words:
ayodhya.40.cau3: Mother, tell me the cause of my father's grief, so that some means may be tried to remove it.
Kaikeyī said: Listen, Rāma; the whole cause is this: the king loves you dearly.
ayodhya.40.cau4: He offered me two boons, and I asked for whatever I liked.
Hearing it, the king was troubled at heart, for he cannot set aside his tender regard for you.
ayodhya.40.do40: Love for his son on this side, his word on that: the king is caught in a strait.
If you can, take the command on your head and end his bitter distress.
ayodhya.41.cau1: Seated without a qualm, Kaikeyī speaks bitter words; hearing them, even harshness grew deeply uneasy.
Her tongue is the bow, her words are many arrows, and the king, it seems, is a soft target.
ayodhya.41.cau2: Hardness, it seems, has become flesh: a fine warrior at his archery practice.
She has laid the whole matter before Śrī Rāma and sits there as if cruelty had taken a body.
ayodhya.41.cau3: Smiling to himself, Śrī Rāma, sun of the solar line and by his very nature a store of joy,
answered in gentle, graceful words with no flaw in them, words like jewels worn by speech:
ayodhya.41.cau4: Listen, Mother: the fortunate son is the one who holds dear what his father and mother say.
Mother, one who keeps his parents content is a son seldom found anywhere in the world.
ayodhya.41.do41: Above all, the forest will bring me the company of sages, and that does me good in every way;
and with it come my father's command and, Mother, your own consent.
ayodhya.42.cau1: The kingdom goes to Bharata, whom I love as my life; every way I look, fate smiles on me today.
Were I to stay back from the forest when the cause is this, the first name on the roll of fools should be mine.
ayodhya.42.cau2: Those who give up the wish-granting tree to tend the castor plant, who put nectar aside and ask for poison,
even they, given such a chance, would not let it slip; consider it in your mind, Mother.
ayodhya.42.cau3: One sorrow weighs on me above the rest, Mother: the king, lord of men, so wholly distraught.
The matter is small, yet my father's grief is heavy; Mother, my mind will not accept it.
ayodhya.42.cau4: The king is steadfast, an ocean of virtues too deep to sound; so the fault, and a grave one, lies with me,
since the king says nothing to me. Swear by me, and tell me truly.
ayodhya.42.do42: Simple and straight by nature were Śrī Rāma's words; the queen's warped mind read them as crooked,
as the leech moves on a crooked course through water, though the water is the same throughout.
ayodhya.43.cau1: Finding Śrī Rāma so minded, the queen was glad, and, feigning affection, she said:
On oath by you and by Bharata, I know of no other reason.
ayodhya.43.cau2: Offence and you, my son, have nothing to do with each other; mother, father and brothers all find joy in you.
Rāma, every word you say is true; your heart is set on what your father and mother say.
ayodhya.43.cau3: Bless you, my son: reason with your father and tell him what will spare him disgrace in his old age.
Sons like you are the fruit of his merit; he should not make light of it.
ayodhya.43.cau4: How do these fair words look in that evil mouth? Like Gayā and the other holy places in the land of Magadha.
Śrī Rāma liked every word his mother spoke, as water grows lovely once it has reached the Gaṅgā.
ayodhya.43.do43: Coming out of his faint with Śrī Rāma in his thoughts, the king turned on his side.
The minister said that Śrī Rāma was here and spoke to the king humbly, as the hour required.
ayodhya.44.cau1: Word reached the king that Śrī Rāma was there; gathering his courage, he let his eyes open.
The minister held him and sat him up, and there before him was Śrī Rāma, bowing down at his feet.
ayodhya.44.cau2: Love left him helpless; he clasped Śrī Rāma close, like a snake that has its lost jewel back.
His eyes stayed fixed on Śrī Rāma while the tears ran down in a steady flow.
ayodhya.44.cau3: Grief has him so in its grip that no word comes; over and over he holds Śrī Rāma to his breast.
Silently the king entreats the Creator: let it come about that Śrī Rāma does not leave for the forest.
ayodhya.44.cau4: Then, calling Śiva to mind, he pleads with him: Hear my prayer, O Sadāśiva.
You are quickly pleased and give freely without reckoning; knowing me for your humble servant, take away my distress.
ayodhya.44.do44: You are the one who moves every heart from within; give Rāma such a mind
that he sets aside my word and stays at home, putting away his good nature and his love.
ayodhya.45.cau1: Disgrace in the world, the loss of my good name, a fall into hell, heaven gone: I accept them all.
Lay on me every pain too hard to bear, only keep Rāma before my eyes.
ayodhya.45.cau2: So the king pondered in his mind and said nothing; his heart trembled like a pipal leaf.
Śrī Rāma saw that his father was overcome by love, and guessed that his mother would speak again.
ayodhya.45.cau3: Then, weighing his words to suit the place, the time and the occasion, he spoke humbly:
Father, forgive me for daring to speak; if anything I say is improper, put it down to my youth.
ayodhya.45.cau4: It is a very slight matter to have caused you pain, and no one let me know of it first.
I saw my lord and asked Mother; once I had heard the whole of it, my whole body felt cool and at ease.
ayodhya.45.do45: Father, at this auspicious hour, put away the worry that love has brought you,
and give me your leave with a glad heart. As he said this, the Lord thrilled from head to foot.
ayodhya.46.cau1: A son's birth on earth is a blessed thing when his father hears of his deeds and is glad.
Whoever holds father and mother as dear as life has all four ends of life, dharma, wealth, desire and liberation, within his grasp.
ayodhya.46.cau2: I will carry out your order, reap the reward of being born, and be back before long; only let the word be given.
I will just say goodbye to Mother and come back, bow at your feet, and be off to the forest.
ayodhya.46.cau3: Having said this, Śrī Rāma went; grief held the king, and no reply came from him.
The stinging news ran through the whole city, as a scorpion's venom rises through all the body the moment it touches.
ayodhya.46.cau4: The news left every man and woman in turmoil, like creepers and trees that have caught sight of a forest fire.
Each one, wherever the news finds him, beats his head where he stands; the grief runs deep, and nobody can steady himself.
ayodhya.46.do46: Mouths are dry, eyes run with tears, and the grief is more than hearts can hold;
it is as if the army of pathos had descended on Avadh with beating drums.
ayodhya.47.cau1: Just as all was coming together, fate spoiled it. Everywhere people cursed Kaikeyī:
What came over this sinful woman, that she set fire to a house just roofed?
ayodhya.47.cau2: She would tear out her eyes with her own hand and then look; she would throw away nectar and taste poison.
Crooked, hard, ill-minded and ill-fated, she has become the fire in the bamboo forest of Raghu's line.
ayodhya.47.cau3: Seated on its shoots, she has cut down the tree; right in the heart of happiness she has laid out the whole array of grief.
To her Śrī Rāma has always been like her own life; what cause could turn her to such crooked purpose?
ayodhya.47.cau4: The poets have it right: there is no grasping a woman's nature by any means; it is deep past sounding and keeps its secrets.
A man may perhaps lay hold of his own reflection, brother; a woman's ways cannot be known.
ayodhya.47.do47: What can fire not burn? What can the ocean not hold?
What will a weak woman not do once she gains strength? And whom in the world does death not devour?
ayodhya.48.cau1: What fate first let us hear, and what it has made us hear now; what it showed us, and what it would show us now!
Some say: It was wrong of the king to grant the ill-minded queen her boon without thinking.
ayodhya.48.cau2: By his own stubbornness he has made himself the vessel of every sorrow; in a woman's power, his wisdom and virtue seem to have left him.
Others, wise men who know how far dharma reaches, do not blame the king.
ayodhya.48.cau3: The tales of Śibi, Dadhīci and Hariścandra pass from one to another, told in full.
Some say Bharata had a hand in it; some listen and keep silent, taking no side.
ayodhya.48.cau4: Some clap their hands over their ears, hold their tongues between their teeth, and cry out that it is a lie.
Talk like this costs you your merit; Bharata loves Śrī Rāma as his own life.
ayodhya.48.do48: The moon may drip sparks of fire and nectar become like poison,
but never, even in a dream, will Bharata do anything against Śrī Rāma.
ayodhya.49.cau1: Some lay the fault on the Creator: he let them see nectar, then handed them poison.
Unrest fills the city and worry fills everyone; an unbearable fire burns in every breast, and gladness has vanished.
ayodhya.49.cau2: Brahmin wives, the respected elder women of the house, and the women Kaikeyī held dearest of all
set about advising her, speaking well of her character; to her each word feels like an arrow.
ayodhya.49.cau3: They said: You have never tired of saying that Bharata is less dear to you than Rāma; all the world is aware of it.
Your love for Śrī Rāma comes by nature; what wrong of his makes you give him the forest today?
ayodhya.49.cau4: Rivalry with a co-wife was never in you; your love and your good faith are known across the land.
So how has Kausalyā wronged you now, for you to strike the city with a thunderbolt?
ayodhya.49.do49: Will Sītā leave her beloved's side? Will Lakṣmaṇa remain in the palace?
Will Bharata enjoy the kingdom in the city? Will the king live on without Śrī Rāma?
ayodhya.50.cau1: Weigh this in your heart and let go of your anger; do not turn yourself into a home for grief and shame.
Let Bharata be made heir, surely, but what business has Śrī Rāma in the forest?
ayodhya.50.cau2: Śrī Rāma does not crave a kingdom; the yoke of dharma rests on him, and the senses' pleasures leave him cold.
Ask the king for this instead as your second boon: that Śrī Rāma quit his home and stay at his guru's.
ayodhya.50.cau3: Refuse our counsel, and you will end with nothing in your hands.
And if this was meant in fun, declare it plainly so that all may know.
ayodhya.50.cau4: A son such as Rāma, sent to the forest? What will people say of you when word gets out?
Get up now, and find a way to put an end to this grief and this stain.
ayodhya.50.cha1: Find the way by which the grief and the disgrace may pass, and keep the family safe.
Śrī Rāma is on his way to the forest; insist on bringing him back, and bring up nothing else.
As a day is without the sun, a body without its life, a night without the moon,
so would Avadh be without the Lord of Tulasīdāsa; only think of it in your heart, lady.
ayodhya.50.so50: Her friends gave her counsel sweet to hear and good in its outcome,
but the crooked hunchback had already worked on her mind, and she would not listen in the least.
ayodhya.51.cau1: Kaikeyī said not a word in reply, harsh with unbearable fury; her look was that of a starving tigress fixed on does.
Knowing the disease to be past cure, her companions left her and went away calling her dull-witted and ill-fated.
ayodhya.51.cau2: Fate has ruined her in the midst of her royal state; she has done a thing no one would ever do.
So the men and women of the city lamented, and heaped countless curses on the queen who had acted so wickedly.
ayodhya.51.cau3: They burned as with a cruel fever and heaved long sighs: what hope of life is there without Śrī Rāma?
The people were in anguish at so great a separation, like shoals of water creatures when the water is drying up.
ayodhya.51.cau4: Men and women alike were sunk in deep sorrow. Śrī Rāma, the Master, went to his mother.
His face was bright and his heart four times as eager, for the worry that the king might keep him back was gone.
ayodhya.51.do51: Śrī Rāma's mind was like a young elephant, and the kingdom like the post to which it is tethered.
Hearing that he was to go to the forest, he knew himself set free, and the joy in his heart grew.
ayodhya.52.cau1: Śrī Rāma, the jewel of Raghu's line, joined his palms and gladly laid his head at his mother's feet.
Giving her blessing, she drew him to her breast and lavished jewels and garments on him as a loving offering.
ayodhya.52.cau2: Again and again the mother kissed his face; her eyes were wet with love and her body thrilled.
She sat him on her lap and held him to her heart again, and the sweet milk of love flowed from her lovely breasts.
ayodhya.52.cau3: Her love and joy were past telling, as though a pauper had gained the rank of Kubera, lord of wealth.
Gazing fondly at his lovely face, the mother spoke sweetly:
ayodhya.52.cau4: Tell me, my son, your mother would give her life for you: when is that hour of joy and blessing,
the lovely summit of my merit, my good conduct and my happiness, the utmost that my birth could gain;
ayodhya.52.do52: the hour that all the men and women long for in such deep distress
as a thirsty cātaka and his mate long for the rain of the Svāti star in autumn?
ayodhya.53.cau1: My son, I would give my life for you; bathe quickly and eat some sweet thing that you like.
Then go to your father, my boy; it is very late already, and your mother would give her life for you.
ayodhya.53.cau2: He heard his mother's words, so wholly to his liking; they were like blossoms of the wish-granting tree of love,
full of the nectar of happiness and the very root of fortune; yet seeing them, the bee of Śrī Rāma's mind was not drawn to them.
ayodhya.53.cau3: Śrī Rāma, upholder of dharma, knowing the way of dharma, spoke to his mother in the gentlest words:
Father has given me the kingdom of the forest, where in every way a great purpose of mine will be served.
ayodhya.53.cau4: Mother, give me leave with a glad heart, so that I may go to the forest in joy and good fortune.
Do not let love lead you into needless fear; Mother, by your grace all will be joy.
ayodhya.53.do53: When I have lived fourteen years in the forest and made my father's word come true,
I will come back and see your feet again; do not let your heart be downcast.
ayodhya.54.cau1: Śrī Rāma's humble, sweet words struck his mother's heart like arrows and kept on stinging.
Hearing that cool speech she shrank in fear and withered, as the javāsā plant withers when the rains fall on it.
ayodhya.54.cau2: No words could tell the dismay in her heart; she was like a doe at the sound of a lion's roar.
Tears welled in her eyes and she trembled all over, as a fish reels when it has eaten the froth of the first rains.
ayodhya.54.cau3: Steadying herself and looking at her son's face, the mother spoke in a voice choked with feeling:
My son, your father loves you as his own life; he is ever delighted to watch what you do.
ayodhya.54.cau4: To give you the kingdom he had an auspicious day chosen; what wrong of yours now makes him bid you go to the forest?
Tell me the cause, my son: who has become a fire to the line of the Sun?
ayodhya.54.do54: Seeing Śrī Rāma's look, the minister's son explained the whole cause to her.
When she heard what had happened she was left speechless; her state cannot be described.
ayodhya.55.cau1: She could neither keep him nor tell him to go; either way her heart burned terribly.
Setting out to write the moon, the hand wrote Rāhu; the Creator's ways always run against everyone.
ayodhya.55.cau2: Duty and love together hemmed in her mind; she was in the plight of a snake that has seized a muskrat.
If I insist and keep my son here, dharma is lost and brother is set against brother;
ayodhya.55.cau3: and if I tell him to go to the forest, the loss is great. The queen was overwhelmed by this dilemma and her anxiety.
Then, wise as she was, understanding a wife's dharma and holding Śrī Rāma and Bharata both equally her sons,
ayodhya.55.cau4: Śrī Rāma's mother, guileless by nature, summoned great courage and said:
My son, bless you, you have done well; a father's command is the crown of all dharma.
ayodhya.55.do55: To be promised the kingdom and given the forest instead: for that I do not grieve at all;
but without you, Bharata, the king and the people will suffer bitterly.
ayodhya.56.cau1: If it is your father's command alone, my son, then do not go, knowing your mother to be the greater.
But if your mother too joins your father in bidding you go, then the forest will be as good as a hundred Ayodhyās.
ayodhya.56.cau2: The gods of the forest will be your father and its goddesses your mother, and birds and beasts will serve your lotus feet.
Even for a king, forest life befits his last years; but seeing how young you are, my heart is grieved.
ayodhya.56.cau3: Fortunate is the forest and unfortunate Ayodhyā, which you, the jewel of Raghu's line, have forsaken.
Were I to say to you, my son, take me along too, your heart would fall into doubt.
ayodhya.56.cau4: My son, you are dearest of all to everyone, the life of life itself and the breath of every heart.
And you, such as you are, say: Mother, let me go to the forest; and I hear these words and sit here grieving.
ayodhya.56.do56: Thinking this over, I will not insist and make a show of false love.
but, bless you, hold to the bond with your mother, and let the thought of me never fade from you.
ayodhya.57.cau1: My lord, may all the gods and ancestors guard you as the eyelids guard the eyes.
The term of your exile is the water, and your loved ones and household are its fish; you are full of compassion and the upholder of dharma.
ayodhya.57.cau2: Bearing this in mind, find the way to come back and meet everyone while they are still alive.
Bless you, go happily to the forest, leaving your servants, your family and the city without a protector.
ayodhya.57.cau3: Today the fruit of everyone's merit has run out; cruel time has turned adverse.
Lamenting in many ways and counting herself most unfortunate, she clung to his feet.
ayodhya.57.cau4: A dreadful, unbearable burning filled her heart; her many laments are beyond description.
Śrī Rāma raised his mother, held her to his heart, and consoled her again with gentle words.
ayodhya.57.do57: The news reached Sītā just then, and she got up in alarm.
She went and saluted her mother-in-law's two lotus feet, and sat down with bowed head.
ayodhya.58.cau1: Her mother-in-law blessed her in gentle words, and grew anxious to see how very delicate she was.
Sītā, a treasure of beauty, pure in her love for her husband, sat with lowered face and thought:
ayodhya.58.cau2: The lord of my life wishes to go to the forest; who will be blessed to go with him:
my body and my life together, or my life alone? What the Creator will do cannot be known at all.
ayodhya.58.cau3: She scratched the ground with the nails of her lovely feet, and the poet describes the sweet chiming of her anklets
as though, overcome by love, they were praying that Sītā's feet should never leave them.
ayodhya.58.cau4: Tears ran from her lovely eyes; seeing this, Śrī Rāma's mother spoke:
Listen, my son: Sītā is very delicate, and dear to her mother-in-law, her father-in-law and all the family.
ayodhya.58.do58: Her father Janaka is a jewel among kings, her father-in-law the sun of the solar race;
and her husband is the moon to the lily-groves of the Sun's line, a treasury of virtue and beauty.
ayodhya.59.cau1: And then a dear daughter-in-law came to me, a treasure of beauty, lovely in virtue and conduct.
I have made her the pupil of my eye and let my fondness for her grow; my very life I have fixed on Jānakī.
ayodhya.59.cau2: Like a wish-granting creeper I have reared her with every fondness, watering her with love and tending her.
She was coming into flower and fruit, and now the Creator has turned adverse; what will come of it, none can tell.
ayodhya.59.cau3: Apart from couch, seat, lap and swing, Sītā has never set foot on the hard ground.
Like a herb that keeps one alive I have guarded her with care; I never bid her so much as move a lamp's wick.
ayodhya.59.cau4: That same Sītā wishes to go with you to the forest; what is your command, O Lord of the Raghus?
How can a cakorī, who delights in the moon's rays, turn her eyes to face the sun?
ayodhya.59.do59: Elephants, lions, demons and many savage creatures roam the forest.
My son, does a lovely life-giving herb belong in a garden of poison?
ayodhya.60.cau1: For the forest Brahmā made the daughters of the Kol and Kirāta peoples, who know nothing of worldly pleasures;
Their nature is as tough as a stone-worm's, and the forest never brings them hardship.
ayodhya.60.cau2: Or the wives of ascetics are fit for the forest, who have given up all pleasures for the sake of austerity.
My son, how is Sītā to live in the forest, when even a monkey in a picture frightens her?
ayodhya.60.cau3: A swan maiden roams the fair lotus groves of the gods' lake; is a muddy pool any place for her?
Weigh this, and whatever you command, that is the counsel I will give Jānakī.
ayodhya.60.cau4: His mother said: if Sītā stays at home, it will be a great support to me.
Śrī Rāma heard his mother's loving words, steeped as if in the nectar of goodness and affection;
ayodhya.60.do60: with loving and wise words he set his mother's mind at rest,
and began to counsel Jānakī, setting out the good and the bad of the forest.
ayodhya.61.cau1: Śrī Rāma felt shy of speaking before his mother, yet, seeing in his mind what the hour demanded, he said:
Princess, listen to my counsel, and do not take it any other way in your heart.
ayodhya.61.cau2: If it is your good and mine you want, do as I say and remain at home.
Dear lady, my command is kept and your mother-in-law has your service; home is good for you in every way.
ayodhya.61.cau3: There is no higher dharma than to worship, with reverence, the feet of one's mother-in-law and father-in-law.
Whenever my mother remembers me and is overwhelmed with love, her mind bewildered,
ayodhya.61.cau4: then, fair one, tell her the old tales and soothe her in a gentle voice.
I speak plainly, a hundred oaths upon me: lovely one, I keep you here for my mother's good alone.
ayodhya.61.do61: The fruit of dharma approved by the guru and the Veda is gained without hardship.
Driven by obstinacy, the sage Gālava and King Nahuṣa endured every kind of trouble.
ayodhya.62.cau1: Listen, lovely and wise one: as for me, once I have made my father's word good, I shall soon come back.
The days will pass in no time. Listen to my counsel, fair one.
ayodhya.62.cau2: If, out of love, you insist, dear lady, you will come to grief in the end.
The forest is hard and fearsome in the extreme; its heat, cold, rain and winds are fierce.
ayodhya.62.cau3: The paths are strewn with kuśa grass, thorns and stones of many kinds, and you must walk them on foot, without shoes.
Your lotus feet are soft and lovely, and the ways are hard to pass, among mighty mountains.
ayodhya.62.cau4: Caves, ravines, rivers, streams and torrents are so impassable and deep that one cannot bear to look at them.
Bears, tigers, wolves, lions and elephants roar, and at the sound all courage flees.
ayodhya.62.do62: Sleep on the ground, clothes of bark, food of tubers, fruit and roots;
and will even these be there always, every day? Each comes only in its own season.
ayodhya.63.cau1: Demons who feed on men wander there and take on false guises of countless kinds.
Hill water tells badly on the body, and the forest's hardships cannot be put into words.
ayodhya.63.cau2: The forest is dreadful, with fearsome serpents and birds and hordes of demons who carry off women and men.
The thought of that deep forest frightens even the steady, and timidity, doe-eyed one, is in your nature.
ayodhya.63.cau3: You who walk like a swan are not made for the forest; hearing of it, people will blame me.
Would a swan raised on the nectar-sweet water of the Mānasa lake survive in the briny sea?
ayodhya.63.cau4: Would a cuckoo used to roaming young mango groves look well among karīla bushes?
Stay at home, moon-faced one, having weighed this in your heart: the sorrow of the forest is heavy.
ayodhya.63.do63: Whoever does not take to heart the counsel of a natural well-wisher, a guru or a master
repents bitterly at heart, and surely his good comes to harm.
ayodhya.64.cau1: As her beloved spoke so softly and so sweetly, Sītā's lovely eyes brimmed with tears.
His cool counsel scorched her the way an autumn night under the moon scorches the female cakravāka.
ayodhya.64.cau2: No answer came to Vaidehī; she was distraught that her pure and loving lord wished to leave her.
Forcibly holding back the tears in her eyes, the daughter of the Earth gathered courage in her heart,
ayodhya.64.cau3: and, falling at her mother-in-law's feet with joined hands, she said: Forgive, noble lady, my great want of modesty.
What the lord of my life has taught me is the very way to my highest good.
ayodhya.64.cau4: But I too have weighed it in my mind and seen that there is no sorrow in the world like separation from one's beloved.
ayodhya.64.do64: Lord of my life, home of compassion, beautiful, giver of joy, all-knowing,
moon to the night-lotus of Raghu's line, without you heaven itself is like hell.
ayodhya.65.cau1: Mother, father, sister, dear brother, dear family, the company of friends,
mother-in-law, father-in-law, guru, kinsfolk, helpers, and a son fair, good-natured and joy-giving:
ayodhya.65.cau2: whatever ties of love and kinship there are, my Lord, without her beloved they scorch a woman more than the sun.
Body, wealth, home, land, city and kingdom: without her husband all of it is a gathering of grief.
ayodhya.65.cau3: Pleasures are like sickness, ornaments a burden, and the world like the tortures of Yama.
Lord of my life, without you there is nothing anywhere in the world that brings me joy.
ayodhya.65.cau4: A body without life, a river without water: such, my Lord, is a wife without her husband.
With you, my Lord, gazing on your face like the spotless autumn moon, I have every joy.
ayodhya.65.do65: My kin will be the birds and beasts, my city the forest, my spotless fine raiment the bark garments;
and with you, my Lord, a hut of leaves will be the root of joy, like a palace of the gods.
ayodhya.66.cau1: The goddesses and gods of the forest, generous as they are, will care for me as a mother-in-law and father-in-law do.
With my Lord beside me, a pleasant pallet of kuśa and fresh leaves will be as fine as Kāmadeva's mattress.
ayodhya.66.cau2: My food of tubers, roots and fruit will be like nectar, and the hills will be to me as a hundred palaces of Ayodhyā.
Every moment I shall look on my Lord's lotus feet and be glad, like the female cakravāka in daylight.
ayodhya.66.cau3: My Lord, you have told me of the many sorrows of the forest, its many fears, griefs and torments;
yet the least trace of separation from my Lord, treasury of mercy, outweighs them all together.
ayodhya.66.cau4: Crown of the wise, see this in your heart: take me along rather than leave me.
What need have I to plead at length, my Lord? You are full of compassion and know every heart from within.
ayodhya.66.do66: If you keep me in Ayodhyā until the term is over, know that my life will not last,
friend of the lowly, beautiful, giver of joy, treasury of goodness and love.
ayodhya.67.cau1: Gazing on your lotus feet every moment, I shall not tire as I walk the road.
I shall serve my beloved in every way and take away all the weariness of the journey.
ayodhya.67.cau2: I shall wash your feet and, seated in a tree's shade, fan you gladly.
Seeing your dark body beaded with sweat, beholding the lord of my life, where is there time for sorrow?
ayodhya.67.cau3: On level ground this handmaid will lay grass and leaves and rub your feet the whole night through.
Gazing again and again on your gentle form, I shall not feel even the hot wind.
ayodhya.67.cau4: Who could so much as glance at me while my Lord is with me? No more could a hare or a jackal eye the lion's mate.
Am I the delicate one, and my Lord fit for the forest? Is austerity right for you, and pleasure for me?
ayodhya.67.do67: If my heart has not broken even on hearing such harsh words,
then, my Lord, this wretched life will bear the cruel pain of separation from you.
ayodhya.68.cau1: With these words Sītā grew deeply distraught; the very talk of parting was more than she could bear.
Seeing her state, Śrī Rāma knew in his heart that if he kept her back by force she would not keep her life.
ayodhya.68.cau2: Then the compassionate lord of the Sun's line said: Leave off your worry and come along to the forest with me.
Today is no occasion for grief; quickly make ready to set out for the forest.
ayodhya.68.cau3: He calmed his beloved with loving words; then he touched his mother's feet and received her blessing.
His mother said: Come back soon and end the people's sorrow; do not forget your hard-hearted mother.
ayodhya.68.cau4: O Fate, will my fortune ever turn again? Shall I see this lovely pair with my own eyes?
That good day, that happy hour, my son: when will it come, for your mother to look on your moon-like face while she still lives?
ayodhya.68.do68: When again shall I call you my little one, my darling, lord of the Raghus, best of the Raghus, my dear,
and calling you to me, hold you to my heart and gaze on you with joy?
ayodhya.69.cau1: Śrī Rāma saw his mother faint with love; no words would come, and she was deeply distressed.
He comforted her in many ways. That hour and that love are beyond describing.
ayodhya.69.cau2: Then Jānakī touched her mother-in-law's feet and said: Listen, Mother, I am most unfortunate.
Just when it was time to serve you, fate has given me the forest and left my wish unfulfilled.
ayodhya.69.cau3: Put away your grief, but do not withdraw your affection. Destiny is hard; the fault is not mine either.
Hearing Sītā's words her mother-in-law was distraught; how can I describe her state?
ayodhya.69.cau4: Time after time she drew Sītā to her bosom; then, gathering her courage, she gave her counsel and a blessing:
May your married fortune stand unshaken as long as the waters of the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā flow.
ayodhya.69.do69: Her mother-in-law gave Sītā blessings and counsel in many ways;
and bowing her head again and again at her lotus feet with deep love, Sītā departed.
ayodhya.70.cau1: The news reached Lakṣmaṇa; distraught, he sprang up and ran, his face fallen.
Trembling, the hair on his body on end, his eyes wet, and overcome with love, he clasped Śrī Rāma's feet.
ayodhya.70.cau2: He could say nothing and stood gazing, like a wretched fish drawn out of water.
Anxious at heart he thought: O Fate, what is to happen? All our joy and merit is spent.
ayodhya.70.cau3: What will Śrī Rāma say to me? Will he leave me in the palace or take me along?
Śrī Rāma saw his brother with joined hands, having broken every tie with body, home and all.
ayodhya.70.cau4: Śrī Rāma, wise in right conduct, an ocean of goodness, love, simplicity and joy, said:
Dear brother, do not grow faint-hearted out of love; understand in your heart the joy the outcome holds.
ayodhya.70.do70: Those who readily take to heart and follow the counsel of mother, father, guru and master
have won the gain of being born; otherwise one's birth in the world goes to waste.
ayodhya.71.cau1: Brother, take this to heart and listen to my counsel: serve the feet of mother and father.
Bharata and Śatrughna are not at home; the king is old, and grief for me fills his mind.
ayodhya.71.cau2: If I go to the forest taking you with me, Ayodhyā will be left without a protector in every way.
On the guru, father, mother, the people and the household, on all of them, an unbearable weight of sorrow will fall.
ayodhya.71.cau3: Stay, and give comfort to all; otherwise, dear brother, it will be a grave fault.
A king in whose realm his beloved people suffer has surely earned hell.
ayodhya.71.cau4: Weigh this rule of right conduct, dear brother, and stay. Hearing this, Lakṣmaṇa was deeply distressed.
At these cool words he withered, as a lotus withers at the touch of frost.
ayodhya.71.do71: Overcome by love, he could find no answer, and in distress he clasped Śrī Rāma's feet.
He said: My Lord, I am your servant and you are my master; if you leave me behind, what power have I?
ayodhya.72.cau1: My master, the counsel you gave me is good, but in my faint-heartedness it seemed beyond my reach.
Those fit for the teaching of the Vedas and of right conduct are the best of men, steadfast, who bear the yoke of dharma.
ayodhya.72.cau2: I am a child, raised in the Lord's affection. Can swans lift Mount Mandara or Meru?
I know no guru, no father, no mother. I tell you my nature, my Lord; believe me.
ayodhya.72.cau3: All the ties of love and kinship in the world, all the love and trust the Vedas themselves have sung,
are for me you alone, my master, friend of the lowly, who know what lies within the heart.
ayodhya.72.cau4: Teach dharma and right conduct to one who cares for fame, prosperity and a blessed hereafter.
Is one who loves your feet in mind, deed and word to be given up, O ocean of mercy?
ayodhya.72.do72: Hearing the gentle, humble words of his good brother, the Lord, ocean of compassion,
saw that love had made him afraid, and drew him to his heart and reassured him.
ayodhya.73.cau1: Śrī Rāma said: Brother, go and take leave of your mother, then come back quickly and come with me to the forest.
Lakṣmaṇa rejoiced to hear Śrī Rāma's words: a great gain had come, and a great loss had passed.
ayodhya.73.cau2: Glad at heart he came to his mother, like a blind man whose sight has been given back.
He went and bowed his head at her feet, but his mind was with Śrī Rāma and Jānakī.
ayodhya.73.cau3: His mother saw that he was low in spirit and questioned him; Lakṣmaṇa told her everything, in full.
She shrank in fear at the harsh news, like a doe that sees forest fire on every side.
ayodhya.73.cau4: Lakṣmaṇa saw that disaster had struck that day: out of love she would spoil everything.
So, asking leave, he hesitated in fear: O Fate, will she tell me to go with him or not?
ayodhya.73.do73: Sumitrā thought of the beauty, the fine character and the nature of Śrī Rāma and Sītā,
and seeing the king's love for them she beat her head: that sinful woman has played a foul trick.
ayodhya.74.cau1: Knowing the moment to be ill-starred, she steadied herself; then, kind-hearted by nature, she said gently:
Your mother, my son, is Vaidehī; your father is Śrī Rāma, loving towards you in every way.
ayodhya.74.cau2: Ayodhyā is wherever Śrī Rāma dwells; it is day only where the sun gives light.
If Sītā and Śrī Rāma are indeed going to the forest, you have nothing to do in Ayodhyā.
ayodhya.74.cau3: Guru, father, mother, brother, the gods and one's master: all should be served as one cherishes one's own life.
And Śrī Rāma is dear as life itself, the very life of the soul, the selfless friend of all.
ayodhya.74.cau4: Reverence and deepest love are due to anyone only through their relation to Śrī Rāma.
Hold this in your heart, my son: go with him to the forest, and reap the gain of a life in this world.
ayodhya.74.do74: I would give my life for you; you have become a vessel of great fortune, and I with you,
if, putting away all deceit, you have made a home in your heart for Śrī Rāma's feet.
ayodhya.75.cau1: In this world the woman truly blessed with a son is she whose son is a devotee of Śrī Rāma.
Otherwise better to be barren; she who looks for her good from a son turned away from Śrī Rāma has given birth in vain.
ayodhya.75.cau2: It is your own good fortune that takes Śrī Rāma to the forest, my son; there is no other cause.
The great fruit of all merit is this: a natural love for the feet of Śrī Rāma and Sītā.
ayodhya.75.cau3: Attachment, anger, envy, pride and delusion: never fall under their sway, even in a dream.
Casting off every kind of failing, serve them in thought, deed and word.
ayodhya.75.cau4: For you the forest holds every comfort, since you have with you Śrī Rāma and Sītā, your father and mother.
Do whatever spares Śrī Rāma hardship in the forest, my son; this is my counsel.
ayodhya.75.cha1: This is my counsel, my son: act so that through you Śrī Rāma and Sītā may be happy,
and in the forest forget the memory of the comforts of father, mother, dear kin and city.
Tulasīdāsa says: after this counsel to his Lord, Lakṣmaṇa, Sumitrā gave him her leave and then her blessing:
May your love for the feet of Sītā and Śrī Rāma never break, stay pure, and grow new each day.
ayodhya.75.so75: Bowing his head at his mother's feet, he set off at once, uneasy at heart,
like a deer that by good fortune has broken a cruel snare and fled.
ayodhya.76.cau1: Lakṣmaṇa went to where Śrī Rāma, the lord of Jānakī, was, and rejoiced at heart to have the company of his beloved.
He bowed to the lovely feet of Śrī Rāma and Sītā, and they went together to the king's palace.
ayodhya.76.cau2: Men and women of the city were saying among themselves: Fate arranged things well and then undid them.
Their bodies were wasted, their minds in grief, their faces downcast; they were as distraught as bees robbed of their honey.
ayodhya.76.cau3: Wringing their hands and beating their heads, they lamented, as distressed as birds without wings.
A great crowd gathered at the king's court; the boundless sorrow there is beyond description.
ayodhya.76.cau4: The minister helped the king up and seated him, telling him the welcome words: Śrī Rāma has come.
Seeing his two sons with Sītā, the king was overwhelmed with distress.
ayodhya.76.do76: Gazing again and again at his two handsome sons and Sītā, the king was overcome,
and in his love he drew them to his heart time after time.
ayodhya.77.cau1: The king in his distress could not speak; grief had set a terrible burning in his heart.
Then Śrī Rāma rose, bowed his head at his feet with deep love, and asked leave:
ayodhya.77.cau2: Father, give me your blessing and your leave. Why be dismayed at a time of joy?
Dear father, if one falls into neglect out of love for someone dear, one's good name in the world is lost and reproach follows.
ayodhya.77.cau3: Hearing this, the king rose in his love, took Śrī Rāma by the arm and seated him.
He said: Listen, my son; the sages say of you that Rāma is the lord of all that moves and does not move.
ayodhya.77.cau4: God weighs deeds, good and bad, in his heart and gives their fruit accordingly.
The doer of a deed is the one who reaps its fruit: this is the rule of the Vedas, and all say so.
ayodhya.77.do77: Yet one commits the offence and another suffers its fruit.
Most strange are the ways of the Lord; who in the world is able to know them?
ayodhya.78.cau1: To keep Śrī Rāma back, the king tried many means, without any guile.
But seeing the mind of Śrī Rāma, upholder of dharma, steadfast and wise, he knew that he would not stay.
