ayodhya.78.cau2: Then the king drew Sītā to his heart and, with deep affection, counselled her in many ways.
He spoke of the forest's unbearable hardships, and made clear to her the happiness she would have with her parents-in-law and her father.
ayodhya.78.cau3: But Sītā's heart was given to Śrī Rāma's feet; home did not seem easy to her, nor the forest hard.
Everyone else too reasoned with Sītā, telling her again and again how great the perils of the forest were.
ayodhya.78.cau4: The minister's wife and the guru's wife, both wise, spoke to her gently and with affection:
You at least have not been given exile to the forest; do what your father-in-law, the guru and your mother-in-law say.
ayodhya.78.do78: The counsel was cool, kindly, sweet and gentle, but Sītā did not take to it,
just as the cakaī (the ruddy sheldrake hen) grows restless when the light of the autumn moon falls on her.
ayodhya.79.cau1: Held back by modesty, Sītā gave no answer. Hearing all this, Kaikeyī sprang up in a temper,
brought a hermit's garments, ornaments and vessels, set them before Śrī Rāma, and said in a soft voice:
ayodhya.79.cau2: O hero of the Raghus, you are dear as life to the king. Timid as he is, he will not give up his good nature and affection.
Though his merit, his good name and his hereafter be lost, he will never tell you to go to the forest.
ayodhya.79.cau3: Weigh this, and do as you think fit. Śrī Rāma was glad to hear his mother's counsel.
But to the king the words were like arrows; and still his wretched life would not depart.
ayodhya.79.cau4: The people were distraught and the king fell senseless; no one could think what to do.
At once Śrī Rāma put on the dress of a hermit, bowed his head to father and mother, and set out.
ayodhya.79.do79: Making ready all that was needed for the forest, with his wife and brother,
the Lord bowed to the feet of the Brahmins and the guru and set out, leaving everyone stunned.
ayodhya.80.cau1: Coming out, he stood at Vasiṣṭha's door and saw the people scorched by the fire of separation.
With loving words Śrī Rāma consoled them all, and he called for the Brahmins in a body.
ayodhya.80.cau2: Through the guru he gave them provisions for a year, and won them over with honour, gifts and humility.
Those who came begging he contented with gifts and honour; his friends he satisfied with pure love.
ayodhya.80.cau3: Then he summoned the maids and servants, entrusted them to the guru, and said with joined palms:
Master, you will watch over and care for them all as a father and mother would.
ayodhya.80.cau4: Again and again, with both palms joined, Śrī Rāma spoke gently to everyone:
Whoever keeps the king content is, in every way, the one who wishes me well.
ayodhya.80.do80: So that none of my mothers is brought low by grief while I am away,
all of you, most able people of the city, take those very measures.
ayodhya.81.cau1: With everyone thus reassured, Śrī Rāma joyfully touched his head to his guru's lotus feet.
Then he invoked Gaṇeśa, Gaurī and Śiva, lord of the mountain, and with blessings received, Śrī Rāma set out.
ayodhya.81.cau2: As Śrī Rāma set out, a deep gloom fell; the cry of the stricken city was more than anyone could bear to hear.
In Laṅkā there were ill omens, in Ayodhyā bitter sorrow, and the world of the gods was swayed by joy and grief at once.
ayodhya.81.cau3: The faint passed and the king came round; he sent for Sumantra and spoke to him in these words:
Rāma has gone to the forest, and still my life does not leave me. For what happiness does it stay on in this body?
ayodhya.81.cau4: If not this, what grief is strong enough to make the life leave the body?
Then, gathering his courage, the king said: My friend, take the chariot and go with them.
ayodhya.81.do81: The two princes are very tender, and Janaka's daughter is delicate.
Seat them in the chariot, show them the forest, and when four days have passed, come back.
ayodhya.82.cau1: Should the two steadfast brothers not come back — and Rāma, lord of the Raghus, is true to his pledge and firm in his vows —
then press your palms together and beg him: My lord, let the princess of Mithilā return.
ayodhya.82.cau2: If the forest frightens Sītā, wait for the right moment and pass on my counsel to her:
Your mother-in-law and father-in-law have said this: Come home, daughter; the forest brings great hardship.
ayodhya.82.cau3: Stay sometimes in your father's house and sometimes in your husband's, wherever you like.
Try many such ways; her return would be a prop for my life.
ayodhya.82.cau4: Otherwise, in the end, it is death for me. When fate turns against one, nothing is in one's power.
These words spoken, the king fell to the ground in a faint, with the plea: bring Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā and let me see them.
ayodhya.82.do82: Taking the king's command with a bow of the head, Sumantra made the chariot ready in great haste
and went to where the two brothers were with Sītā, outside the city.
ayodhya.83.cau1: Sumantra then passed on the king's words to them, and by entreaty got Śrī Rāma into the chariot.
Once Sītā and the two brothers were aboard, they moved off, inwardly bowing their heads to Ayodhyā.
ayodhya.83.cau2: Seeing Śrī Rāma leave and Ayodhyā bereft of its protector, all the people, distraught, followed him.
The ocean of mercy reasoned with them in many ways; they would turn back, and then, drawn by love, come back again.
ayodhya.83.cau3: Ayodhyā seemed fearful beyond measure, like the dark night of doom.
Its men and women, like dreadful creatures, shrank in fear at the sight of one another.
ayodhya.83.cau4: Homes were like cremation grounds, kinsfolk like ghosts, and sons, well-wishers and friends seemed the messengers of Yama.
In the gardens, trees and creepers withered; rivers and lakes were too sad to look at.
ayodhya.83.do83: Horses and elephants by the million, pet deer, the town's animals, cātaka birds and peacocks,
cuckoos, cakravākas, parrots, mynas, cranes, swans and cakoras —
ayodhya.84.cau1: all these stood here and there, stricken by separation from Śrī Rāma, as though drawn in a picture.
The city was a great thick forest rich in fruit, and its many birds and deer were the men and women who lived there.
ayodhya.84.cau2: Fate made Kaikeyī a Kirāta huntress, who set an unbearable forest fire raging in all ten directions.
That fire of parting from Śrī Rāma was too much to bear, and in distress everyone fled.
ayodhya.84.cau3: Every one of them thought: without Śrī Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā there is no happiness.
Where Śrī Rāma is, there all our company belongs; without him we have nothing to do in Ayodhyā.
ayodhya.84.cau4: With this resolve made firm, they left homes full of comforts hard for even the gods to come by, and went with him.
How could the pleasures of the senses master anyone who loves Śrī Rāma's lotus feet?
ayodhya.84.do84: All the people went with him; the children and the old they left at home.
On the first day Śrī Rāma stayed the night by the river Tamasā.
ayodhya.85.cau1: Seeing how love held his people, Śrī Rāma felt a deep sorrow in his kind heart.
The compassionate Lord Śrī Rāma feels at once whatever pain others suffer.
ayodhya.85.cau2: With gentle, lovely words steeped in love, Śrī Rāma tried every way to make the people understand.
He gave them much teaching on dharma, yet love held them so fast that they would not go back when sent.
ayodhya.85.cau3: Kindness and affection could not be set aside, and Śrī Rāma was caught in a dilemma.
Worn out with grief and toil, the people slept, while a touch of the gods' māyā dulled their wits.
ayodhya.85.cau4: Two watches of the night had gone by when Śrī Rāma spoke lovingly to the minister:
Dear sir, drive the chariot so that its tracks are lost; nothing else will serve.
ayodhya.85.do85: Śrī Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā mounted the chariot and bowed their heads at the feet of Śiva,
and the minister drove off at once, hiding the tracks this way and that.
ayodhya.86.cau1: At daybreak all the people woke; Śrī Rāma was gone, and a great clamour arose.
Nowhere could they find the chariot's tracks; calling Rāma, Rāma, they ran in every direction.
ayodhya.86.cau2: It was as if a ship had gone down at sea and a great band of merchants were left in despair.
They admonished one another: Śrī Rāma left us because he knew the hardship we would face.
ayodhya.86.cau3: They reproached themselves and praised the fish: shame on a life without Śrī Rāma.
If fate meant to part us from our beloved, why did it not grant us death when we asked for it?
ayodhya.86.cau4: So they wept and lamented in many ways, and reached Ayodhyā consumed with grief.
That cruel separation cannot be told; in the hope of the appointed day of return, all of them held on to life.
ayodhya.86.do86: For the sake of seeing Śrī Rāma, men and women took up observances and vows.
They were as forlorn as the cakravāka, his mate and the lotus without the sun.
ayodhya.87.cau1: The two brothers, with Sītā and the minister, came to Śṛṅgaverapura.
At the sight of the river of the gods Śrī Rāma got down, and in great joy fell full length before her.
ayodhya.87.cau2: Lakṣmaṇa, the minister and Sītā bowed as well, and Śrī Rāma rejoiced with them all.
The Gaṅgā is the root of all joy and blessing; she brings every happiness and takes away every pain.
ayodhya.87.cau3: Telling one story and episode after another, countless of them, Śrī Rāma gazed at the waves of the Gaṅgā.
To the minister, to his younger brother and to his beloved he told the great glory of the river of the gods.
ayodhya.87.cau4: The bath took away the weariness of the road, and drinking the pure water gladdened the heart.
Weariness, in one whose remembrance wipes out the heaviest weariness, is nothing but the way of the world.
ayodhya.87.do87: Śrī Rāma, the pure source whose being is truth, consciousness and bliss, the banner of the solar line,
acts in the way of men, and these deeds are a bridge across the ocean of worldly existence.
ayodhya.88.cau1: When Guha the Niṣāda heard this news, he gladly called his dear kinsmen together.
Loading up fruits and roots as gifts, he set out to meet him, his heart filled with boundless joy.
ayodhya.88.cau2: He prostrated himself, laid the gifts before the Lord, and gazed at him with deep love.
Moved by his natural affection, Śrī Rāma seated him close by and asked after his welfare.
ayodhya.88.cau3: Guha said: My Lord, in seeing your lotus feet all is well with me; now I am counted among the fortunate.
My lord, earth, wealth and home are all yours, and I am a lowly servant of yours, with all my family.
ayodhya.88.cau4: Be kind enough to set foot in my town and raise your servant high, so the whole town looks on me with envy.
Śrī Rāma said: Wise friend, all you say is true, but my father has given me another command.
ayodhya.88.do88: For fourteen years I am to dwell in the forest with a hermit's vows, dress and food;
to stay in a village is not right. Hearing this, Guha was sorely grieved.
ayodhya.89.cau1: The village men and women gazed at how lovely Śrī Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā were, and said to one another with love:
Tell me, friend, what kind of father and mother are they who have sent such children to the forest?
ayodhya.89.cau2: One said: The king did well; fate has given us something worth having eyes for.
Then the Niṣāda chief considered in his heart, and a lovely śiṃśapā (sissoo) tree came to his mind.
ayodhya.89.cau3: He took Śrī Rāma there and showed him the place. Śrī Rāma said: It is lovely in every way.
The townsfolk paid their respects and went home, and Śrī Rāma went to perform the evening prayers.
ayodhya.89.cau4: Guha made up a bed of kuśa grass and young leaves, soft and pleasing, and spread it out.
He chose fruits and roots he knew to be pure, sweet and soft, set them out in leaf bowls filled to the brim, and set out water.
ayodhya.89.do89: Śrī Rāma ate bulbs, roots and fruits with Sītā, Sumantra and his brother,
and then the jewel of Raghu's line went to rest, his brother massaging his feet.
ayodhya.90.cau1: Knowing the Lord asleep, Lakṣmaṇa rose and gently told the minister to sleep.
Then, a little way off, he made ready his bow and arrows, sat in the warrior's posture and began to keep watch.
ayodhya.90.cau2: Guha sent for trusty watchmen and lovingly set them at post after post.
He himself, quiver at his waist and arrow set on the bow, went and sat beside Lakṣmaṇa.
ayodhya.90.cau3: As he watched the Lord sleeping, the Niṣāda, overcome by love, grew sorrowful at heart.
His body thrilled, tears flowed from his eyes, and he spoke lovingly to Lakṣmaṇa:
ayodhya.90.cau4: The king's palace has a beauty all its own; Indra's mansion is no match for it.
It has fine upper chambers wrought with jewels, as if the god of love had shaped them with his own hands;
ayodhya.90.do90: pure, richly adorned, full of every comfort and sweet with the scent of flowers,
where there are lovely beds and jewelled lamps, and every ease of every kind.
ayodhya.91.cau1: Clothes of many kinds, pillows and quilts are there, soft as milk-foam, spotless and lovely.
On these Sītā and Śrī Rāma would lie at night, their own beauty robbing Rati and the god of love of their pride.
ayodhya.91.cau2: That same Sītā and Śrī Rāma now sleep on a bed of leaves and grass; weary and without proper clothes, they are a sight too hard to bear.
Mother and father, kinsfolk and citizens, friends of good nature, servants and maids —
ayodhya.91.cau3: all used to guard him like their own life; and that same master, Śrī Rāma, now sleeps on the ground.
She whose father is Janaka, of power famed through the world, whose father-in-law is the king of the Raghus, friend of Indra,
ayodhya.91.cau4: she whose husband is Rāmacandra, that Vaidehī, sleeps on the ground. Against whom does fate not turn?
Are Sītā and Śrī Rāma fit for the forest? People speak the truth when they say that karma rules all.
ayodhya.91.do91: Kaikeyī, the dull-witted daughter of Kekaya, has played a harsh and crooked part,
bringing sorrow to Śrī Rāma and Sītā at a time meant for joy.
ayodhya.92.cau1: She has become an axe to the tree of the solar race; in her folly she has brought grief to the whole world.
Seeing Śrī Rāma and Sītā sleeping on the ground, the Niṣāda chief was overcome with grief.
ayodhya.92.cau2: Then, in sweet and gentle words steeped in knowledge, dispassion and devotion, Lakṣmaṇa said:
Brother, no one gives joy or sorrow to anyone; each reaps the fruit of the deeds he himself has done.
ayodhya.92.cau3: Union and parting, pleasures good and bad, those who wish us well or ill and those who are neither — all these are snares of delusion.
Birth and death, fortune and misfortune, karma and time — the whole net of the world, as far as it reaches,
ayodhya.92.cau4: earth, home, wealth, city and family, heaven and hell — all the dealings of life,
and all that is seen, heard and pondered in the mind, has its root in delusion; there is no ultimate truth in it.
ayodhya.92.do92: In a dream a king may become a beggar, or a pauper the lord of heaven;
on waking there is neither gain nor loss. See this world in your heart in the same way.
ayodhya.93.cau1: Thinking this over, one should not be angry, nor blame anyone in vain.
All are asleep in the night of delusion, and in their sleep they see dreams of many kinds.
ayodhya.93.cau2: In this night of the world the yogīs stay awake, seekers of the highest truth, detached from the world's show.
Know that a soul has woken in the world only when it has turned away from every pleasure of the senses.
ayodhya.93.cau3: When discernment dawns and the error of delusion flees, then love is born for the feet of Śrī Rāma.
Friend, this is the highest good of all: love for Śrī Rāma's feet in thought, deed and word.
ayodhya.93.cau4: Śrī Rāma is Brahman, the very form of the highest truth: beyond knowing, beyond sight, without beginning, beyond compare.
He is free of every change and beyond all distinction; the Vedas ever describe him as neti, not this.
ayodhya.93.do93: For the good of devotees, the earth, Brahmins, cows and gods, that compassionate Lord
takes a human body and performs his deeds; on hearing of them, the snares of the world are undone.
ayodhya.94.cau1: Understanding this, friend, give up delusion and give yourself to the feet of Sītā and Śrī Rāma.
As he spoke of Śrī Rāma's virtues, day broke, and the Lord who brings the world blessing and joy awoke.
ayodhya.94.cau2: When he had finished all his morning duties, Śrī Rāma bathed; then, pure and wise, he sent for the milky sap of the banyan.
With his younger brother he matted the hair of his head; seeing this, Sumantra's eyes filled with tears.
ayodhya.94.cau3: His heart burning and his face downcast, Sumantra folded his hands and said, in most humble words:
My Lord, the lord of Kosala told me this: Take the chariot and go with Rāma;
ayodhya.94.cau4: show them the forest, let them bathe in the Gaṅgā, and bring the two brothers back quickly.
Clear away every doubt and hesitation, and bring Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma and Sītā back.
ayodhya.94.do94: So the king said. Now, my master, whatever you say I will do; my life is yours.
Having made his plea, he fell at Śrī Rāma's feet and wept like a child.
ayodhya.95.cau1: Sumantra spoke again: Dear one, be gracious and do what will keep Ayodhyā from being left without a protector.
Śrī Rāma raised the minister and consoled him: Father, you have searched out every teaching of dharma.
ayodhya.95.cau2: For dharma's sake Śibi, Dadhīci and King Hariścandra endured countless sufferings.
Rantideva and Bali, wise kings, kept to dharma while bearing troubles of many kinds.
ayodhya.95.cau3: There is no dharma equal to truth; so the Āgamas, the Vedas and the Purāṇas declare.
That dharma has come to me easily; if I give it up, disgrace will spread through the three worlds.
ayodhya.95.cau4: For a man of honour, to earn disgrace is a dreadful burning, like dying ten million deaths.
Father, why should I say much to you? Merely by answering you back I would incur sin.
ayodhya.95.do95: Clasp my father's feet, give him my bows ten million times, and with folded hands entreat him:
Father, do not worry about me in any way.
ayodhya.96.cau1: You too, like my father, wish me every good. Father, with folded hands I beg you:
your duty in every way is to see that my father does not suffer from grief over us.
ayodhya.96.cau2: Hearing this talk between Śrī Rāma and the minister, the Niṣāda chief and his people were stricken with distress.
Then Lakṣmaṇa said some bitter words; the Lord, knowing them to be most improper, stopped him.
ayodhya.96.cau3: Abashed, Śrī Rāma bound Sumantra by an oath on himself not to repeat Lakṣmaṇa's message when he went back.
Then Sumantra delivered the king's message: Sītā will be unable to bear the hardships of the forest.
ayodhya.96.cau4: So whatever brings Sītā back to Ayodhyā, that is what Rāma and you must do.
Otherwise, left with no support at all, I shall not live, as a fish cannot live without water.
ayodhya.96.do96: At her father's house and at her husband's she has every comfort; wherever and whenever her heart wishes,
there let Sītā live happily, until this calamity passes and morning comes.
ayodhya.97.cau1: The way the king made his plea, the anguish and the love in it, is beyond telling.
Hearing his father's message, Śrī Rāma, the treasury of mercy, counselled Sītā in countless ways.
ayodhya.97.cau2: Mother-in-law, father-in-law, guru and dear family: if you go back, the anxiety of them all will be ended.
Hearing her husband's words, Vaidehī said: Listen, lord of my life, my dearest love.
ayodhya.97.cau3: My Lord, you are full of compassion and supremely wise. How can a shadow be held back, apart from its body?
Where can the light go, leaving the sun? Where can moonlight go, leaving the moon?
ayodhya.97.cau4: Having made this loving plea to her husband, Sītā spoke to the minister in gracious words:
You wish me well as my father and father-in-law do; to answer you back is most improper of me.
ayodhya.97.do97: Father, it is my distress that makes me stand up to you; do not take it amiss.
Without the lotus feet of my noble lord, every tie there is counts for nothing.
ayodhya.98.cau1: I have seen the splendour and luxury of my father, whose footstool is touched by the jewelled crowns of kings.
Yet such a house of every joy as my father's does not please my heart, even by mistake, without my beloved.
ayodhya.98.cau2: My father-in-law, the king of Kosala, is an emperor whose power is known in all fourteen worlds;
Indra himself comes forward to receive him and gives him half of his own throne.
ayodhya.98.cau3: Such a father-in-law, a home in Ayodhyā, a loving family, mothers-in-law who are like mothers —
without the dust of Śrī Rāma's lotus feet, none of these has ever seemed a joy to me, even in a dream.
ayodhya.98.cau4: Hard paths, forest lands and mountains, elephants and lions, lakes and rivers without end,
the Kol and Kirāta forest peoples, deer and birds — with the lord of my life, all of them bring me joy.
ayodhya.98.do98: Fall at the feet of my mother-in-law and father-in-law and make my plea on my behalf:
let them not worry about me at all; in the forest I am happy by my very nature.
ayodhya.99.cau1: The lord of my life and my dear brother-in-law are with me, foremost of heroes, bearing bow and quiver.
So my mind feels no weariness of the road, no bewilderment, no sorrow; do not worry about me, even by mistake.
ayodhya.99.cau2: Hearing Sītā's cool words, Sumantra was as distraught as a serpent that has lost its jewel.
His eyes could not see, his ears could not hear; utterly overwrought, he could say nothing.
ayodhya.99.cau3: Śrī Rāma consoled him in many ways, yet his heart found no relief.
He tried many ways to go along with them, but Śrī Rāma met each with a fitting answer.
ayodhya.99.cau4: There was no undoing Śrī Rāma's command; the way of karma is hard, and no one can prevail against it.
He bowed down, head to the feet of Śrī Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, and went home like a trader who has lost his capital.
ayodhya.99.do99: He drove the chariot on, but the horses kept looking back at Śrī Rāma and neighing.
Seeing this, the Niṣādas, overwhelmed with grief, beat their heads and lamented.
ayodhya.100.cau1: If even beasts are so distraught at parting from him, how will his people, his mother and his father live?
Śrī Rāma sent Sumantra back against his will, and then came himself to the bank of the Gaṅgā.
ayodhya.100.cau2: He asked for the boat; the boatman would not fetch it, but said: I have found out your secret.
Everyone says the dust of your lotus feet is a herb of some kind that makes things human.
ayodhya.100.cau3: At its touch a rock became a lovely woman, and wood is no harder than stone.
My boat too would become a sage's wife; I would be robbed on the road, and my boat would simply fly away.
ayodhya.100.cau4: By this I support my whole family; I know no other trade.
My Lord, if you must cross over, then tell me to wash your lotus feet.
ayodhya.100.cha1: Only when I have washed your lotus feet will I take you on board, my Lord; I want no fare for the crossing.
O Rāma, I swear by you and by Daśaratha that all I say is true.
Lakṣmaṇa may shoot arrows at me if he likes, but till I have washed your feet,
until then, compassionate Lord of Tulasīdāsa, I will not ferry you across.
ayodhya.100.so100: Hearing the boatman's quaint words, wrapped in love,
Śrī Rāma, abode of compassion, looked towards Jānakī and Lakṣmaṇa and laughed.
ayodhya.101.cau1: The ocean of mercy said with a smile: Do whatever will keep your boat from being lost.
Bring water quickly and wash my feet; time is slipping by, so ferry us over.
ayodhya.101.cau2: He whose name people need remember but once to cross the boundless ocean of worldly existence,
he who made the world too small for three of his steps, that same compassionate Lord is entreating a boatman.
ayodhya.101.cau3: Seeing the nails of his feet, Gaṅgā, river of the gods, rejoiced; yet hearing the Lord's words, her mind was drawn into delusion.
Receiving Śrī Rāma's command, the boatman filled a wooden basin with water and brought it.
ayodhya.101.cau4: Overflowing with joy and love, he began to wash the lotus feet.
All the gods rained flowers and envied him: none has a store of merit to equal his.
ayodhya.101.do101: Having washed his feet and drunk that water himself, together with all his family,
he first brought his forefathers across, then gladly took the Lord to the other shore.
ayodhya.102.cau1: Stepping down, Sītā and Śrī Rāma, with Guha and Lakṣmaṇa, stood on the sandbank of the Gaṅgā.
The boatman stepped down and prostrated himself; the Lord felt abashed that he had given him nothing.
ayodhya.102.cau2: Sītā, who knew her beloved's heart, gladly drew off her jewelled ring.
The compassionate Lord said: Take your fare. The boatman, distraught, clasped his feet.
ayodhya.102.cau3: The boatman said: My Lord, what have I not received today? My faults, my sorrows and the burning of poverty are gone.
Long have I laboured for wages; today the Creator has paid me well and in full.
ayodhya.102.cau4: My Lord, there is nothing I want now, by your grace, O you who are kind to the lowly.
Whatever you give me on your way back, I shall take as your blessed gift and place it on my head.
ayodhya.102.do102: The Lord, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā pressed him hard, but the boatman would take nothing.
Then the abode of compassion sent him away, granting him the boon of pure devotion.
ayodhya.103.cau1: Then Śrī Rāma bathed, worshipped an earthen image of Śiva and bowed his head.
Sītā, with joined palms, said to Gaṅgā: Mother, fulfil my wish,
ayodhya.103.cau2: so that, home again in safety with my husband and his brother, I may offer you worship.
When Gaṅgā heard Sītā's prayer, steeped in the delight of love, a noble voice then came from her pure waters:
ayodhya.103.cau3: Listen, Vaidehī, beloved of the hero of the Raghus: who in the world does not know your power?
Those on whom your glance falls become guardians of the worlds; all the siddhis stand before you with joined palms to serve you.
ayodhya.103.cau4: That you have made so humble a prayer to me is your kindness to me; it has honoured me.
Even so, goddess, I shall bless you, so that my own words may bear fruit.
ayodhya.103.do103: Coming back safe to Kosala with the lord of your life and his younger brother,
you will have every wish of your heart fulfilled, and your fair fame will remain spread over the world.
ayodhya.104.cau1: Hearing Gaṅgā's words, the root of all good, Sītā was glad to find the river of the gods favourable.
Then the Lord told Guha to return home. Hearing it, Guha's face went dry and a burning rose in his breast.
ayodhya.104.cau2: Guha, with joined palms, spoke humbly: O jewel of the Raghu line, hear my prayer.
My Lord, I would stay with you, show you the way and serve your feet for a few days;
ayodhya.104.cau3: in whatever forest you go to live, O Lord of the Raghus, I will build a lovely hut of leaves.
Then whatever command you give me, that I will do; I swear it by the hero of the Raghus.
ayodhya.104.cau4: Seeing his natural love, Śrī Rāma took him along, and Guha's heart was full of joy.
Then Guha called all his kinsmen and, having set their minds at rest, sent them back.
ayodhya.104.do104: Then the Lord remembered Gaṇeśa and Śiva and bowed his head to Gaṅgā;
and with his friend, his younger brother and Sītā, Śrī Rāma set out for the forest.
ayodhya.105.cau1: That day they lodged beneath a tree, and Lakṣmaṇa and the friend made them comfortable in every way.
At daybreak, his morning observances done, Śrī Rāma went on, and the Lord set eyes on Prayāga, king of all holy places.
ayodhya.105.cau2: Truth is the minister of this king, Faith his beloved queen, and a friend such as Veṇīmādhava his well-wisher.
His treasury is filled with the four aims of life, and that holy region is his most beautiful realm.
ayodhya.105.cau3: The holy region is his fortress, hard to reach, strong and lovely, which no enemy has won even in a dream.
All the holy places are the fine warriors of his army, steady in battle, crushing the forces of sin.
ayodhya.105.cau4: The confluence makes his throne, splendid beyond measure; for parasol he has the undying banyan, which holds even sages' minds enthralled.
His fly-whisks are the ripples of the Yamunā and the Gaṅgā; sorrow and poverty are shattered at the sight of them.
ayodhya.105.do105: The virtuous, pure and holy serve him and obtain all they desire.
The Vedas and the hosts of Purāṇas are his heralds, who sing his spotless virtues.
ayodhya.106.cau1: Who can tell the glory of Prayāga, a lion to the elephant herds of sin?
Seeing so lovely a king of holy places, Śrī Rāma, the ocean of joy, himself found joy.
ayodhya.106.cau2: To Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa and his friend the Lord spoke, telling them from his own holy lips how great the king of holy places is.
Bowing to it, and looking at the woods and gardens as he spoke of its glory with deep love,
ayodhya.106.cau3: he came in this way and beheld the Triveṇī, the confluence that grants every blessing to those who but remember it.
Gladly he bathed, served Śiva and duly worshipped the gods of the holy place.
ayodhya.106.cau4: Then the Lord came to Bharadvāja; even as he prostrated, the sage clasped him to his heart.
The joy in the sage's mind cannot be told; it was as if he had gained a store of the bliss of Brahman.
ayodhya.106.do106: The chief of sages gave his blessing, and his heart was full of joy as he thought
that the Creator had, as it were, brought the fruit of his merit and set it before his eyes.
ayodhya.107.cau1: Asking after their welfare, the sage gave them seats, worshipped them and filled them with love.
He brought them fine tubers, roots, fruits and tender shoots, as if made of nectar.
ayodhya.107.cau2: With Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa and his devoted attendant, Śrī Rāma ate the lovely roots and fruits with great relish.
Rested from his weariness, Śrī Rāma was at ease, and Bharadvāja spoke gently:
ayodhya.107.cau3: Today my austerity, pilgrimage and renunciation are rewarded; today japa, yoga and dispassion are rewarded too.
All my good practices and their whole array have borne fruit, Rāma, now that I behold you today.
ayodhya.107.cau4: There is no gain beyond this, no joy beyond this; in seeing you all my hopes are fulfilled.
Now be gracious and give me this boon too: natural love for your lotus feet.
ayodhya.107.do107: Until a person, casting off deceit in deed, word and mind, becomes your servant,
he finds no happiness even in a dream, though he try ten million remedies.
ayodhya.108.cau1: Hearing the sage's words Śrī Rāma was abashed, and was filled with the joy of his love and devotion.
Then Śrī Rāma told everyone the sage's fair renown in countless ways.
ayodhya.108.cau2: Śrī Rāma said: Great is he, and the home of every virtue, O chief of sages, whom you honour.
So the sage and Śrī Rāma bowed to each other and knew a joy beyond words.
ayodhya.108.cau3: On hearing this news, the people of Prayāga, students, ascetics, sages, siddhas and recluses,
all came to Bharadvāja's hermitage to see the handsome sons of Daśaratha.
ayodhya.108.cau4: Śrī Rāma bowed to every one of them, and they rejoiced to gain the reward of their eyes.
Filled with supreme joy they gave their blessings, and went back praising his beauty.
ayodhya.108.do108: Śrī Rāma rested for the night, and in the morning bathed at Prayāga;
then, gladly bowing his head to the sage, he set out with Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa and his devoted attendant.
ayodhya.109.cau1: Śrī Rāma said lovingly to the sage: My lord, tell us which way we should go.
Smiling inwardly, the sage said to Śrī Rāma: Every road is easy for you.
ayodhya.109.cau2: The sage called his disciples to go with them; hearing it, some fifty came, glad at heart.
All of them had boundless love for Śrī Rāma, and every one said: We have seen the way.
ayodhya.109.cau3: Then the sage sent four young students with them, who had done every kind of good deed through many births.
Bowing to the seer and receiving his leave, Śrī Rāma set off with a glad heart.
ayodhya.109.cau4: When they pass near a village, men and women run out to see them.
Gaining the fruit of their birth, they feel they have found a protector, and turn back sad, sending their hearts along with them.
ayodhya.109.do109: Śrī Rāma sent the students back with courteous entreaty, and they returned with their hearts' desire.
Then, going down to the river, they bathed in the water of the Yamunā, dark as Śrī Rāma's own body.
ayodhya.110.cau1: Hearing of it, the men and women who lived on the bank ran out, their own tasks forgotten.
Seeing the beauty of Lakṣmaṇa, Śrī Rāma and Sītā, they praised their own good fortune.
ayodhya.110.cau2: Great longing filled their minds, but they were shy to ask names and village.
Those among them who were older and wise recognised Śrī Rāma by shrewd reckoning.
ayodhya.110.cau3: They told everyone the whole story: that they were going to the forest at their father's command.
Hearing it, all grieved and lamented: the queen and the king have not done right.
ayodhya.110.cau4: Just then an ascetic came there, a mass of radiance, young and handsome.
Poets could not trace his ways; he wore the dress of a renunciant and loved Śrī Rāma in mind, deed and word.
ayodhya.110.do110: With tears in his eyes and his body thrilling, he recognised his own chosen deity;
he fell flat on the ground like a staff, and his state cannot be described.
ayodhya.111.cau1: Śrī Rāma, thrilled with love, clasped him to his heart, as if a man in utter poverty had found the philosopher's stone.
Everyone said it was as if love and the supreme truth had taken bodies and were meeting.
ayodhya.111.cau2: Then he fell at Lakṣmaṇa's feet, and Lakṣmaṇa, overflowing with love, raised him up.
Then he placed the dust of Sītā's feet on his head, and she, as a mother, blessed him as her own child.
ayodhya.111.cau3: The Niṣāda prostrated himself before him; seeing in him one who loved Śrī Rāma, the ascetic met him gladly.
With the cups of his eyes he drinks the nectar of Śrī Rāma's beauty, as glad as a hungry man who has found good food.
ayodhya.111.cau4: The women say to one another: Tell me, friend, what kind of father and mother are they, who sent such children to the forest?
At the sight of Śrī Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā in their beauty, men and women are overwhelmed with love.
ayodhya.111.do111: Then Śrī Rāma gave his friend the Niṣāda chief counsel in many ways.
Taking Śrī Rāma's command upon his head, he went back to his home.
ayodhya.112.cau1: Then Sītā, Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa folded their hands and bowed once more to the Yamunā.
The two brothers went on gladly with Sītā, praising the Yamunā, daughter of the Sun.
ayodhya.112.cau2: Many travellers meet them on the way; seeing the two brothers, they say lovingly:
We see the marks of kingship in every limb of yours, and our hearts are deeply troubled.
ayodhya.112.cau3: And yet you walk the road on foot: to our mind, astrology is false.
The way is hard, through mountains and dense forests, and with you on it is a delicate young woman.
ayodhya.112.cau4: The forest, with its elephants and lions, is fearful even to look at. If you permit, we will come with you.
We will take you as far as you are going, then bow our heads to you and come back.
ayodhya.112.do112: So they ask, overcome by love, their bodies thrilling and their eyes full of tears.
Śrī Rāma, the ocean of mercy, turns them back with humble, gentle words.
ayodhya.113.cau1: The towns and villages that lie along the road are envied by the cities of the Nāgas and the gods:
By what virtuous soul, at what hour, were these founded? They are blessed, full of merit and supremely lovely.
ayodhya.113.cau2: Wherever Śrī Rāma's feet tread, not even Amarāvatī equals those places.
Those who live near the road are heaps of merit; the dwellers of heaven praise them,
ayodhya.113.cau3: who gaze their eyes' fill on Śrī Rāma, dark as a rain-cloud, with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
The lakes and rivers in which Śrī Rāma bathes are praised by the lakes and rivers of the gods.
ayodhya.113.cau4: The tree under which the Lord goes and sits is extolled by the wish-granting trees.
Touched by the pollen of Śrī Rāma's lotus feet, the earth counts herself greatly blessed.
ayodhya.113.do113: Clouds give shade; the hosts of gods rain flowers and look on with longing.
Śrī Rāma goes along the road, looking at the hills and forests, the birds and beasts.
ayodhya.114.cau1: When Śrī Rāma, with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, passes close by a village,
all who hear of it, children and the old, men and women, set out at once, forgetting their household work.
ayodhya.114.cau2: Gazing on the beauty of Śrī Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, they win the reward of having eyes and are happy.
With tearful eyes and bodies thrilling, all were lost in joy at the sight of the two heroes.
ayodhya.114.cau3: Their state is past describing: it was as though paupers had come upon a heap of wish-granting gems.
Some call to others and advise them: Take the gain of your eyes this very moment.
ayodhya.114.cau4: Some, seeing Śrī Rāma, are so moved with love that they walk along with him, gazing at him.
Others draw his image through their eyes into their hearts, and body, mind and fair speech all go limp in them.
ayodhya.114.do114: Some, seeing the pleasant shade of a banyan, spread soft grass and leaves
and say: Rest from your weariness a moment; then go now, or in the morning.
ayodhya.115.cau1: Some bring a pitcher filled with water and say in gentle words: My Lord, please drink.
Hearing their loving words and seeing their deep love, Śrī Rāma, compassionate and gracious above all,
ayodhya.115.cau2: knowing in his heart that Sītā was tired, rested a while in the shade of the banyan.
Men and women gaze with delight at the beauty; the peerless form has charmed their eyes and minds.
ayodhya.115.cau3: All around, they stand with unblinking gaze, lovely as cakora birds before the moon of Śrī Rāma's face.
His body, the colour of a young tamāla tree, shines; the sight of it enchants the minds of countless Kāmadevas.
ayodhya.115.cau4: Lakṣmaṇa, the colour of lightning, is exceedingly handsome, lovely from toe-nail to crown and dear to the heart.
With hermits' cloth and quivers bound at their waists, they hold bows and arrows that shine in their lotus hands.
ayodhya.115.do115: On their heads are lovely crowns of matted hair; their chests, arms and eyes are large.
On their fair faces, like the moon of an autumn full-moon night, a network of beads of sweat glistens.
ayodhya.116.cau1: The charming pair cannot be described: the beauty is great and my wit is small.
All gaze at the beauty of Śrī Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā with heart, mind and understanding intent upon it.
ayodhya.116.cau2: The men and women, thirsting with love, stood still, like does and stags that have seen a lamp.
The village women go up to Sītā, but in their great affection they are shy to ask.
ayodhya.116.cau3: Again and again they all touch her feet and speak gentle words, simply and naturally:
Princess, we have a request; but, being women, we are timid to ask anything.
ayodhya.116.cau4: Lady, forgive our boldness, and take no offence, knowing us to be simple village women.
These two princes are lovely by nature; emerald and gold owe their lustre to them.
ayodhya.116.do116: One is dark and one fair; both are fine youths, handsome, homes of all grace.
Their faces are like the autumn moon, their eyes like the autumn lotus.
ayodhya.117.cau1: They put countless Kāmadevas to shame. Tell us, fair-faced one, who are they to you?
Hearing their sweet words full of affection, Sītā was abashed and smiled within herself.
ayodhya.117.cau2: She looks at them, then looks down at the ground: the fair lady is held back by a shyness from two sides.
Shyly and lovingly, she whose eyes are a fawn's and whose voice is a cuckoo's spoke sweet words:
ayodhya.117.cau3: This one, simple of nature, handsome and fair, is Lakṣmaṇa, my husband's younger brother.
Then, covering her moon-like face with the end of her sari, she looked towards her beloved, arched her brows,
ayodhya.117.cau4: and with a sidelong glance of her lovely wagtail eyes, Sītā made known to them by signs that this was her own husband.
The young village wives were all overjoyed, as if paupers had plundered a king's treasure.
ayodhya.117.do117: With great love they fall at Sītā's feet and bless her in many ways:
May you ever remain a happy wife, as long as the earth rests on the serpent's head.
ayodhya.118.cau1: May you be dear to your lord as Pārvatī is to hers. Goddess, do not withdraw your affection from us.
Again and again we pray with folded hands: if you come back this way,
ayodhya.118.cau2: grant us the sight of you, knowing us as your own servants. Sītā saw that they all thirsted with love.
With sweet words, again and again, she satisfied them, as moonlight nourishes the night-lilies.
ayodhya.118.cau3: Then Lakṣmaṇa, knowing Śrī Rāma's wish, gently asked the people the way.
At this the men and women grew sad; their bodies thrilled and their eyes filled with tears.
ayodhya.118.cau4: Their joy vanished and their hearts sank, as if the Creator were taking back a treasure he had given.
Understanding the ways of karma, they took heart, and having worked out an easy road, told it to them.
ayodhya.118.do118: Then Śrī Rāma set out with Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā.
He sent them all back with kind words, but took their hearts along with him.
ayodhya.119.cau1: As they go back, the men and women grieve deeply and blame fate in their hearts.
Sorrowfully they say to one another: All the Creator's doings are perverse.
ayodhya.119.cau2: He is wholly unchecked, cruel and fearless: he made the moon sickly and stained.
He made the wish-granting tree a mere tree and the ocean salt; it is he who has sent these princes to the forest.
ayodhya.119.cau3: If he has given them exile in the forest, the Creator made pleasures and luxuries for nothing.
These walk the road without shoes; then the Creator made all kinds of mounts and carriages for nothing.
ayodhya.119.cau4: These lie on the ground on a bed of kuśa grass and leaves: why does the Creator make lovely beds?
The Creator has given them a home under great trees; then his toil in building white palaces was wasted.
ayodhya.119.do119: If hermits' clothes and matted hair are for these two, so handsome and so tender,
then the Maker fashioned jewels and garments of every kind in vain.
ayodhya.120.cau1: If these eat bulbs, roots and fruit, then nectar and all such food in the world is in vain.
Some say: They are lovely by nature; they appeared of themselves and were not made by the Creator.
ayodhya.120.cau2: All the Creator's work that the Vedas tell of, all that ear, eye and mind can reach:
search through all fourteen worlds and see: where is such a man, where such a woman?
ayodhya.120.cau3: At the sight of them the Creator's heart was charmed, and he set about making others to match them.
He toiled hard, but not one came up to them; so, out of envy, he brought them to the forest and hid them.
ayodhya.120.cau4: Others say: We do not know much, but we count ourselves supremely blessed.
And in our reckoning they too are heaps of merit who see them, who will see them, and who have seen them.
ayodhya.120.do120: Saying such loving words over and over, they fill their eyes with tears:
How will bodies so very delicate travel the hard road?
ayodhya.121.cau1: Overcome by love, the women grow distraught, looking like female cakravāka birds at dusk.
Knowing how soft are these lotus feet and how hard the road, they speak fine words with full hearts:
ayodhya.121.cau2: Their soft red feet touch the earth, and it shrinks back as our hearts shrink.
If the Lord of the world has given them the forest, why did he not make the road all of flowers?
ayodhya.121.cau3: Friend, if Brahmā granted what we asked of him, we would keep them within our eyes.
The men and women who missed that moment could not see Sītā and Śrī Rāma.
ayodhya.121.cau4: Hearing of their beauty, they ask in distress: Brother, how far will they have gone by now?
Those who are able run off and see them, and come back overjoyed, having won the fruit of their birth.
ayodhya.121.do121: Women, children and the old, who cannot go, wring their hands and grieve.
So, wherever Śrī Rāma goes, the people there are overpowered by love.
ayodhya.122.cau1: In village after village there is such joy at the sight of Śrī Rāma, the moon to the water-lilies of the solar line.
Those who come to hear something of the news lay the blame on the king and the queen.
ayodhya.122.cau2: Some say the king is very good, for he has given our eyes this gain.
Men and women talk among themselves in words that are simple, loving and sweet.
ayodhya.122.cau3: Blessed are the father and mother who bore them, and blessed the city they have come from.
Blessed the land, the hill, the forest and the village, and blessed every place they go to.
ayodhya.122.cau4: Brahmā found joy in making that one to whom these two are bound in love in every way.
The lovely tale of Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa on their journey spread along the whole road and through the forest.
ayodhya.122.do122: So Śrī Rāma, the sun to the lotus of Raghu's line, gladdening the people on the road,
goes on his way with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, looking at the forest.
ayodhya.123.cau1: Śrī Rāma walks in front and Lakṣmaṇa looks fine behind him; in the garb of ascetics they shine.
Between the two Sītā looks as māyā does between Brahman and the individual soul.
ayodhya.123.cau2: Again, I tell the picture as it lives in my mind: it is as if Rati shone between Madhu, the spring, and Kāma.
Again, searching my heart, I give another likeness: it is as if Rohiṇī shone between Budha and the moon.
ayodhya.123.cau3: Sītā sets her feet down between the Lord's footprints, walking the road with fearful care.
Lakṣmaṇa walks clear of the footprints of Sītā and Śrī Rāma, keeping their track to his right.
ayodhya.123.cau4: The lovely affection of Śrī Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā lies beyond words; how could it be told?
Birds and beasts are lost in wonder at the sight; Śrī Rāma the traveller has stolen their hearts.
ayodhya.123.do123: All who saw those dear travellers, the two brothers with Sītā,
have come to the end of the hard road of worldly existence joyfully and without toil.
ayodhya.124.cau1: Even now, if ever, even in a dream, the travellers Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā and Śrī Rāma come to dwell in anyone's heart,
he will find the way to Śrī Rāma's abode, the way that only now and then some sage finds.
ayodhya.124.cau2: Then Śrī Rāma, seeing that Sītā was tired, noticed a banyan and cool water close by.
They stayed there and ate bulbs, roots and fruits; at dawn Śrī Rāma bathed and went on.
ayodhya.124.cau3: The Lord came to Vālmīki's hermitage, taking in the lovely woods, lakes and hills on the way.
To Śrī Rāma the sage's dwelling looked delightful: a beautiful hill, woods and holy water.
ayodhya.124.cau4: Lotuses bloom in the lakes and trees in the forest, and bees hum sweetly, lost in the nectar.
Birds and beasts in great numbers fill the air with their cries and roam glad at heart, with no enmity among them.
ayodhya.124.do124: Seeing the pure, beautiful hermitage, the lotus-eyed Lord was glad.
Hearing that Śrī Rāma had come, the sage came out ahead to bring him in.
ayodhya.125.cau1: Śrī Rāma prostrated himself before the sage, and that great Brahmin gave his blessing.
His eyes were soothed by the sight of Śrī Rāma's beauty, and with honour he brought them into the hermitage.
ayodhya.125.cau2: The great sage, having guests as dear to him as life, had sweet bulbs, roots and fruits brought.
Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa and Śrī Rāma ate the fruit, and then the sage gave them pleasant places in the hermitage.
ayodhya.125.cau3: Gazing with his own eyes on the embodiment of all that is auspicious, Vālmīki felt great joy in his heart.
Then Śrī Rāma joined his lotus hands and spoke words that delighted the ear:
ayodhya.125.cau4: Lord of sages, you see past, present and future; the whole world is to you like a jujube berry held in your hand.
With these words the Lord told the whole story of how the queen had given him the forest.
ayodhya.125.do125: My father's word, then my mother's good, a brother like Bharata becoming king,
and, my lord, the sight of you granted to me: all of this is the fruit of my merit.
ayodhya.126.cau1: King of sages, in seeing your feet all our good deeds have borne fruit.
Now let us stay wherever you bid us, but in a place where no sage will suffer any disturbance.
ayodhya.126.cau2: Kings who bring suffering on sages and ascetics burn without any fire.
The contentment of Brahmins is the root of all good, and a Brahmin's anger burns up millions of families.
ayodhya.126.cau3: Knowing this, tell me the place where I may go with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
and there, O kind one, build a pretty hut of leaves and grass and live for a while.
ayodhya.126.cau4: Hearing the natural, guileless words of Śrī Rāma, the wise sage said: Well spoken, well spoken.
Banner of Raghu's line, how could you not speak so? It is you who forever guard the bounds the Vedas set.
ayodhya.126.cha1: Rāma, you are the Lord of the world who guards the bounds of the Vedas, and Jānakī is māyā,
who creates, sustains and takes away the world at a sign from you, the treasury of grace.
Lakṣmaṇa is the thousand-headed king of serpents who holds up the earth, master of all that moves and does not move.
For the gods' sake you have taken the body of a king and set out to destroy the army of the wicked demons.
ayodhya.126.so126: Rāma, your true being is out of the reach of speech and beyond the mind.
It is unknowable, unutterable and boundless; the Vedas ever say of it neti neti, not this, not this.
ayodhya.127.cau1: The world is a show and you are the one who watches it; you make even Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva dance.
Not even they know your secret; who else, then, could know you?
ayodhya.127.cau2: Only he knows you whom you allow to know you, and in knowing you he becomes none other than you.
Only by your own grace, Delight of the Raghus, do devotees know you, you who are sandal-paste to their hearts.
ayodhya.127.cau3: Your body is made of consciousness and bliss and is free of every change; those fit for it know this.
For the work of saints and gods you have put on a human body, and you speak and act as an ordinary king would.
ayodhya.127.cau4: Rāma, seeing and hearing of your deeds, the dull are bewildered and the wise are glad.
All that you say and do is right, for as one dresses for the part, so must one dance.
ayodhya.127.do127: You ask me where to live, and I am shy of asking you in turn:
name any place where you are not, and I will show you a place to stay.
ayodhya.128.cau1: Hearing the sage's words, steeped in the sweetness of love, Śrī Rāma was abashed and smiled to himself.
Vālmīki laughed and spoke again, in sweet words soaked in nectar:
ayodhya.128.cau2: Hear me, Rāma: now I will name the homes in which you may dwell with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
Those whose ears are like the sea, and your stories the many lovely rivers,
ayodhya.128.cau3: which keep filling with them and are never full: their hearts are fine homes for you.
Those who have made their eyes into cātaka birds, ever longing for the rain cloud of your sight,
ayodhya.128.cau4: who scorn the great rivers, oceans and lakes and are made happy by a single drop of the water of your beauty:
in their hearts, homes that give joy, dwell with your brother and Sītā, O Lord of the Raghus.
ayodhya.128.do128: One whose tongue is a swan on the clear Mānasa lake of your fame,
picking up the pearls of your many virtues: Rāma, dwell in his heart.
ayodhya.129.cau1: One whose nose daily and reverently takes in the pure, lovely fragrance of what is offered to the Lord;
those who eat only what has been offered to you, and wear clothes and ornaments that are the Lord's gift,
ayodhya.129.cau2: whose heads bow with love and deep humility when they see gods, their guru or Brahmins,
whose hands worship Śrī Rāma's feet every day, and whose hearts trust in Śrī Rāma and no other,
ayodhya.129.cau3: whose feet carry them to Śrī Rāma's holy places: Rāma, dwell in their minds.
Those who chant your king of mantras every day and worship you together with your household,
ayodhya.129.cau4: who make libations and fire offerings in many ways, feed Brahmins and give them many gifts,
who in their hearts hold their guru greater even than you and serve him with all their heart, honouring him,
ayodhya.129.do129: and, having done all this, ask for one fruit alone, love for Śrī Rāma's feet:
in the temple of their minds dwell, Sītā and you, delight of the Raghus, both of you.
ayodhya.130.cau1: Those in whom there is no desire, anger, pride, conceit or delusion, no greed, unrest, attachment or malice,
and no deceit, hypocrisy or guile: in their hearts dwell, O Lord of the Raghus.
ayodhya.130.cau2: Those who are dear to all and do good to all, to whom sorrow and joy, praise and abuse are the same,
who think before they speak words that are true and kind, and who, waking or sleeping, rest in your refuge,
ayodhya.130.cau3: who have no other refuge but you: Rāma, dwell in their minds.
Those who look on another man's wife as a mother, and for whom another's wealth is a poison worse than poison,
ayodhya.130.cau4: who rejoice to see another's prosperity and are deeply grieved at another's misfortune,
and for whom you, Rāma, are as dear as life: their minds are fair homes for you.
ayodhya.130.do130: My dear, those for whom you are everything, master, friend, father, mother and guru:
in the temple of their minds dwell, you two brothers, with Sītā.
ayodhya.131.cau1: Those who leave aside faults and take up the virtues of all, and bear hardship for the good of Brahmins and cows,
whose skill in right counsel is renowned in the world: their good mind is your home.
ayodhya.131.cau2: He who counts the virtues as yours and the faults as his own, who relies on you in every way,
and to whom the devotees of Rāma are dear: dwell in his heart, with Sītā.
ayodhya.131.cau3: Caste and kin, wealth, dharma, standing, a dear family and a happy home:
he who leaves them all and holds you alone to his heart: dwell in his heart, O Lord of the Raghus.
ayodhya.131.cau4: He for whom heaven, hell and liberation are alike, who sees you everywhere holding bow and arrows,
who is your servant in deed, word and mind: take up your lodging in his heart, O Rāma.
ayodhya.131.do131: He who never wants anything at all, and whose love for you comes naturally:
dwell for ever in his mind; it is your very own home.
ayodhya.132.cau1: Thus the great sage Vālmīki showed the dwellings, and his loving words delighted Śrī Rāma's heart.
The sage said: Listen, O leader of the solar race; I will tell you of a hermitage that will bring you comfort at this time.
ayodhya.132.cau2: Make your home on Mount Citrakūṭa; there you will be at ease in every way.
The mountain is lovely and the forest fair, and elephants, lions, deer and birds roam there.
ayodhya.132.cau3: There is a holy river, sung in the Purāṇas, which Atri's wife brought there by the power of her austerities.
This stream of the Gaṅgā, named Mandākinī, devours all the brood of sin as a ḍākinī devours infants.
ayodhya.132.cau4: Many great sages, Atri among them, live there, practising yoga, japa and austerity and disciplining their bodies.
Go there and make the labours of all bear fruit, Rāma, and grant honour to that noble mountain as well.
ayodhya.132.do132: The great sage sang of the boundless glory of Citrakūṭa.
The two brothers came there with Sītā and bathed in that excellent river.
ayodhya.133.cau1: Śrī Rāma said: Lakṣmaṇa, this is a good ghāṭ; now make some arrangement for us to stay somewhere.
Lakṣmaṇa looked at the high northern bank of the Payasvinī, with a stream curving round it on every side like a bow.
ayodhya.133.cau2: Lakṣmaṇa said: The river is the bowstring, calm of mind, self-restraint and giving are the arrows, and all the sins of the Kali age are the many kinds of game.
Citrakūṭa is like a hunter who never moves; his aim never misses, and he strikes face to face.
ayodhya.133.cau3: Saying this, Lakṣmaṇa pointed out the place, and Śrī Rāma was glad to see the spot.
The gods knew that Śrī Rāma's heart had settled there, and they set out with Viśvakarmā, the chief builder of the gods.
ayodhya.133.cau4: They all came dressed as Kols and Kirātas and built charming homes of leaves and grass.
There were two lovely huts, beyond describing, one small and graceful, the other spacious.
ayodhya.133.do133: The Lord, with Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, shines in the lovely dwelling,
like Kāmadeva in the garb of a sage, with Rati and the Spring beside him.
ayodhya.134.cau1: At that time gods, nāgas, kinnaras and the guardians of the quarters came to Citrakūṭa.
Śrī Rāma bowed to every one of them, and the gods rejoiced at gaining the reward of their eyes.
ayodhya.134.cau2: Showering flowers, the assembled gods said: Lord, today we have a protector.
With prayers they told of their unbearable sufferings, then went happily each to their own abode.
ayodhya.134.cau3: Śrī Rāma has made his home at Citrakūṭa: as they heard the news, sage after sage came.
Seeing the joyful company of sages coming, Śrī Rāma bowed down full length before them.
ayodhya.134.cau4: The sages clasp Śrī Rāma to their hearts and bless him, so that their blessings may bear fruit.
They gaze on the beauty of Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa and Śrī Rāma, and count all their spiritual practice as fulfilled.
ayodhya.134.do134: The Lord honoured each as was due and bade the company of sages farewell.
In their own hermitages they practise yoga, japa, sacrifice and austerity unhindered.
ayodhya.135.cau1: When the Kols and Kirātas heard this news, they were as glad as if the nine treasures had come to their homes.
Filling leaf-cups to the brim with tubers, roots and fruits, they set off like the poor rushing to plunder gold.
ayodhya.135.cau2: As they went along the way, the others questioned those among them who had seen the two brothers.
So, talking and hearing of Śrī Rāma's beauty, everyone arrived and set eyes on him.
ayodhya.135.cau3: Setting their gifts before him, they greeted him and gazed at the Lord with great love.
They stood here and there as still as figures in a painting, their bodies thrilling and their eyes filling with tears.
ayodhya.135.cau4: Śrī Rāma saw that they were all lost in love, and with kind words he honoured every one.
Bowing to the Lord again and again, with joined palms they spoke humbly:
ayodhya.135.do135: Lord, now that we have seen your feet, we all have a protector.
It is our good fortune, O King of Kosala, that you have come here.
ayodhya.136.cau1: Blessed are the ground, the woods, the paths and the hills, wherever, Lord, you have set your feet.
Blessed are the birds and beasts that roam the forest: seeing you, their birth has found its reward.
ayodhya.136.cau2: We too are blessed, all of us and our families, for we have seen you to our eyes' content.
You have thought it over and made your home in a good place; here you will be comfortable in every season.
ayodhya.136.cau3: We will serve you in every way, keeping elephants, lions, snakes and tigers away from you.
The forests and ravines, the hills, caves and hollows: every step of them, Lord, we have explored.
ayodhya.136.cau4: From place to place we will take you hunting and show you lakes, waterfalls and pools.
We and our families are your servants; Lord, never hesitate to command us.
ayodhya.136.do136: The Lord, home of compassion, whom the words of the Vedas and the minds of sages cannot reach,
listened to the words of the Kirātas as a father listens to his child's prattle.
ayodhya.137.cau1: To Śrī Rāma only love is dear; let whoever would understand, understand this.
Then Śrī Rāma contented all the forest folk, speaking gentle words that nurtured their love.
ayodhya.137.cau2: When he gave them leave, they bowed their heads and went, and reached home speaking and hearing of the Lord's virtues.
Thus the two brothers lived in the forest with Sītā, giving joy to gods and sages.
ayodhya.137.cau3: Ever since Śrī Rāma came to live there, the forest has been a source of blessing.
Trees of every sort flower and fruit, and fine, lovely creepers spread in canopies all around.
ayodhya.137.cau4: They are lovely by nature like the trees of paradise, as though they had left the forests of the gods and come here.
Rows of bees hum most sweetly, and a pleasant breeze blows, cool, gentle and fragrant.
ayodhya.137.do137: Blue jays, cuckoos, parrots, cātakas, cakravākas and cakoras:
birds of every kind call in their many voices, delighting the ear and stealing the heart.
ayodhya.138.cau1: Elephants, lions, monkeys, boars and deer, their enmity forgotten, all roam side by side.
As Śrī Rāma roams on the hunt, herds of deer delight all the more in the sight of his beauty.
ayodhya.138.cau2: The forests of the gods, as many as there are in the world, all look with envy on Śrī Rāma's forest.
The Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī, the Yamunā, daughter of the Sun, the Narmadā, daughter of Mekala, the blessed Godāvarī,
ayodhya.138.cau3: all the lakes and seas, and rivers great and small, sing the praises of the Mandākinī.
The mountains of the sunrise and the sunset, Kailāsa, Mandara and Meru, all the dwellings of the gods,
ayodhya.138.cau4: and Himālaya and every other mountain there is, all sing of Citrakūṭa's fame.
The Vindhya rejoices, his joy overflowing, for he has won great glory without effort.
ayodhya.138.do138: The birds and beasts, creepers, trees and every kind of grass of Citrakūṭa
are all blessed, stores of merit: so the gods say day and night.
ayodhya.139.cau1: Those who have eyes look on Śrī Rāma, reap the fruit of their birth and are freed from sorrow.
Things that cannot move are made happy by the touch of the dust of his feet, and have become worthy of the supreme state.
ayodhya.139.cau2: That forest and hill are lovely by nature, full of blessing, purifying even the purest.
How can one speak of the glory of the place where the ocean of joy has made his home?
ayodhya.139.cau3: Where Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa and Śrī Rāma have come to live, leaving the ocean of milk and forsaking Ayodhyā,
even a hundred thousand thousand-mouthed Śeṣas could not tell the splendour of that forest.
ayodhya.139.cau4: How then shall I describe it? Can a tortoise from a puddle lift Mount Mandara?
Lakṣmaṇa serves him in deed, mind and speech; his goodness and love cannot be put into words.
ayodhya.139.do139: Seeing the feet of Sītā and Śrī Rāma moment by moment, and knowing their love for him,
Lakṣmaṇa never, even in a dream, turns his thoughts to brothers, mother, father or home.
ayodhya.140.cau1: Sītā lives happily with Śrī Rāma, the thought of city, kin and home forgotten.
Gazing every moment at her beloved's moon-like face, she is overjoyed like a young cakora bird.
ayodhya.140.cau2: Seeing her lord's love grow day by day, she stays as joyful as the cakravākī in daylight.
Sītā's heart is devoted to Śrī Rāma's feet, and the forest is as dear to her as a thousand Ayodhyās.
ayodhya.140.cau3: With her dearest, the hut of leaves is dear to her, and the deer and birds are her beloved family.
The sages' wives and the great sages are like her mother-in-law and father-in-law, and a meal of tubers, roots and fruits tastes like nectar.
ayodhya.140.cau4: With her lord, a simple bed of grass is lovely, giving her the comfort of a hundred beds of Kāmadeva.
She whose mere glance makes beings guardians of the worlds: can sensual pleasure ever charm her?
ayodhya.140.do140: Remembering Śrī Rāma, his devotees cast away sense pleasures like straw;
in Sītā, Śrī Rāma's beloved and the mother of the world, this is no wonder at all.
ayodhya.141.cau1: Whatever would make Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa happy, that Śrī Rāma did and that he said.
He told ancient stories and tales, and Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā listened in great delight.
ayodhya.141.cau2: Each time Ayodhyā came to Śrī Rāma's mind, tears welled up in his eyes.
Remembering his mother and father, his family and his brothers, and Bharata's love, gentleness and service,
ayodhya.141.cau3: the Lord, ocean of mercy, grew sorrowful, but seeing that the times were hard he held to his patience.
Seeing him so, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa grew troubled, as a shadow follows a man.
ayodhya.141.cau4: Śrī Rāma, steadfast and compassionate, cooling sandal to the hearts of his devotees, saw how it was with his beloved and his brother.
He began to tell some holy stories, and in hearing them Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā found happiness.
ayodhya.141.do141: Śrī Rāma, with Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, looked lovely in the hut of leaves
as Indra lives in the city of the gods with Śacī and Jayanta.
ayodhya.142.cau1: How did the Lord watch over Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa? As the eyelids guard the eyeballs.
And Lakṣmaṇa served Sītā and Śrī Rāma as a man without discernment tends his own body.
ayodhya.142.cau2: So the Lord, the friend of birds and beasts, gods and ascetics, lived happily in the forest.
I have told the lovely tale of Śrī Rāma's going to the forest; now hear how Sumantra came back to Ayodhyā.
ayodhya.142.cau3: Having escorted the Lord, the Niṣāda chief turned back, and on arriving he saw the chariot with the minister.
When he saw how distraught the minister was, the grief that came upon him was beyond words.
ayodhya.142.cau4: Crying out Rāma, Rāma, Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, the minister fell to the ground in deep distress.
The horses looked towards the south and neighed, restless as birds without wings.
ayodhya.142.do142: They would not graze or drink water, and tears ran from their eyes.
Seeing Śrī Rāma's horses so, all the Niṣādas were grieved.
ayodhya.143.cau1: Then the Niṣāda chief steadied himself and said: Sumantra, put away your grief now.
You are learned and know the highest truth. Seeing that fate has turned away, be firm.
ayodhya.143.cau2: Speaking gently to him of many things, he brought him along and made him sit in the chariot against his will.
But Sumantra, faint with grief, could not drive; the pain of parting from Śrī Rāma lay sharp in his heart.
ayodhya.143.cau3: The horses floundered and would not keep to the road, as though wild beasts had been brought and yoked to the chariot.
They stumbled and fell, and turned to look behind them, distressed by the sharp pain of separation from Śrī Rāma.
ayodhya.143.cau4: If anyone spoke the name of Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa or Vaidehī, the horses neighed again and again and looked at him with love.
How can the horses' anguish of separation be told?
They were as distressed as a serpent that has lost its gem.
ayodhya.143.do143: Seeing the minister and the horses, the Niṣāda chief was overcome with sorrow.
Then he called four trusty servants and sent them along with the charioteer.
ayodhya.144.cau1: Guha saw the charioteer off and turned home; his grief at the parting cannot be described.
The Niṣādas set out for Ayodhyā with the chariot, sinking into sorrow moment after moment.
ayodhya.144.cau2: Sumantra, distraught and wretched with grief, thought: Shame on a life without Śrī Rāma.
This base body will not last in the end anyway; it could have won honour by falling the moment he parted from me, and it did not.
ayodhya.144.cau3: This life of mine has become a vessel of disgrace and sin; why does it not depart?
Alas, my dull mind let the moment slip by. Even now my heart does not break in two.
ayodhya.144.cau4: He wrung his hands and beat his head in remorse, as a miser does when his heap of riches is gone.
He went on his way like a warrior who had put on the badge of valour and been hailed a great hero, and then fled the battle.
ayodhya.144.do144: Think of a Brahmin, discerning, learned in the Vedas, esteemed by the good and of noble birth,
who has drunk wine by mistake: such was the minister's anguish.
ayodhya.145.cau1: As a wife of good family, virtuous and wise, who holds her husband as her god in deed, thought and word,
burns when fate forces her to live apart from him, so fierce was the burning in the minister's heart.
ayodhya.145.cau2: His eyes were full of tears and his sight grew dim; his ears did not hear, and his troubled mind was lost.
His lips were parched and his mouth dry; yet life did not leave him, for the appointed term of exile stood as a door across his heart.
ayodhya.145.cau3: He had turned so pale that one could not bear to look at him, as if he had slain his own father and mother.
Loss and remorse weighed heavy on his mind, like the dread of a sinner on the road to the realm of Yama.
ayodhya.145.cau4: No words came to him, and he grieved within: What shall I see when I reach Ayodhyā?
Whoever sees the chariot without Śrī Rāma will be loath to look at me.
ayodhya.145.do145: When the stricken men and women of the city come running to question me,
I shall give every one of them an answer, with a thunderbolt set upon my heart.
ayodhya.146.cau1: All the mothers, forlorn and grieving, will ask me; O Creator, what shall I tell them?
When Lakṣmaṇa's mother asks, what happy message shall I give her?
ayodhya.146.cau2: When Śrī Rāma's mother comes running, like a cow that has lately calved and remembers her young,
I shall answer her question with this: Śrī Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Vaidehī have gone to the forest.
ayodhya.146.cau3: Whoever asks, this is the answer I must give; this is the joy that awaits me now in Ayodhyā.
When the king, broken with grief, whose very life hangs on Śrī Rāma, asks me,
ayodhya.146.cau4: how shall I face him and answer that I have seen the princes safely there and come home?
Hearing what Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā and Śrī Rāma have to say, the king will give up his body as one drops a blade of grass.
ayodhya.146.do146: Mud cracks apart when its beloved water leaves it, but my heart did not break at the parting;
by this I know that the Creator has given me this body only to suffer torment.
ayodhya.147.cau1: So he lamented all along the way, and the chariot soon reached the bank of the Tamasā.
There the minister humbly bade the Niṣādas farewell, and they fell at his feet and turned back, overcome with sorrow.
ayodhya.147.cau2: The minister shrank from entering the city, as though he had killed his teacher, a Brahmin or a cow.
Under a tree he sat out the day, and at evening his chance came.
ayodhya.147.cau3: He entered Ayodhyā in the dark, left the chariot at the gate and went into the palace.
All who heard the news came to the king's gate to see the chariot.
ayodhya.147.cau4: Recognising the chariot and seeing the horses in distress, they wasted away like hailstones in the sun.
How troubled were the men and women of the city? Like fish when the water runs low.
ayodhya.147.do147: As soon as they heard that the minister had come, all the queens' quarters were in turmoil.
To him the palace seemed a place of terror, as if spirits of the dead lived there.
ayodhya.148.cau1: All the queens questioned him in deep distress, but no answer would come; his voice faltered.
His ears did not hear and his eyes saw nothing; to everyone before him he put one question: Tell me, where is the king?
ayodhya.148.cau2: The maids saw the minister's distress and led him to Kausalyā's apartments.
How did Sumantra find the king when he got there? Like the moon without its nectar.
ayodhya.148.cau3: Without seat, bed or ornaments, utterly forlorn, he lay on the bare ground.
Heaving long sighs, he grieved like Yayāti fallen from heaven.
ayodhya.148.cau4: Every moment his breast heaved with grief, like Sampāti fallen with his wings burnt.
The king who so loved Rāma cried Rāma, Rāma, and then again, Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Vaidehī.
ayodhya.148.do148: Seeing him, the minister cried, Victory and long life, and bowed down full length.
Hearing it, the king rose up in distress and said: Sumantra, tell me, where is Rāma?
ayodhya.149.cau1: The king drew Sumantra to his breast, like a drowning man who has found something to hold.
Lovingly he made him sit beside him, and with tears brimming in his eyes the king questioned him:
ayodhya.149.cau2: Dear friend, tell me how Rāma fares. Where are Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Vaidehī?
Have you brought them back, or have they gone on to the forest? At this the minister's eyes filled with tears.
ayodhya.149.cau3: Distraught with grief, the king pressed him again: What message did Sītā, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa send?
Calling to mind again and again Śrī Rāma's beauty, virtues, kindness and nature, the king grieved in his heart.
ayodhya.149.cau4: I told him he would be king and then gave him exile, and hearing it his mind felt neither joy nor sorrow.
Parted from such a son, my life did not leave me; who is so great a sinner as I?
ayodhya.149.do149: Friend, wherever Rāma, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa may be, bring me there too.
Otherwise, I tell you truly, my life is ready to leave me now.
ayodhya.150.cau1: Again and again the king asked the minister: Tell me what my dearest sons said.
Friend, quickly find some way to bring Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā before my eyes.
ayodhya.150.cau2: The minister steadied himself and said gently: Your Majesty, you are learned and wise.
My lord, you are brave, deeply steadfast, foremost among those who bear great burdens, and you have always served the company of the good.
ayodhya.150.cau3: Birth and death, every taste of joy and sorrow, loss and gain, meeting and parting with those we love:
all these, my master, come about under the sway of time and karma, as surely as night and day.
ayodhya.150.cau4: The foolish exult in joy and wail in sorrow, while the steadfast hold the two as one in their minds.
You who do good to all, weigh this with discernment, take heart and let go of grief.
ayodhya.150.do150: The first night's halt was at the Tamasā, the second on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
There the two heroes and Sītā bathed and kept themselves on water alone.
ayodhya.151.cau1: The boatman did them much service, and that night was spent at Śṛṅgaverapura.
At daybreak Śrī Rāma sent for the milky sap of the banyan and with it made of his hair a crown of matted locks.
ayodhya.151.cau2: Then Śrī Rāma's friend had a boat brought. Śrī Rāma helped his beloved aboard and then boarded himself.
Lakṣmaṇa set the bow and arrows in their place and, at the Lord's bidding, came aboard himself.
ayodhya.151.cau3: Seeing me distraught, Śrī Rāma steadied himself and spoke sweet words:
Father, give my father my salutation, and clasp his lotus feet again and again.
ayodhya.151.cau4: Then fall at his feet and plead with him: Father, have no anxiety for me.
On the forest road we are blessed and safe through your grace, your favour and your merit.
ayodhya.151.cha1: By your favour, Father, I shall find every happiness as I go to the forest,
and having carried out your command I shall come back again, safe and well, to see your feet.
Comfort all the mothers, falling at their feet again and again and pleading with them earnestly.
Tulasīdāsa says: make every effort that keeps the lord of Kosala well.
ayodhya.151.so151: Clasp the guru's lotus feet again and again and give him my message:
let him give the king of Avadh such counsel that he does not grieve for me.
ayodhya.152.cau1: Father, entreat all the townspeople and the household and give them my plea:
whoever keeps the king happy is in every way the one who does me good.
ayodhya.152.cau2: When Bharata comes, give him my message: do not forsake right counsel on gaining the throne;
protect the people in deed, mind and word, and serve all the mothers, counting them equal.
ayodhya.152.cau3: And, brother, keep faith with our brotherhood to the end, serving father, mothers and the good.
Dear one, look after the king so that he never grieves over me.
ayodhya.152.cau4: Lakṣmaṇa spoke a few harsh words. Śrī Rāma checked him and then pleaded with me,
and again and again made me swear by him: Father, do not tell of Lakṣmaṇa's boyish rashness.
ayodhya.152.do152: Sītā sent her salutation and began to say something more, but love overcame her;
her words stopped short, tears welled in her eyes, and her whole body thrilled.
ayodhya.153.cau1: At that moment, taking his cue from Śrī Rāma, the boatman pushed the boat off for the far shore.
So the jewel of the Raghu line went away, and I stood there watching, a thunderbolt laid upon my breast.
ayodhya.153.cau2: How can I tell you my own anguish? I have come back alive, bringing Śrī Rāma's message.
With these words the minister's voice broke off, and he was overcome by loss, remorse and grief.
ayodhya.153.cau3: The moment he heard the charioteer's words the king fell to the ground, a terrible burning in his breast.
He writhed, his mind stunned by a fearful swoon, like a fish seized by the froth of the first rains.
ayodhya.153.cau4: All the queens wept and lamented; how could so great a calamity be told?
Hearing their cries, sorrow itself felt sorrow, and patience itself lost its patience.
ayodhya.153.do153: Hearing the cries from the king's palace, a great uproar broke out in Ayodhyā,
as if a hard thunderbolt had fallen at night upon a forest full of birds.
ayodhya.154.cau1: The king's life rose to his throat; he was like a serpent in torment, robbed of its jewel.
All his senses were in great distress, like lotus-clumps in a pond whose water has gone.
ayodhya.154.cau2: Kausalyā saw the king wilting and knew in her heart that the sun of the solar line was on the point of setting.
Then Śrī Rāma's mother gathered her courage and spoke words fitting the hour:
ayodhya.154.cau3: My lord, understand this and weigh it in your mind: parting from Rāma is a shoreless ocean.
You are at the helm of the ship that is Ayodhyā, and all who are dear to us have boarded it as fellow travellers.
ayodhya.154.cau4: If you hold fast to courage, the far shore can be reached; if not, the whole family will drown.
Should you hold my plea in your heart, beloved, Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā will meet us once more.
ayodhya.154.do154: Hearing his beloved's gentle words, the king opened his eyes and looked,
as when cool water is sprinkled on a fish that lies writhing and faint.
ayodhya.155.cau1: Gathering his courage, the king sat up and asked: Sumantra, where is Rāma, the gracious one?
Where is Lakṣmaṇa, where my loving Rāma, and where Vaidehī, my son's dear wife?
ayodhya.155.cau2: Distraught, the king lamented in many ways; the night grew as long as an age and would not end.
He remembered the blind ascetic's curse, and told Kausalyā the whole story.
ayodhya.155.cau3: As he told it he was overcome: Shame on the hope of living without Rāma!
This body did not keep my vow of love: why should I hold on to it?
ayodhya.155.cau4: Alas, delight of the Raghus, dear as my life! Many days have gone by while I live on without you.
Alas, Jānakī! Lakṣmaṇa! Alas, best of the Raghus! Alas, rain-cloud to the cātaka of your father's loving heart!
ayodhya.155.do155: Crying Rāma, Rāma, crying Rāma, then Rāma, Rāma, and Rāma once more,
the king gave up his body in separation from Śrī Rāma and went to the abode of the gods.
ayodhya.156.cau1: Daśaratha won the reward of both living and dying; his spotless fame spread through many universes.
Living, he gazed on Śrī Rāma's moon-like face; and dying of separation from Śrī Rāma, he made his death a thing of beauty.
ayodhya.156.cau2: All the queens, distraught with grief, wept as they recalled his beauty, his goodness, his strength and his splendour.
They lamented in many ways and fell to the ground again and again.
ayodhya.156.cau3: Menservants and maidservants lamented in distress, and in house after house the citizens wept.
Today the sun of the solar dynasty has set, the utmost bound of dharma, the treasury of virtue and beauty.
ayodhya.156.cau4: Everyone heaped abuse on Kaikeyī, who had left the world without its eyes.
