So the night passed in lamentation, and then all the great and wise sages came.
ayodhya.156.do156: Then the sage Vasiṣṭha told many ancient histories suited to the hour,
and with the light of his realised knowledge drove away the grief of all.
ayodhya.157.cau1: He had a boat-shaped vessel filled with oil and the king's body laid in it; then he called the envoys and said:
Hurry, run to Bharata. Say nothing of the king to anyone anywhere.
ayodhya.157.cau2: When you get there, tell Bharata only this: the guru has sent for both brothers.
Hearing the sage's order, the couriers ran off, outstripping the finest horses and shaming them with their speed.
ayodhya.157.cau3: From the time disaster began in Ayodhyā, ill omens had been coming to Bharata.
At night he saw fearful dreams, and when he woke countless bitter fancies filled his mind.
ayodhya.157.cau4: Each day he fed Brahmins and gave gifts, and bathed Śiva's image in worship with many rites.
Praying to Maheśa in his heart, he asked for the welfare of his mother and father, his kin and his brothers.
ayodhya.157.do157: Bharata was brooding in this way when the couriers arrived.
When his ears had taken in the guru's command, he invoked Gaṇeśa and set out.
ayodhya.158.cau1: Bharata drove on with horses swift as the wind, crossing rivers, mountains and trackless forests.
His heart was heavy with care and nothing could please him; he wished in his heart that he could fly there.
ayodhya.158.cau2: Each moment dragged by like a year. So Bharata came close to the city.
As he entered it, ill omens appeared: crows perched in unlucky places cawed harshly.
ayodhya.158.cau3: Donkeys and jackals gave inauspicious cries, and hearing them again and again Bharata's mind was pierced.
Lakes, rivers, woods and gardens had lost their glory, and the city above all looked fearful.
ayodhya.158.cau4: No one could bear to look at the birds and beasts, the horses and elephants; parting from Śrī Rāma had worn them down like a wasting disease.
Women and men in the city were in deep misery, as if every one of them had been robbed of all they had.
ayodhya.158.do158: The townspeople came up to him without a word, quietly made their bow and moved away.
Bharata, his mind gripped by fear and gloom, could not ask them how things stood.
ayodhya.159.cau1: The markets and roads were dreadful to see, as if a forest fire had caught the city on all ten sides.
Hearing that her son was coming, Kaikeyī rejoiced, she who was moonlight to the lotus of the solar race.
ayodhya.159.cau2: She prepared the ārati, rose and hurried out in delight, met him right at the door and led him into the palace.
Bharata saw the family in sorrow, like a lotus grove nipped by frost.
ayodhya.159.cau3: Kaikeyī's joy was that of a Kirāta woman who has set fire to a forest and is glad of it.
Seeing her son troubled and downcast, she asked: Is all well at my parents' home?
ayodhya.159.cau4: Bharata gave her good news of everyone there, then asked how his own house fared:
Tell me, where is Father? Where are all the mothers? Where is Sītā, and where are Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, my dear brothers?
ayodhya.159.do159: Hearing her son's loving words, the sinful woman filled her eyes with false tears
and spoke words that went like a spike into Bharata's ears and heart:
ayodhya.160.cau1: My son, I had arranged it all, and poor Mantharā was a help.
But Fate spoilt the work a little along the way: the king has set foot in the city of Indra.
ayodhya.160.cau2: At these words Bharata was helpless with grief, as an elephant shrinks in fear when a lion roars.
Crying Father, Father, alas, Father, he fell to the ground in utter distress.
ayodhya.160.cau3: I could not even see you as you went, Father, and you did not give me into Śrī Rāma's keeping.
Then, taking heart, he gathered himself and rose, and said: Mother, tell me why Father died.
ayodhya.160.cau4: Hearing her son's words, Kaikeyī began to speak, as though slitting a vital spot and pouring poison in.
Crooked and hard, she described everything she had done, from the start, and took pleasure in the telling.
ayodhya.160.do160: At the news of Śrī Rāma's going to the forest, Bharata forgot that his father had died.
Knowing in his heart that he himself was the cause, he stood stunned and fell silent.
ayodhya.161.cau1: Seeing her son distraught, Kaikeyī set about consoling him, as if rubbing salt into a burn.
Dear son, the king is not one to grieve for: he earned merit and fame and enjoyed their fruits as well.
ayodhya.161.cau2: While he lived he won every fruit that a birth can yield, and at the end he went to the abode of Indra.
Reasoning so, put away your grief, and with all the court about you rule the kingdom of this city.
ayodhya.161.cau3: Hearing this, the prince was badly shaken, as if a live coal had touched a festering wound.
Steadying himself and drawing long sighs, Bharata said: Sinful woman, you have ruined the family in every way.
ayodhya.161.cau4: If you harboured such evil intent, why did you not kill me the moment I was born?
You have cut down the tree to water its leaves, and bailed out the water to keep the fish alive.
ayodhya.161.do161: My line is the solar line, my father is Daśaratha, my brothers are such as Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa;
and you, mother, were the one to become my mother. Against the Creator no one has any power.
ayodhya.162.cau1: When your evil mind resolved on this evil scheme, your heart did not even break in pieces.
Asking for the boons, you felt no pang; your tongue did not rot, nor did worms fill your mouth.
ayodhya.162.cau2: How could the king have put his trust in you? At the hour of his death the Creator took away his judgement.
The workings of a woman's heart were beyond even Brahmā; it is a mine of all deceit, sin and wrong.
ayodhya.162.cau3: The king was guileless, kindly and given to dharma; how was he to know a woman's nature?
In all the world, what living being is there that does not hold Śrī Rāma dear as life?
ayodhya.162.cau4: Even Śrī Rāma seemed to you a bitter enemy. Who are you? Tell me the truth.
Whatever you are, so be it: blacken your face, get up, and go and sit where my eyes cannot see you.
ayodhya.162.do162: The Creator made me come forth from a heart that is hostile to Śrī Rāma.
Who is as great a sinner as I? Whatever I say to you is said in vain.
ayodhya.163.cau1: Śatrughna heard of the mother's crookedness; his whole body burned with anger, and yet he could do nothing.
At that very moment the hunchback Mantharā came in, decked out in all kinds of clothes and jewels.
ayodhya.163.cau2: At the sight of her, Lakṣmaṇa's younger brother Śatrughna was filled with rage, like a blazing fire fed an offering of ghee.
Leaping forward, he took aim and kicked her on the hump; she fell on her face to the ground, crying out.
ayodhya.163.cau3: Her hump broke, her head split, her teeth were smashed and blood poured from her mouth.
Mantharā cried: Alas, O fate, what harm have I done? For doing good I have reaped evil.
ayodhya.163.cau4: At these words Śatrughna, seeing she was rotten from head to toe, took her by the hair again and again and began to drag her along.
Bharata, that treasury of mercy, freed her, and the two brothers went to Kausalyā.
ayodhya.163.do163: Kausalyā was in soiled clothes, her colour gone, distraught, her body worn thin under the weight of sorrow,
like a fine golden wish-granting creeper in the forest blighted by frost.
ayodhya.164.cau1: Seeing Bharata, the mother rose and ran to him, but a swoon came over her and she fell senseless to the ground.
At the sight Bharata was overcome with distress and, forgetting all about himself, fell at her feet.
ayodhya.164.cau2: Bharata said: Mother, where is my father? Let me see him. And Sītā and the two brothers Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, where are they?
Why was Kaikeyī ever born into the world? And if she was born, why was she not barren,
ayodhya.164.cau3: she who bore me, the stain on my family, the vessel of infamy, the betrayer of those I love?
Who in the three worlds is as unlucky as I, because of whom, mother, you have come to such a state?
ayodhya.164.cau4: My father is in heaven, Śrī Rāma in the forest, and I alone, like the baleful Ketu, am the cause of all these calamities.
Shame on me! I was born as the fire in a forest of bamboo, and have earned unbearable burning, sorrow and blame.
ayodhya.164.do164: Hearing Bharata's gentle words, the mother gathered herself and rose again.
She lifted him up and held him to her heart, tears streaming from her eyes.
ayodhya.165.cau1: The mother, simple-hearted, took Bharata to her heart with such love that it was as if Śrī Rāma had returned.
Then she embraced Śatrughna too, the younger brother of Lakṣmaṇa; her heart could not contain its grief and love.
ayodhya.165.cau2: Seeing her nature, everyone said: How could Śrī Rāma's mother be otherwise?
The mother sat Bharata on her lap, wiped away his tears and spoke gentle words:
ayodhya.165.cau3: My child, I would give my life for you; even now take heart; see that the times are hard, and let go of grief.
Knowing that the course of time and karma cannot be turned aside, do not take loss and remorse to heart.
ayodhya.165.cau4: Dear son, do not blame anyone. Fate has turned against me in every way,
keeping me alive even through such sorrow. Who knows, even now, what more it wishes?
ayodhya.165.do165: Dear son, at his father's command Śrī Rāma laid aside his ornaments and robes.
With neither dismay nor joy in his heart, he put on garments of bark.
ayodhya.166.cau1: His face was serene, and in his heart was neither attachment nor anger; having contented everyone in every way,
he set out for the forest. Hearing of it, Sītā went along with him; devoted to Śrī Rāma's feet, she would not stay behind.
ayodhya.166.cau2: As soon as he heard, Lakṣmaṇa too rose and went with them; for all Śrī Rāma's efforts he would not stay.
Then Śrī Rāma bowed his head to all and set out with Sītā and his younger brother.
ayodhya.166.cau3: Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā went away to the forest; I did not go with them, nor did I send my life after them.
Before these eyes of mine all this came to pass, and even then this wretched soul did not quit the body.
ayodhya.166.cau4: Looking at my own love I feel no shame, I, the mother of a son like Rāma.
Of living and dying, it was the king who knew the right way; my heart is as hard as a hundred thunderbolts.
ayodhya.166.do166: At Kausalyā's words the whole of the queens' household, Bharata with them, broke into anguished weeping;
it was as if the royal house had become the home of grief itself.
ayodhya.167.cau1: Both brothers, Bharata and Śatrughna, wept in distress, and Kausalyā drew them to her heart.
She consoled Bharata in many ways, speaking words full of discernment.
ayodhya.167.cau2: Bharata in turn consoled all the mothers, telling them beautiful stories from the Purāṇas and the Vedas.
Then, with folded hands, Bharata spoke in words pure, simple, kind and free of guile:
ayodhya.167.cau3: The sins of killing a mother, a father or a son, of burning down a cow-pen or a town of Brahmins,
the sins of slaying a woman or a child, of giving poison to a friend or to a king,
ayodhya.167.cau4: and all the greater and lesser sins that poets say arise from deed, word and thought:
may those sins, O Creator, fall on me, if this was done with my consent, mother.
ayodhya.167.do167: Those who forsake the feet of Śrī Hari and Śiva to worship the dreadful hosts of spirits:
may the Creator give me their fate, mother, if this had my consent.
ayodhya.168.cau1: Those who sell the Vedas and milk dharma for gain, who carry tales and spread abroad the sins of others,
who are deceitful, crooked, quarrelsome and wrathful, who revile the Vedas and set themselves against the whole world,
ayodhya.168.cau2: the greedy, the lustful, those who live by craving, those who eye another's wealth and another's wife:
may I meet their dreadful end, mother, if this had my approval.
ayodhya.168.cau3: those who have never loved the company of the good, the unfortunate who have turned their backs on the path to the highest good,
those who, though born in a human body, do not worship Śrī Hari, and whom the fair fame of Śrī Hari and Śiva does not please,
ayodhya.168.cau4: those who leave the path of the Vedas to walk the contrary way, the cheats who put on false guises to deceive the world:
may Śiva give me their fate, mother, if I knew anything of this secret.
ayodhya.168.do168: Hearing Bharata's words, true and guileless by nature, the mother said:
Dear son, in word, thought and deed Śrī Rāma has always been dear to you.
ayodhya.169.cau1: Rāma means more to you than life itself, and you are dearer than life to Śrī Rāma.
The moon might drip poison, frost rain down fire, a creature of the water turn away from water,
ayodhya.169.cau2: and delusion might remain even after knowledge has dawned, but you will never turn against Śrī Rāma.
Those in the world who say this was your will shall not find happiness or a blessed end even in a dream.
ayodhya.169.cau3: So saying, the mother held Bharata to her heart; her breasts flowed with milk and tears filled her eyes.
Lamenting much in this way, they sat on until the whole night had passed.
ayodhya.169.cau4: Then came Vāmadeva and Vasiṣṭha, who had all the ministers and the chief men of the city called.
The sage counselled Bharata in many ways, speaking fitting words of the highest truth.
ayodhya.169.do169: Vasiṣṭha said: Dear son, keep your heart steady, and do what today's occasion asks of you.
Bharata rose at his guru's words and bade them prepare all that was needed.
ayodhya.170.cau1: The king's body was bathed as the Vedas prescribe, and a most wonderful bier was built.
Bharata held every mother back by clasping her feet, and the queens lived on, longing to see Śrī Rāma.
ayodhya.170.cau2: Many loads of sandalwood and aloe-wood arrived, with countless lovely fragrances of every kind.
On the bank of the Sarayū a pyre was carefully built, like a lovely stairway to heaven.
ayodhya.170.cau3: Thus all the rites of the cremation were performed, and after bathing in due form the offering of sesame and water was made.
Then, having searched all the Smṛtis, Vedas and Purāṇas, Bharata performed the ten-day rite of Daśagātra.
ayodhya.170.cau4: Wherever the great sage gave an instruction, Bharata carried it all out just so, in a thousand ways.
When he was purified he gave every kind of gift: cows, horses, elephants and conveyances of many kinds,
ayodhya.170.do170: thrones, ornaments, clothes, grain, land, wealth and houses;
all these Bharata gave, and the Brahmins who received them had every wish fulfilled.
ayodhya.171.cau1: What Bharata did for his father's sake could not be told even with a hundred thousand mouths.
Then, having fixed an auspicious day, the great sage Vasiṣṭha came and called together all the ministers and leading citizens.
ayodhya.171.cau2: They all went and took their seats in the royal court, and sent for the two brothers, Bharata and Śatrughna.
Vasiṣṭha seated Bharata near him and spoke words full of right counsel and dharma.
ayodhya.171.cau3: First the great sage told the whole story of what the scheming Kaikeyī had done.
Then he praised the king's vow of dharma and his truthfulness, for he had given up his body to keep faith with his love.
ayodhya.171.cau4: As he spoke of Śrī Rāma's virtues, gentleness and nature, the king of sages' eyes filled with tears and he thrilled all over.
Then, telling of the love of Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, the wise sage was lost in grief and affection.
ayodhya.171.do171: The lord of sages said sorrowfully: Listen, Bharata, destiny is mighty.
Loss and gain, life and death, fame and ill fame all lie in the hands of the Creator.
ayodhya.172.cau1: Seeing this, whom should one blame, and with whom be angry in vain?
Think it over in your mind, dear son: King Daśaratha is not one to be grieved for.
ayodhya.172.cau2: One should grieve for the Brahmin who is without the Vedas and, leaving his own dharma, is sunk in the pleasures of the senses.
One should grieve for the king who does not know right counsel and to whom his subjects are not as dear as life.
ayodhya.172.cau3: One should grieve for the Vaiśya who is wealthy yet miserly, and not skilled in serving guests or in devotion to Śiva.
One should grieve for the Śūdra who slights Brahmins, talks too much, craves honour and is vain of his learning.
ayodhya.172.cau4: One should grieve, too, for the woman who deceives her husband, is crooked, loves quarrels and goes her own way.
One should grieve for the student who abandons his vow and does not follow his guru's commands.
ayodhya.172.do172: One should grieve for the householder who, under the sway of delusion, abandons the path of action.
One should grieve for the ascetic who is caught up in worldly affairs and has lost discernment and dispassion.
ayodhya.173.cau1: That forest hermit is to be grieved for who has left austerity and finds pleasure in enjoyments.
One should grieve for the slanderer who is angry without cause and hostile to mother, father, guru and brothers.
ayodhya.173.cau2: In every way one should grieve for him who harms others, feeds only his own body and is utterly without pity.
And in every way he is to be grieved for who does not give up deceit and become a devotee of Śrī Hari.
ayodhya.173.cau3: The king of Kosala is not to be grieved for; his power is manifest in all the fourteen worlds.
Bharata, there has never been, there is not, nor will there now be a king such as your father.
ayodhya.173.cau4: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Indra and the guardians of the quarters all tell the tale of Daśaratha's virtues.
ayodhya.173.do173: Tell me, dear son, how can anyone praise him enough,
whose pure sons are such as Śrī Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, you and Śatrughna?
ayodhya.174.cau1: The king was fortunate in every way; to mourn for him is in vain.
Hear this, understand it and let go of your grief; take the king's command upon your head and carry it out.
ayodhya.174.cau2: The king has given the throne to you; you must make your father's word come true.
For that word's sake he gave up Śrī Rāma, and in the fire of parting from Śrī Rāma he left his body.
ayodhya.174.cau3: To the king his word was dear, not his life; so, dear son, make your father's word good.
Bow your head to the king's command and carry it out; in that lies your good in every way.
ayodhya.174.cau4: Paraśurāma kept his father's command and killed his mother, as all the worlds bear witness.
Yayāti's son gave his youth to his father; obeying his father's command brought him neither sin nor disgrace.
ayodhya.174.do174: Those who, setting aside all thought of right and wrong, keep their father's word
become worthy of happiness and good fame and dwell in the abode of Indra, lord of the immortals.
ayodhya.175.cau1: Be sure to make the king's word true; protect the people and set grief aside.
The king in heaven will be content, and to you will come merit and good name, not blame.
ayodhya.175.cau2: The Vedas declare it and all agree: the one whom the father appoints receives the tilaka of kingship.
So rule the kingdom, cast off your remorse, and accept my words, knowing them to be for your good.
ayodhya.175.cau3: Śrī Rāma and Sītā will be glad to hear of it, and no learned man will call it wrong.
All the mothers, Kausalyā and the rest, will rejoice as well when the people are happy.
ayodhya.175.cau4: Whoever knows the supreme bond between you and Śrī Rāma will think well of you in every way.
When Śrī Rāma comes back, hand the kingdom over to him and serve him with a fair and loving heart.
ayodhya.175.do175: The ministers said with joined palms: You must surely do as your guru commands.
When Śrī Rāma returns, you can then do whatever is fitting.
ayodhya.176.cau1: Kausalyā, steadying herself, said: My son, your guru's command is wholesome for you.
Honour it and carry it out, knowing it is for your good, and give up your sorrow, knowing the ways of time.
ayodhya.176.cau2: Śrī Rāma is in the forest, the king is in heaven, and you, dear son, lose heart like this.
My son, for the household, the people, the ministers and all your mothers, you alone are the support.
ayodhya.176.cau3: Seeing that fate is against us and the times are hard, take heart; your mother would give her life for you.
Take your guru's command upon your head and follow it; protect the people and take away the sorrow of the household.
ayodhya.176.cau4: Bharata heard the guru's words and the ministers' approval; they were like sandal-paste to his heart, cooling and soothing it.
Then he heard his mother's gentle words, steeped in the sweetness of kindness, love and sincerity.
ayodhya.176.cha1: Hearing his mother's words, steeped in the sweetness of sincerity, Bharata was overcome.
His lotus eyes streamed with tears, watering the new shoots of separation in his heart.
Seeing his state at that time, everyone lost all awareness of their own bodies.
Tulasīdāsa says: all reverently praised him as the very limit of natural love.
ayodhya.176.so176: Bharata, foremost of the steadfast, gathered his courage and joined his lotus hands,
and gave everyone a fitting reply in words that seemed dipped in nectar.
ayodhya.177.cau1: My guru has given me good counsel, and the people, the ministers and everyone agree with it.
My mother, too, has given her command as she thought right, and I truly wish to bow my head to it and carry it out.
ayodhya.177.cau2: The words of a guru, father, mother, master or well-wisher should be heeded with a glad heart, knowing them to be good.
To stop and weigh whether they are right or wrong is to lose dharma and to take a load of sin upon one's head.
ayodhya.177.cau3: You are giving me plain advice, the very kind that will do me good if I follow it.
And though I understand this well, my heart is not at peace.
ayodhya.177.cau4: Now hear my plea and give me counsel that suits my state.
Forgive the fault of my answering you; the good do not count the faults and merits of one in distress.
ayodhya.177.do177: My father is in heaven, Sītā and Śrī Rāma are in the forest, and you tell me to rule.
Do you see my good in this, or some great purpose of your own?
ayodhya.178.cau1: My good lies in serving Sītā's lord, and my mother's cunning has snatched that away.
I have weighed it in my mind and seen that by no other means can good come to me.
ayodhya.178.cau2: Without the sight of the feet of Lakṣmaṇa, Śrī Rāma and Sītā, what is this kingdom, this heap of sorrows, worth?
Ornaments are a useless burden without clothing; reflection on Brahman is useless without dispassion.
ayodhya.178.cau3: To a sick body many pleasures are useless; without devotion to Śrī Hari, japa and yoga go to waste.
A fair body without life is useless; without Śrī Rāma all that I have is useless.
ayodhya.178.cau4: Give me leave to go to Śrī Rāma; in this one thing, beyond doubt, lies my good.
And when you seek your own good by making me king, that too you say under the spell of love's blindness.
ayodhya.178.do178: I am Kaikeyī's son, crooked of mind, turned away from Śrī Rāma and without shame.
Under delusion you hope for happiness from the rule of so low a man as I.
ayodhya.179.cau1: I speak the truth; hear it, all of you, and believe it: a king must be devoted to dharma.
The moment you force the kingdom on me, the earth will sink into the netherworld.
ayodhya.179.cau2: Who is such a home of sin as I, for whose sake Sītā and Śrī Rāma were sent to live in the forest?
The king gave Śrī Rāma the forest, and as he parted from him he went to the city of the immortals.
ayodhya.179.cau3: I, the wretch who am the cause of all this ruin, sit here fully aware and hear it all.
I have seen the house without Śrī Rāma, and borne the world's mockery, and still my life has stayed.
ayodhya.179.cau4: My life has no taste for the holy delight of Śrī Rāma; greedy, it hungers for land and pleasures.
How far can I tell the hardness of my heart, which has outdone even the thunderbolt and won fame for it?
ayodhya.179.do179: An effect is harder than its cause; the fault is not mine.
The thunderbolt, made from bone, and iron, from stone, are fiercer and harder than what they came from.
ayodhya.180.cau1: My base life, clinging to this body born of Kaikeyī, is wretched through and through.
If even in separation from my beloved my life is still dear to me, I shall see and hear much more yet.
ayodhya.180.cau2: Kaikeyī gave the forest to Lakṣmaṇa, Śrī Rāma and Sītā, and did her husband a kindness by sending him to heaven.
She took widowhood and disgrace on herself, and gave the people grief and anguish.
ayodhya.180.cau3: To me she gave happiness, fair fame and a fine kingdom; Kaikeyī has served everyone's ends.
What could be better for me now than this? And on top of it you tell me you will crown me.
ayodhya.180.cau4: Born into the world from Kaikeyī's womb, I find nothing in this unfitting for me.
Fate itself has arranged all my affairs; why then do the people and you elders lend it a hand?
ayodhya.180.do180: A man seized by an evil planet, then struck by a disorder of the wind, and then stung by a scorpion,
is given wine to drink: tell me, what kind of cure is that?
ayodhya.181.cau1: Whatever in the world befits a son of Kaikeyī, that very thing the clever Creator has given me.
The greatness of being Daśaratha's son and Śrī Rāma's younger brother, fate gave me for nothing.
ayodhya.181.cau2: All of you tell me to receive the mark of coronation; the king's command seems good to everyone.
How am I to answer each one of you? Let each speak freely, as he pleases.
ayodhya.181.cau3: Leave aside me and my wicked mother, and tell me: who else will say that good was done here?
In all creation, moving and unmoving, who is there but me to whom Sītā and Śrī Rāma are not dear as life?
ayodhya.181.cau4: What is the utmost loss, everyone takes for a great gain; these are my evil days, and no one is to blame.
You are swayed by doubt, by courtesy and by love; so whatever you say is all fitting.
ayodhya.181.do181: Śrī Rāma's mother is utterly simple of heart and holds me in special love.
Seeing my wretched state, she speaks as her nature moves her, overcome by affection.
ayodhya.182.cau1: The world knows the guru to be an ocean of discernment; to him the whole universe is like a jujube berry in the hand.
Even he is preparing my coronation. When fate turns away, everyone turns away.
ayodhya.182.cau2: Apart from Sītā and Śrī Rāma, no one in the world will say that I did not consent to this.
I shall hear it and bear it and count it a joy; in the end there is mud only where there is water.
ayodhya.182.cau3: I do not fear that the world will call me vile, nor do I care about the world to come.
One unbearable forest fire alone burns in my heart: because of me Sītā and Śrī Rāma have come to grief.
ayodhya.182.cau4: It is Lakṣmaṇa who has truly won life's prize: he gave up all and gave his heart to Śrī Rāma's feet.
My birth was only for Śrī Rāma's exile to the forest; why should I, ill-fated as I am, lament in vain?
ayodhya.182.do182: Bowing my head to you all, I tell you of my dreadful plight:
until I see the feet of Śrī Rāma, the burning of my heart will not leave me.
ayodhya.183.cau1: No other way occurs to me; who but Śrī Rāma can understand what is in my heart?
This one resolve alone is in my mind: at daybreak I shall set out for the Lord.
ayodhya.183.cau2: Though I am wicked and a wrongdoer, and all this calamity has come about because of me,
yet when he sees me before him seeking refuge, he will forgive it all and show me special grace.
ayodhya.183.cau3: Śrī Rāma is gracious, modest and utterly simple of nature, a home of mercy and love.
Śrī Rāma has never harmed even an enemy; and I, perverse though I am, am his child and his servant.
ayodhya.183.cau4: You elders too, seeing my good in this, give me your leave and your blessing in kind words,
so that Śrī Rāma may hear my plea, know me for his servant, and come back to the capital.
ayodhya.183.do183: Though I was born of a wicked mother, and am a rogue, ever full of faults,
I trust that Śrī Rāma, knowing me for his own, will not cast me off.
ayodhya.184.cau1: Bharata's words were dear to all, as though steeped in the nectar of love for Śrī Rāma.
The people, scorched by the cruel poison of separation, woke as if on hearing a mantra with its seed-syllable.
ayodhya.184.cau2: The mothers, the ministers, the guru, and all the men and women of the city were deeply overcome with love.
Praising Bharata again and again, they say: your body is love for Śrī Rāma in visible form.
ayodhya.184.cau3: Dear Bharata, why should you not speak so? You are as dear to Śrī Rāma as his own life.
Any base man who in his folly suspects you because of your mother's crookedness,
ayodhya.184.cau4: that wretch, along with millions of his forebears, will dwell in hell for a hundred kalpas.
The gem does not take on the serpent's sin and faults; rather it draws out poison and burns away sorrow and poverty.
ayodhya.184.do184: Let us go, by all means, to the forest where Śrī Rāma is; Bharata, you have resolved well.
To all who were drowning in an ocean of grief, you have given something to hold on to.
ayodhya.185.cau1: No small joy filled every heart, as the cātaka bird and the peacock rejoice at the sound of thunder.
Seeing this good resolve to set out at dawn, all came to hold Bharata dear as life.
ayodhya.185.cau2: Saluting the sage and bowing to Bharata, all took their leave and went home.
Blessed in the world is Bharata's life, they say as they go, praising his goodness and his love.
ayodhya.185.cau3: They say to one another: a great thing has come about; and all get ready for the journey.
Anyone they ask to stay behind and guard the house feels as though his neck had been struck.
ayodhya.185.cau4: Someone says: let no one be told to stay; who in the world does not want this, the gain of a lifetime?
ayodhya.185.do185: Let them burn, the wealth, the home, the comfort, the friend, the mother, the father and the brother
who will not gladly help a man to turn towards Śrī Rāma's feet.
ayodhya.186.cau1: In house after house people make ready vehicles of every kind, glad at heart to set out at daybreak.
Bharata went home and reflected: the city, the horses and elephants, the palaces and the treasury,
ayodhya.186.cau2: all this wealth belongs to Śrī Rāma. If I go and leave it with no care taken for it,
no good will come to me in the end; betraying one's master is the crown of all sins.
ayodhya.186.cau3: He alone is a servant who does his master good, though someone lay a million faults at his door.
With this in mind he called for trusty servants who had never swerved from their duty even in a dream.
ayodhya.186.cau4: He told them the whole of the matter, set out their duty clearly, and put each to the task he was fit for.
When every arrangement was made and the guards were posted, Bharata went to Śrī Rāma's mother.
ayodhya.186.do186: Bharata, who knew well the ways of love, saw that all the mothers were in distress,
and gave orders to make ready palanquins and to fit out comfortable litters.
ayodhya.187.cau1: Like the cakravāka and his mate, the city's men and women longed for morning, their hearts sorely troubled.
All night they lay awake until the dawn came; then Bharata sent for his wise ministers.
ayodhya.187.cau2: He said: take with you everything for the coronation; the sage will give Śrī Rāma the kingdom in the forest itself.
Go quickly. Hearing this the ministers bowed, and at once had horses, chariots and elephants made ready.
ayodhya.187.cau3: Vasiṣṭha, chief of sages, with Arundhatī and the things for the sacred fire, mounted his chariot and set out first.
Then the Brahmins in their hosts, every one a treasury of austerity and radiance, followed on vehicles of many kinds.
ayodhya.187.cau4: All the people of the city fitted out their vehicles and set off for Citrakūṭa.
The queens, one and all, mounted palanquins too fine for words and went on their way.
ayodhya.187.do187: Having entrusted the city to faithful servants and sent everyone on ahead with honour,
the two brothers, Bharata and Śatrughna, remembered the feet of Śrī Rāma and Sītā and then set out.
ayodhya.188.cau1: Drawn by the longing to see Śrī Rāma, all the men and women went on like elephants and their mates heading for water.
Mindful that Sītā and Śrī Rāma were in the forest, Bharata and his younger brother went on foot.
ayodhya.188.cau2: Seeing their love, the people too were moved to love; they got down and walked, leaving horses, elephants and chariots.
Then Śrī Rāma's mother came near, had her palanquin set down, and spoke in gentle words:
ayodhya.188.cau3: My son, get into the chariot, your mother begs you; else all your dear family will suffer.
If you walk, everyone will walk, and all are worn thin with grief and unfit for the road.
ayodhya.188.cau4: The two brothers took her word upon their heads, bowed low at her feet, climbed into a chariot and went on.
On the first day they halted at the Tamasā; the second halt was on the bank of the Gomatī.
ayodhya.188.do188: Some of the people lived on milk, some on fruit, and some took a single meal at night.
For Śrī Rāma's sake they kept rules and vows, giving up ornaments and pleasures.
ayodhya.189.cau1: They spent the night on the bank of the Saī and moved on at dawn, and all drew near Śṛṅgaverapura.
The Niṣāda chief heard all the news, and with a heavy heart he turned it over in his mind:
ayodhya.189.cau2: For what cause is Bharata going to the forest? There is some deceit in his mind.
If there were no crookedness in his heart, why has he brought an army with him?
ayodhya.189.cau3: He thinks: I shall kill Śrī Rāma and his younger brother, and then rule in comfort with no rival in my way.
Bharata has given no thought to statecraft; then he earned only disgrace, now he will lose his life.
ayodhya.189.cau4: Even if all the gods and demons, warriors every one, were to join together, none could defeat Śrī Rāma in battle.
What wonder that Bharata acts like this? A poisonous creeper does not bear the fruit of nectar.
ayodhya.189.do189: Having weighed this, Guha said to his kinsmen: be on your guard, all of you.
Take the boats in hand and sink them, and let the landing be barred.
ayodhya.190.cau1: Arm yourselves and hold the landings; all of you make every preparation for death.
I shall cross weapons with Bharata face to face, and while I live I shall not let him cross the Gaṅgā.
ayodhya.190.cau2: Death in battle, and on the bank of the Gaṅgā at that, in Śrī Rāma's service, and this body passes in a moment.
Bharata is Śrī Rāma's brother and a king, and I a lowly servant; such a death is won only by great good fortune.
ayodhya.190.cau3: For my master's cause I shall do battle, and make my fame shine bright through all the fourteen worlds.
If I give up my life for Śrī Rāma, both my hands hold sweets of joy.
ayodhya.190.cau4: One who has no place in the company of the good, who has no standing among Śrī Rāma's devotees,
lives in the world for nothing: a weight on the earth, an axe laid to the tree of his mother's youth.
ayodhya.190.do190: The Niṣāda chief, his dejection gone, raised everyone's spirits,
and remembering Śrī Rāma he called at once for his quiver, his bow and his armour.
ayodhya.191.cau1: Guha said: Hurry, brothers, make your gear ready. Hearing Guha's command, no one holds back.
All of them answer gladly: Very well, master; and each fires the other's zeal.
ayodhya.191.cau2: The Niṣādas set off, saluting their chief again and again; all were brave men who relished the clash of battle.
Remembering the sandals of Śrī Rāma's lotus feet, they tied on their quivers and strung their bows.
ayodhya.191.cau3: They put on armoured jackets and set iron helmets on their heads, and make ready their axes, bamboo staves and spears.
Some, highly skilled with shield and broadsword, leap into the air as though they had left the ground behind.
ayodhya.191.cau4: Each having fitted out his own gear and band, they went and saluted Guha, their chief.
Looking at the fine warriors, he judged every one of them fit, and honoured them all, calling each by name.
ayodhya.191.do191: Guha said: Brothers, let there be no failing; a great task lies before me today.
Hearing this, the warriors answered hotly: Hero, do not be anxious.
ayodhya.192.cau1: By Śrī Rāma's glory and by your strength, master, we will leave that army with neither warriors nor horses.
While we live we will not set a foot back; we will strew the earth with headless trunks and heads.
ayodhya.192.cau2: The Niṣāda chief saw that the band was a good one and said: Beat the war drum.
The words were hardly out when someone sneezed on the left; the readers of omens said: The field looks fair.
ayodhya.192.cau3: An old man, weighing the omen, said: Go and meet Bharata; there will be no fight.
Bharata is on his way to win Śrī Rāma back; the omen says there is no hostility here.
ayodhya.192.cau4: Hearing this, Guha said: The old man speaks well; fools act in haste and repent of it.
To come to blows without understanding Bharata's nature and conduct, without knowing him, would do great harm to our own good.
ayodhya.192.do192: Warriors, gather together, all of you, and hold the landing-places; I shall go, meet him and learn his mind.
When I have found out whether he comes as friend, as foe or as neither, I shall come back and act accordingly.
ayodhya.193.cau1: His love will show itself in his natural, gracious bearing; enmity and love do not stay hidden, however one hides them.
So saying, Guha began to make ready gifts, and sent for tubers, roots and fruits, birds and deer.
ayodhya.193.cau2: Porters brought load upon load of fat, full-grown pāṭhīna fish.
With the gifts for the meeting set out, Guha went to meet Bharata, and good omens, the root of all blessing, came his way.
ayodhya.193.cau3: Seeing Vasiṣṭha, chief of sages, from afar, Guha called out his own name and fell prostrate before him.
Knowing him to be dear to Śrī Rāma, the chief of sages blessed him, and told Bharata plainly who he was.
ayodhya.193.cau4: Hearing that this was Śrī Rāma's friend, Bharata left his chariot, got down and went forward, his love welling up.
Guha told him his village, his people and his name, and saluted him with his forehead to the ground.
ayodhya.193.do193: Seeing him lie prostrate, Bharata clasped him to his heart.
It was as if he had met Lakṣmaṇa; his love was more than his heart could hold.
ayodhya.194.cau1: Bharata embraces him with deep love, and the people look on that way of loving with longing.
Cries of Blessed, blessed! go up, the root of all good, and the gods, praising him, rain down flowers.
ayodhya.194.cau2: The gods say: He whom the world and the Veda alike hold low in every way, whose very shadow, if it touches one, calls for a sprinkling of water,
him Śrī Rāma's younger brother takes into his arms, his body thrilling all over as they meet.
ayodhya.194.cau3: Those who so much as yawn saying Rāma, Rāma, are not faced by heaps of sin.
This man Śrī Rāma himself clasped to his heart, and made him, with all his family, a purifier of the world.
ayodhya.194.cau4: When the water of the Karmanāśā falls into the Gaṅgā, tell me, who does not put it on his head?
The world knows that by repeating the Name backwards Vālmīki became equal to Brahman.
ayodhya.194.do194: The Śvapaca, the Śabara, the Khasa and the Yavana, the dull and the lowly, the Kol and the Kirāta,
by saying Rāma become supremely pure and renowned through the worlds.
ayodhya.195.cau1: This is no wonder; it has been so age after age. Whom has Śrī Rāma not raised to greatness?
So the gods tell the glory of Rāma's Name, and the people of Ayodhyā, hearing it again and again, rejoice.
ayodhya.195.cau2: Bharata met Śrī Rāma's friend lovingly and asked after his health, his fortune and his well-being.
Seeing Bharata's gentleness and love, the Niṣāda chief at that moment forgot his own body.
ayodhya.195.cau3: Diffidence, love and joy swelled in his heart; he stood gazing at Bharata without a blink.
Then, steadying himself, he bowed at his feet once more and, with joined palms, lovingly made his humble plea.
ayodhya.195.cau4: Guha said: Having seen your lotus feet, the root of all welfare, I count myself well in past, present and future.
Now, my lord, by your supreme grace, it is well with me and with ten million generations of my line.
ayodhya.195.do195: Weighing my deeds and my birth, and seeing in one's heart the greatness of the Lord,
whoever still does not worship Śrī Rāma's feet is the one in the world whom Fate has cheated.
ayodhya.196.cau1: I am deceitful, cowardly, of evil mind and low birth, outside the pale of the world and the Veda in every way.
Yet from the moment Śrī Rāma made me his own, I have been an ornament of the world.
ayodhya.196.cau2: Seeing his love and hearing his fine, humble words, Bharata's younger brother Śatrughna embraced him in turn.
Then the Niṣāda chief, giving his name in gentle words, respectfully saluted all the queens.
ayodhya.196.cau3: Holding him equal to Lakṣmaṇa, the queens bless him: Live happily for a hundred lakh years.
The men and women of the city looked at the Niṣāda chief and were glad, as if they were looking at Lakṣmaṇa.
ayodhya.196.cau4: They say: He has won the reward of life, for Śrī Rāma folded him in his arms.
Hearing his good fortune so praised, the Niṣāda chief, overjoyed at heart, led them all on.
ayodhya.196.do196: He signalled to all his servants, and they went off, taking their master's cue,
and made lodgings ready in houses, under trees, by lakes, in gardens and in groves.
ayodhya.197.cau1: When Bharata saw Śṛṅgaverapura, all his limbs went weak with love.
Leaning on the Niṣāda chief, he looked as though Humility and Love had taken bodily form.
ayodhya.197.cau2: So Bharata, the whole army with him, went on and beheld the Gaṅgā, purifier of the world.
He bowed to Rāma's landing-place, and his heart was as rapt as if he had met Śrī Rāma himself.
ayodhya.197.cau3: The men and women of the city bow, rejoicing as they gaze on the water that is Brahman itself.
After bathing they ask with joined palms for love of Śrī Rāma's feet, and no small love.
ayodhya.197.cau4: Bharata said: River of the gods, your very sands give joy to all and are a wish-granting cow to your servants.
With joined palms I ask this boon: a natural love for the feet of Sītā and Śrī Rāma.
ayodhya.197.do197: In this way Bharata bathed and received his guru's leave;
then, knowing that all the mothers had bathed, he led them to the camp.
ayodhya.198.cau1: The people camped here and there, and Bharata saw to the needs of everyone.
Having worshipped the gods and received leave, the two brothers went to Śrī Rāma's mother.
ayodhya.198.cau2: Pressing their feet and speaking gentle words again and again, Bharata showed honour to all the mothers.
Then he left the mothers' care to his brother and himself called the Niṣāda chief.
ayodhya.198.cau3: He walked with his hand in his friend's, his body faint, for his love was no small thing.
He asks his friend: Show me that place, so that I may cool a little the burning of my eyes and heart.
ayodhya.198.cau4: The place where Sītā, Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa slept that night. At these words the corners of his eyes brimmed with tears.
Hearing Bharata's words, the Niṣāda chief was filled with grief, and took him there at once.
ayodhya.198.do198: Where Śrī Rāma had rested beneath the holy śiṃśapā tree,
there Bharata, with deep love and reverence, fell prostrate.
ayodhya.199.cau1: Seeing the lovely bed of kuśa grass, he walked round it and bowed to it.
He touched the dust of the footprints to his eyes; the fullness of his love is beyond telling.
ayodhya.199.cau2: He saw a few specks of gold there and set them on his head, holding them as dear as Sītā herself.
With tears in his eyes and anguish in his heart, he speaks to his friend in gentle words:
ayodhya.199.cau3: Parted from Sītā, these have lost their beauty and their lustre, as the men and women of Ayodhyā have faded.
Her father is Janaka: with whom can I compare him, who holds in his palm both the world's enjoyment and yoga?
ayodhya.199.cau4: Her father-in-law was King Daśaratha, sun of the solar line, whom even Indra, lord of Amarāvatī, envied.
The lord of her life is her master Śrī Rāma, by whose greatness alone anyone who is great becomes great.
ayodhya.199.do199: Even as I look on the bed of Sītā, jewel of noble wives who hold their husband as their god,
my heart does not shudder and break apart; O Śiva, it is harder even than the thunderbolt.
ayodhya.200.cau1: Lakṣmaṇa, young and lovely, was made to be cherished; no brother like him has ever been, or is, or ever will be.
He is beloved of the townsfolk, the darling of his father and mother, and dear as life to Sītā and Śrī Rāma.
ayodhya.200.cau2: His form is gentle and his nature tender; my friend, not even a breath of wind ever touched his body.
He is enduring every kind of hardship in the forest; this breast of mine has put ten million thunderbolts to shame.
ayodhya.200.cau3: By his birth Śrī Rāma brought light to the world; he is an ocean of beauty, goodness, joy and every virtue.
Townsfolk and household, guru, father and mother: to all of them Śrī Rāma's nature brings joy.
ayodhya.200.cau4: Even his enemies praise Śrī Rāma; his way of speaking, his way of meeting and his humility win their hearts.
Ten million Sarasvatīs and a thousand million Śeṣas could not reckon up the host of the Lord's virtues.
ayodhya.200.do200: He who is joy itself, the jewel of the Raghu line, the treasury of blessing and delight,
sleeps on kuśa grass spread on the bare ground. The workings of Fate are mighty indeed.
ayodhya.201.cau1: Śrī Rāma never heard of sorrow even with his ears; the king tended him as one tends the tree of life.
As the eyelids guard the eyes and a serpent guards its gem, so all the mothers watched over him day and night.
ayodhya.201.cau2: And he now roams the woods on foot, eating bulbs, roots, fruits and flowers.
Shame on Kaikeyī, the root of all ill! You turned against the one dearest to you as life.
ayodhya.201.cau3: Shame, shame on me, an ocean of sin and ill-starred, for whose sake all this calamity came about.
The Creator made me a stain on the family, and a wicked mother made me a traitor to my lord.
ayodhya.201.cau4: Hearing this, the Niṣāda chief consoled him lovingly: My lord, why grieve in vain?
You are dear to Śrī Rāma and Śrī Rāma is dear to you; that much is certain, and the fault lies with the Creator, who has turned adverse.
ayodhya.201.cha1: When the Creator turns adverse, his doing is harsh: it was he who made your mother lose her senses.
That very night the Lord spoke of you again and again with praise and respect.
Tulasīdāsa says: no one is as dear to Śrī Rāma as you are; I say it on oath.
Know that the outcome will be good, and bring patience into your heart.
ayodhya.201.so201: Śrī Rāma knows every heart; he is considerate and loving, an abode of grace.
Come now and rest; think on this and make your mind firm.
ayodhya.202.cau1: Hearing his friend's words, Bharata took heart and went to his lodging, remembering Śrī Rāma.
When they heard of it, the men and women of the city, deeply distressed, went to see the place.
ayodhya.202.cau2: They walked round it, bowed down, and heaped blame on Kaikeyī.
Again and again their eyes filled with tears, and they blamed the Creator who had turned against them.
ayodhya.202.cau3: Some praised Bharata's love; others said the king had been true to his love.
Praising the Niṣāda chief, they spoke ill of themselves; no one could put into words the bewilderment and sorrow of that hour.
ayodhya.202.cau4: So all the people stayed awake through the night. At daybreak the ferrying began.
The guru was seated in a fine boat, and all the mothers in handsome new boats.
ayodhya.202.cau5: In four daṇḍas (about an hour and a half) all were across; then Bharata landed and saw to everyone.
ayodhya.202.do202: Bharata performed the morning rites, saluted the feet of his mothers and bowed before the guru;
then he sent the bands of Niṣādas ahead and started the army on its march.
ayodhya.203.cau1: The Niṣāda chief went ahead to lead the way, and all the mothers' palanquins were set going.
Bharata called his younger brother and sent him with them; the guru set out with the Brahmins.
ayodhya.203.cau2: Bharata himself bowed to the Gaṅgā and remembered Sītā and Śrī Rāma, with Lakṣmaṇa.
He went on foot, and the horses went alongside, riderless, led by the rein.
ayodhya.203.cau3: His faithful servants said again and again: My lord, please mount a horse.
Bharata said: Śrī Rāma went on his own two feet; were chariots, elephants and horses made for me?
ayodhya.203.cau4: It would befit me to go walking on my head; a servant's dharma is the hardest of all.
As they saw Bharata's state and heard his gentle words, every one of the servants sank down in shame.
ayodhya.203.do203: In the third watch of the day Bharata entered Prayāga,
saying Rāma Siya, Rāma Siya, as his love welled up again and again.
ayodhya.204.cau1: The blisters on his feet glistened like drops of dew in the cup of a lotus.
Hearing that Bharata had come on foot that day, the whole company was saddened.
ayodhya.204.cau2: When he had learned that all the people had bathed, he came to the Triveṇī and bowed to it.
He bathed with due rites in the white and dark waters, gave gifts and honoured the Brahmins.
ayodhya.204.cau3: At the sight of the waves, dark and white, Bharata thrilled all over and joined his palms.
O king of holy places, you grant every wish; the Vedas tell of your power, and the world sees it plainly.
ayodhya.204.cau4: Setting aside my own dharma, I beg alms of you; what wrong will one in distress not do?
Knowing this in their hearts, wise and generous givers in this world grant what the beggar asks.
ayodhya.204.do204: Wealth, dharma, pleasure: I care for none of them, nor do I ask for the state of nirvāṇa.
This alone is the boon I ask, and no other: love for Śrī Rāma's feet in birth after birth.
ayodhya.205.cau1: Śrī Rāma may count me false, and people may name me traitor to guru and master;
yet may my love for the feet of Sītā and Śrī Rāma increase from day to day, by your favour.
ayodhya.205.cau2: The cloud may forget the cātaka all its life, and when asked for water hurl thunderbolts and hailstones;
yet if the cātaka's cry grows less, it is the cātaka that is lessened, and if its love grows, that is good in every way.
ayodhya.205.cau3: As gold takes on lustre in the fire, so one who keeps his vow to the beloved's feet comes to shine.
The Triveṇī heard Bharata's words, and from its midst came a gentle voice that brought great blessing:
ayodhya.205.cau4: Bharata, dear son, you are a true saint in every way, and there is no fathoming your love for Śrī Rāma's feet.
This remorse in your mind is needless; to Śrī Rāma no one is as dear as you.
ayodhya.205.do205: At the Triveṇī's kindly words Bharata thrilled all over and his heart was glad.
The gods, delighted, cried that Bharata was blessed, blessed, and rained down flowers.
ayodhya.206.cau1: The dwellers of Prayāga, king of holy places, were overjoyed: hermits, young students, householders and renunciants.
Gathering in tens and fives, they said to one another: Bharata's love and goodness are pure and true.
ayodhya.206.cau2: Listening to the many lovely virtues of Śrī Rāma, Bharata came to the great sage Bharadvāja.
Seeing him stretched full length in obeisance, the sage felt that his own good fortune had taken bodily shape.
ayodhya.206.cau3: The sage ran to raise him and held him to his heart; he blessed him and made his life fulfilled.
He gave him a seat; Bharata bowed his head and sat, as if longing to run and hide in the house of shyness.
ayodhya.206.cau4: His great fear was that the sage would ask him something. Seeing his modesty and diffidence, the seer said:
Listen, Bharata, we have heard everything; against what the Creator does, no one has any power.
ayodhya.206.do206: Do not let remorse fill your heart, thinking of what your mother did.
Dear son, the fault is not Kaikeyī's; Sarasvatī led her mind astray and went her way.
ayodhya.207.cau1: Yet no one will call it right even to say this, for the wise hold by both the world's way and the Veda.
Dear son, by singing your spotless fame both the world and the Veda will gain in glory.
ayodhya.207.cau2: All say what the world and the Veda agree upon: the one to whom the father gives the kingdom receives it.
Had the truth-vowed king called you and given you the kingdom, it would have brought happiness, dharma and honour.
ayodhya.207.cau3: Śrī Rāma's going to the forest is the root of the calamity; hearing of it, the whole world was in anguish.
That came about by destiny; the foolish queen did wrong and in the end repented of it too.
ayodhya.207.cau4: Whoever says that even in this there is the least fault of yours is base, ignorant and wicked.
If you had ruled, you would have been blameless, and the news would only have pleased Śrī Rāma.
ayodhya.207.do207: Now, Bharata, you have done very well; this resolve is the right one for you.
In this world the root of every blessing is love for Śrī Rāma's feet.
ayodhya.208.cau1: That love is your wealth, your life and your breath; who is as fortunate as you?
This is no wonder in you, dear son, the son of Daśaratha and Śrī Rāma's beloved brother.
ayodhya.208.cau2: Listen, Bharata: in Śrī Rāma's heart there is no one so dear as you.
Lakṣmaṇa, Śrī Rāma and Sītā love you deeply; the whole night was spent in praising you.
ayodhya.208.cau3: I learned the secret when they bathed at Prayāga: they were lost in love for you.
Śrī Rāma's love for you is like a dull man's clinging to a happy life in the world.
ayodhya.208.cau4: Nor does this add much to Śrī Rāma's praise: he protects and sustains the whole family of anyone who bows to him.
But you, Bharata, in my view, are love for Śrī Rāma itself in bodily form.
ayodhya.208.do208: For you, Bharata, this is a stain; for all of us it is a lesson.
For the perfecting of the joy of devotion to Śrī Rāma, this hour has become a Gaṇeśa, the auspicious beginning.
ayodhya.209.cau1: Dear son, your spotless fame is a moon of a new kind, and Śrī Rāma's servants are its night-lotuses and cakora birds.
It is always risen and will never set; in the sky of the world it will not wane, but grow twofold day by day.
ayodhya.209.cau2: The three worlds, like the cakravāka bird, will love it dearly, and the sun of the Lord's glory will not dim its beauty.
Night and day it will always give joy to all, and Kaikeyī's deed, a Rāhu, will never eclipse it.
ayodhya.209.cau3: It is full of the nectar of pure love for Śrī Rāma, and no taint of dishonouring the guru mars it.
Now let Śrī Rāma's devotees drink their fill of this nectar; you have made nectar easy to find even on earth.
ayodhya.209.cau4: King Bhagīratha brought down the Gaṅgā, the mere remembrance of whom is a mine of every blessing.
Daśaratha's many virtues are beyond telling; there is none in the world to equal him, let alone surpass him.
ayodhya.209.do209: Bound by his love and his regard, Śrī Rāma came and was made manifest:
Śrī Rāma, whom Śiva has never tired of gazing on with the eyes of his heart.
ayodhya.210.cau1: You have made a peerless moon of fame, on which love for Śrī Rāma dwells as the deer-mark.
Dear son, it is for nothing that you feel remorse in your heart; you have found the philosopher's stone and still fear poverty.
ayodhya.210.cau2: Listen, Bharata, we speak no untruth: we stand apart from the world, we live by austerity, and our dwelling is the forest.
We have gained the fair fruit of every spiritual practice: the sight of Lakṣmaṇa, Śrī Rāma and Sītā.
ayodhya.210.cau3: And the fruit of that fruit is the sight of you: great is our fortune, and Prayāga's with it.
Blessed are you, Bharata; your fame has won the world. So saying, the sage was lost in love.
ayodhya.210.cau4: Hearing the sage's words, all in the assembly rejoiced; the gods cried Well done! in praise and showered flowers.
Cries of Blessed, blessed! rang out in the sky and through Prayāga; hearing them again and again, Bharata was lost in love.
ayodhya.210.do210: Thrilled all over, with Śrī Rāma and Sītā in his heart and his lotus eyes full of tears,
he bowed to the gathering of sages and, his voice breaking with feeling, said:
ayodhya.211.cau1: Before this assembly of sages and in Prayāga, king of holy places, even a true oath is a grave wrong.
If anything made up were said in this place, there could be no sin or baseness greater than that.
ayodhya.211.cau2: You know all things, and I speak from a sincere heart; and Śrī Rāma dwells within the heart and knows it.
I am not troubled by what my mother did, nor grieved at heart that the world will think me vile.
ayodhya.211.cau3: I have no fear that my next world will be ruined, nor do I grieve even for my father's death.
His merit and fair fame fill the worlds with their beauty; he won sons like Lakṣmaṇa and Śrī Rāma.
ayodhya.211.cau4: He gave up his fleeting body in separation from Śrī Rāma; what cause is there to grieve for the king?
Śrī Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, with nothing on their feet and in the garb of hermits, wander from forest to forest.
ayodhya.211.do211: Deerskin is their clothing and fruit their food; they sleep on the ground on a bed of kuśa grass and leaves,
and living under the trees they bear cold, heat, rain and wind day after day.
ayodhya.212.cau1: The burning of this grief scorches my breast day after day; I have no hunger by day, no sleep at night.
No medicine exists for this cruel sickness; in my mind I have searched the whole universe.
ayodhya.212.cau2: My mother's evil design is the carpenter, the root of sin; out of our own good it made its adze.
From the bad wood of discord it shaped an evil charm, and buried it, chanting over it the harsh spell of the fixed term.
ayodhya.212.cau3: For my sake she set up this evil scheme and scattered the whole world to ruin.
This evil conjunction will pass, and Ayodhyā be peopled again, when Śrī Rāma comes back, and not otherwise.
ayodhya.212.cau4: Hearing Bharata's words the sage was glad, and everyone praised him in many ways.
The sage said: Dear son, do not grieve so much; all sorrow will end when you see Śrī Rāma's feet.
ayodhya.212.do212: Having comforted him, the great sage said: Be our guests, dear to us in love.
Accept with affection the tubers, roots, fruits and flowers that we offer.
ayodhya.213.cau1: Bharata's heart grew uneasy at the sage's words; it was an ill-timed moment, and a hard scruple arose.
Then, knowing that his guru's word carried weight, he bowed at his feet and spoke with joined palms:
ayodhya.213.cau2: To take your command on my head and carry it out is, my lord, our highest dharma.
Bharata's words pleased the great sage; he called his pure-hearted servants and disciples to him.
ayodhya.213.cau3: Bharata must be given hospitality; go and bring tubers, roots and fruits.
Saying, Very well, my lord, they bowed their heads and went off gladly, each to his own task.
ayodhya.213.cau4: The sage was concerned: he had invited a great guest, and as the deity is, so must the worship be.
Hearing this, the Riddhis and the Siddhis, Aṇimā and the rest, came and said: Whatever you command, master, we will do.
ayodhya.213.do213: Bharata, with his younger brother and all his company, is distraught at parting from Śrī Rāma.
Receive them as guests and take away their weariness: so the glad king of sages said.
ayodhya.214.cau1: The Riddhis and Siddhis took the great sage's word on their heads and counted themselves most fortunate.
Together the Siddhis said among themselves: Śrī Rāma's younger brother is a guest without equal.
ayodhya.214.cau2: Let us bow at the sage's feet and do today what will make the whole royal company happy.
So saying, they built fine dwellings of many kinds, at whose sight even the aerial cars of heaven pine with envy.
ayodhya.214.cau3: They stocked them with abundant comforts and riches, at the sight of which the immortals were filled with longing.
Maids and menservants held every requisite ready and kept careful watch, their minds given wholly to the minds of those they served.
ayodhya.214.cau4: In a moment the Siddhis furnished it all, with joys not found in heaven even in a dream.
First of all they gave everyone lodgings, lovely and pleasant, each to his own liking.
ayodhya.214.do214: Then Bharata and his household were given theirs, for such was the sage's command.
Such was the splendour the great sage raised by the strength of his austerity that it would leave even Brahmā amazed.
ayodhya.215.cau1: When Bharata saw what the sage's power could do, every realm of the world's guardians seemed small to him.
No words can tell that array of delights; a wise man seeing it might forget his dispassion.
ayodhya.215.cau2: There were seats, beds, fine clothes and canopies, woods and gardens, and birds and beasts of many kinds;
fragrant flowers, fruits like nectar, and clear pools of every design.
ayodhya.215.cau3: The food and drink were pure, like the very nectar of nectar; seeing them, the people held back like men under vows of restraint.
At every lodging stood the cow of the gods and the wish-granting tree, and seeing them even Indra and Śacī longed for them.
ayodhya.215.cau4: It was spring; the threefold breeze was blowing, cool, gentle and fragrant, and the four aims of life were within easy reach of all.
Seeing garlands, sandalwood, women and other pleasures, the people were overcome by joy and wonder.
ayodhya.215.do215: Wealth was the female cakavā bird, Bharata the male, and the sage's command the keeper at play;
it held the two together through that night in the hermitage's cage, and so day broke.
ayodhya.216.cau1: Bharata bathed in Prayāga, king of holy places, and with all his company bowed his head to the sage.
Taking the sage's leave and blessing on his head, he fell prostrate before him and spoke many humble words.
ayodhya.216.cau2: Taking everyone along with men skilled in the road, they set out, their hearts fixed on Citrakūṭa.
With his hand on Śrī Rāma's friend Guha, he walks like love itself in bodily form.
ayodhya.216.cau3: There is nothing on his feet, no shade over his head; his love, his observances, his vow and his dharma are without guile.
He asks his friend the tale of the journey of Lakṣmaṇa, Śrī Rāma and Sītā, and Guha tells it in gentle words.
ayodhya.216.cau4: When he sees the places where Śrī Rāma stayed and the trees there, the love in his heart will not be held back.
At the sight of his state the gods shower flowers; the ground turned soft, and the way became a root of all that is auspicious.
ayodhya.216.do216: Clouds go along giving shade, and a sweet, pleasant breeze blows.
The way had not been such for Śrī Rāma as it became for Bharata as he went.
ayodhya.217.cau1: Along the way were countless beings, moving and unmoving; those who had looked on the Lord, and those on whom the Lord had looked,
had all become fit for the supreme state; now the sight of Bharata cured them of the disease of worldly existence.
ayodhya.217.cau2: For Bharata, whom Śrī Rāma himself remembers in his mind, this is nothing great.
Whoever in the world utters the name Rāma even once becomes one who crosses over and carries others across.
ayodhya.217.cau3: Bharata is dear to Śrī Rāma, and his younger brother besides; how could the road not bring him blessings?
So say the siddhas, saints and great sages, and gazing on Bharata they rejoice at heart.
ayodhya.217.cau4: Seeing Bharata's power, Indra grew anxious; to the good the world looks good, to the bad it looks bad.
He said to his guru: My lord, do something so that Śrī Rāma and Bharata do not meet.
ayodhya.217.do217: Śrī Rāma is full of scruple and ruled by love, and Bharata is an ocean of love.
The thing that was achieved is about to be spoilt; search out some trick and find a way.
ayodhya.218.cau1: Hearing these words, Bṛhaspati, the guru of the gods, smiled; he saw that the thousand-eyed one had no eyes.
He said: If anyone works māyā on a servant of the Lord of māyā, O king of the gods, it turns back on the one who works it.
ayodhya.218.cau2: That time, something was done knowing Śrī Rāma's wish; now any foul play will only bring harm.
Listen, Indra, to Śrī Rāma's nature: he is never angered by an offence against himself.
ayodhya.218.cau3: But whoever wrongs his devotee burns in the fire of Śrī Rāma's wrath.
The accounts of it are known in the world and in the Veda; Durvāsā knows this greatness well.
ayodhya.218.cau4: Who loves Śrī Rāma as Bharata does? The world repeats the name of Rāma, and Śrī Rāma repeats his.
ayodhya.218.do218: Lord of the immortals, do not let even a thought of harming a devotee of Śrī Rāma into your mind;
such a thought earns disgrace here and sorrow hereafter, and a load of grief that grows day by day.
ayodhya.219.cau1: Listen, Indra, to my counsel: to Śrī Rāma his servant is supremely dear.
He takes joy in service done to his servant, and counts enmity to his servant as the greater enmity.
ayodhya.219.cau2: Though he is the same to all, with no attachment or anger in him, and sin and merit, virtue and fault do not cling to him,
he has set action at the head of the world, and as one acts, so is the fruit one tastes.
ayodhya.219.cau3: Even so, he deals evenly with one and unevenly with another, as the heart of devotee or non-devotee may be.
Śrī Rāma, beyond all attributes, stainless, free of pride and ever the same, became the Lord with form because his devotees' love held him.
ayodhya.219.cau4: Always Śrī Rāma has kept to what his servant wishes; the Vedas, the Purāṇas, saints and gods are witness to it.
Knowing this in your heart, leave your crooked ways, and foster a fair love for Bharata's feet.
ayodhya.219.do219: Devotees of Śrī Rāma are bent on the good of others; another's pain is their pain, and they are kind.
Bharata is foremost among devotees: guardian of the gods, have no fear of him.
ayodhya.220.cau1: The Lord keeps his promises and seeks the good of the gods; Bharata walks by Śrī Rāma's command.
You are distraught, swayed by self-interest; the fault is not Bharata's but your own delusion.
ayodhya.220.cau2: At the noble words of the gods' guru, joy filled the mind of the best of the gods, and his dejection passed.
Rejoicing, the king of the gods rained flowers and began to praise Bharata's nature.
ayodhya.220.cau3: So Bharata goes on along the road; seeing his state, sages and siddhas long for it.
Whenever he sighs out the name Rāma, love seems to well up on every side.
ayodhya.220.cau4: Hearing his words, thunderbolt and stone would melt; the love of the townspeople is beyond telling.
After a halt on the way they reached the Yamunā; at the sight of its water their eyes filled with tears.
ayodhya.220.do220: Seeing the lovely water, the very colour of Śrī Rāma, Bharata and all his company
were sinking in the ocean of separation, but climbed aboard the ship of discernment.
ayodhya.221.cau1: That day they camped by the Yamunā, and all had such comfort as the time allowed.
That very night boats came from ghat after ghat, countless beyond telling.
ayodhya.221.cau2: At dawn all crossed in a single passage, well pleased with the service of Śrī Rāma's friend.
Having bathed and bowed their heads to the river, the two brothers set out with the lord of the Niṣādas.
ayodhya.221.cau3: In front go the great sages on fine mounts, and the whole royal train follows behind them.
After it come the two brothers on foot, their ornaments, clothes and dress utterly plain.
ayodhya.221.cau4: With them go servants, friends and the minister's son, keeping Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā and Śrī Rāma in remembrance.
Wherever Śrī Rāma had stayed or rested, there they bow down in love.
ayodhya.221.do221: The men and women who live along the road, hearing of it, leave house and work and run out.
Seeing their beauty and their love, all rejoice, for they have won the reward of being born.
ayodhya.222.cau1: Lovingly the women say to one another: Friend, can these be Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, or are they not?
They have the same years, the same build, colouring and looks, friend; the same goodness and warmth, and the very same gait.
ayodhya.222.cau2: But, friend, theirs is not that dress, nor is Sītā with them, and an army of four arms marches ahead of them.
Their faces are not glad and there is sorrow in their hearts; friend, it is this difference that makes me doubt.
ayodhya.222.cau3: Her reasoning won over the women's minds, and they all said that none was as shrewd as she.
Then another woman praised her, honoured her words as true, and spoke in sweet words.
ayodhya.222.cau4: Lovingly she told the whole story of how the joy of Śrī Rāma's crowning was spoilt.
Then that fortunate woman began to praise Bharata's goodness, his love and his nature.
ayodhya.222.do222: Walking on foot, eating only fruit, having left the kingdom his father gave him,
Bharata is going to win Śrī Rāma back: who today is his equal?
ayodhya.223.cau1: Bharata's love for his brother, his devotion and his conduct take away sorrow and fault from all who tell of them or hear of them.
Whatever I say of him, friend, falls short; how should Śrī Rāma's brother be other than this?
ayodhya.223.cau2: Having seen Bharata with his younger brother, all of us are now counted among blessed women.
As they hear of his virtues and see the state he is in, they grieve: Such a son is not fit for a mother like Kaikeyī.
ayodhya.223.cau3: One said: The queen is not to blame; it is all the work of the Creator, who has been kind to us.
For what are we? Women without the rules of the world or of the Vedas, lowly, of humble birth and unclean deeds,
ayodhya.223.cau4: humble women who live in a poor land, in a poor village; and how far beyond such as us is this sight, the fruit of merit!
In every village there was such joy and wonder, as though a wishing tree had sprung up in a desert.
ayodhya.223.do223: The moment they saw Bharata, the fortune of the people along the way opened up,
as though, by a turn of fate, the dwellers of Siṃhala had found Prayāga at their door.
ayodhya.224.cau1: Hearing the tale of Śrī Rāma's virtues, and of his own with it, Bharata goes on his way with Śrī Rāma in remembrance.
At the sight of holy places, hermitages of sages and temples of the gods, he bathes and bows down.
ayodhya.224.cau2: Within his heart he asks one boon: love for the lotus feet of Sītā and Śrī Rāma.
He meets Kirātas, Kols and other people of the forest, hermits of the third stage of life, young brahmacārins, ascetics and men detached from the world.
ayodhya.224.cau3: Bowing to each he meets, he asks in which forest Lakṣmaṇa, Śrī Rāma and Vaidehī are.
They give him every word of news about the Lord, and in seeing Bharata they win the reward of their birth.
ayodhya.224.cau4: Those who tell him they saw them safe and well he holds as dear as Śrī Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
So, asking everyone with gentle words and hearing the story of Śrī Rāma's life in the forest,
ayodhya.224.do224: he halted there that day and set out at daybreak, remembering Śrī Rāma.
All who were with him longed for the sight of Śrī Rāma as Bharata did.
ayodhya.225.cau1: Auspicious omens come to everyone; eyes and arms throb, foretelling joy.
Bharata and all his company are full of eager hope: Śrī Rāma will be found, and the burning of grief will be over.
ayodhya.225.cau2: Each forms such hopes as are in his heart, and all go on drunk with the wine of love.
Their limbs are slack, their feet stumble on the road, and overcome by love they speak in faltering words.
ayodhya.225.cau3: At that moment Śrī Rāma's friend showed them the crest-jewel of mountains, lovely by its very nature,
close to which the two heroes live with Sītā beside the Payasvinī river.
ayodhya.225.cau4: Seeing it, all fall prostrate, crying: Glory to Śrī Rāma, the life of Jānakī.
The royal company is so lost in love, it is as if the king of the Raghus were already on his way back to Ayodhyā.
ayodhya.225.do225: Bharata's love at that hour was such that not even Śeṣa could tell it.
It is beyond the poet's reach, as the bliss of Brahman is beyond those stained by I and mine.
ayodhya.226.cau1: All were slackened by love for Śrī Rāma, and by the time the sun sank they had gone only two kos.
Finding water and level ground they halted, and when the night was over, Śrī Rāma's beloved Bharata moved on.
ayodhya.226.cau2: Meanwhile Śrī Rāma woke while some of the night still remained. Sītā had seen a dream:
it seemed that Bharata had come with all his company, their bodies burning in the fire of separation from their lord.
ayodhya.226.cau3: All were downcast, humbled and in sorrow, and her mothers-in-law looked other than themselves.
Sītā's dream brought tears to Śrī Rāma's eyes, and the releaser from care fell under care.
ayodhya.226.cau4: He said: Lakṣmaṇa, no good will come of this dream; someone will bring us harsh and evil tidings.
With these words he bathed with his brother, worshipped Śiva, the foe of Tripura, and honoured the holy men.
ayodhya.226.cha1: Having honoured the gods and saluted the sages, he sat down and looked towards the north.
There was dust in the sky, and birds and beasts in great numbers fled in alarm to the Lord's hermitage.
Tulasīdāsa says: seeing this, the Lord rose, wondering what the cause could be, and stood startled at heart.
Just then Kirātas and Kols arrived and gave him the whole report.
ayodhya.226.so226: As he heard the joyful tidings his heart filled with delight and his body thrilled all over.
Tulasīdāsa says: his eyes, like lotuses of autumn, filled with tears of love.
ayodhya.227.cau1: Then Sītā's lord grew anxious again: what could be the reason for Bharata's coming?
Then someone came and said further: With him is an army of four arms, and no small one.
ayodhya.227.cau2: Hearing this, Śrī Rāma was deeply troubled: here his father's word, there his concern for his brother.
As he weighed Bharata's nature in his heart, the Lord's mind could not settle where the right course lay.
ayodhya.227.cau3: Then his mind was set at rest, knowing this: Bharata keeps to my word; he is good and wise.
Lakṣmaṇa saw the unease in the Lord's heart, and spoke counsel of policy that suited the hour.
ayodhya.227.cau4: My master, I speak a little unasked; when the hour calls for it, a servant's boldness is no insolence.
You, my Lord, are the crown of all who know all things; I, your follower, say what I myself understand.
ayodhya.227.do227: My Lord, you are a true friend to all, wholly guileless of heart, a treasury of goodness and affection.
You hold everyone in love and trust, and in your heart you think all are as you are.
ayodhya.228.cau1: When power comes to dull souls caught up in sense-pleasure, delusion takes hold of them and their nature shows.
Bharata is true to right conduct, good and discerning; all the world knows how he loves the Lord's feet.
ayodhya.228.cau2: Yet he too, having gained Śrī Rāma's seat today, has set out to break the bounds of dharma.
The crooked, wicked brother, watching for an evil hour and knowing that Śrī Rāma is alone in his forest exile,
ayodhya.228.cau3: has laid evil plans in his heart and gathered his host, and comes to make his rule free of every thorn.
Devising crooked schemes in a million ways, the two brothers have come with an army they have raised.
ayodhya.228.cau4: If there were no guile and ill intent in his heart, who would care for chariots, horses and lines of elephants?
Yet there is no cause to single out Bharata for blame: the world goes mad when it comes to a throne.
ayodhya.228.do228: The Moon went to the wife of his guru; Nahuṣa rode in a litter borne by Brahmins;
and Vena turned from the world's ways and the Vedas, lower than any other.
ayodhya.229.cau1: Sahasrabāhu, Indra lord of the gods, Triśaṅku: whom has the pride of kingship not disgraced?
Bharata has taken a fitting step, for of an enemy or a debt one should never leave the least part.
ayodhya.229.cau2: But one thing Bharata has done ill: he has slighted Śrī Rāma, thinking him without help.
That too he will understand full well today, when in battle he sees Śrī Rāma's face in anger.
ayodhya.229.cau3: With these words Lakṣmaṇa lost the mood of counsel; the tree of the warlike mood blossomed, its flowers the hair standing on end over his body.
He bowed at the Lord's feet, set their dust upon his head, and spoke the truth of his own inborn strength.
ayodhya.229.cau4: My Lord, do not take what I say amiss; Bharata has provoked us in no small measure.
How long are we to suffer it and crush our feelings? Our Lord is at our side and the bow in our hands.
ayodhya.229.do229: A kṣatriya by race, born in the line of Raghu, and known to the whole world as Śrī Rāma's follower:
what is as lowly as dust? Yet kick it, and even dust rises to the head.
ayodhya.230.cau1: He stood, folded his hands and begged leave; it was as though the heroic mood had woken from its sleep.
He tied his matted hair up on his head, girded the quiver tight at his waist, readied his bow and took up an arrow.
ayodhya.230.cau2: Today I shall earn the glory of a true servant of Śrī Rāma, and in battle Bharata shall learn from me.
Paid in full for scorning Śrī Rāma, the two brothers shall sleep on the bed of war.
ayodhya.230.cau3: The whole company has gathered here, and well it has; today I shall let out all my old anger.
As a lion crushes a herd of elephants and a hawk wraps up a quail in its talons,
ayodhya.230.cau4: even so shall I scorn Bharata and strike him down on the field, with his army and his younger brother.
Should Śaṅkara himself come to help him, I will still kill him in battle; I swear it by Śrī Rāma.
ayodhya.230.do230: Seeing Lakṣmaṇa beside himself with fury and hearing his oath, which was certain to be kept,
all the worlds were struck with fear, and their guardians wished to flee in panic.
ayodhya.231.cau1: The world was sunk in fear. Then a voice spoke from the sky, extolling the great strength of Lakṣmaṇa's arms:
Dear one, who can tell of your valour and your might, and who is there who knows them?
ayodhya.231.cau2: Whatever the task, right or wrong, all agree that it is best done with understanding.
Those who act in haste and repent afterwards are not wise, say the Vedas and the learned.
ayodhya.231.cau3: At the words of the gods Lakṣmaṇa was abashed, and Śrī Rāma and Sītā honoured him with kindly regard.
Śrī Rāma said: Dear brother, what you said is sound policy. Of all things, brother, the intoxication of kingship is the hardest.
ayodhya.231.cau4: It is the kings who have never waited upon the assembly of saints that grow drunk on it at the first sip.
Listen, Lakṣmaṇa: anyone as good as Bharata has never been heard of or seen in all the Creator's world.
ayodhya.231.do231: Even were he to gain the rank of Brahmā, Viṣṇu or Śiva, Bharata would not be drunk with power.
Can drops of sour gruel ever turn the ocean of milk?
ayodhya.232.cau1: Darkness may yet swallow the blazing midday sun, the sky may sink into the clouds and be lost in them;
Agastya may drown in the water of a cow's hoofprint, and the earth may give up her natural forbearance;
ayodhya.232.cau2: a mosquito's puff may blow Mount Meru away; but pride of kingship can never touch Bharata, brother.
Lakṣmaṇa, I swear by you and by our father: there is no brother so pure and so good as Bharata.
ayodhya.232.cau3: Virtue is milk, dear brother, and fault is water; the Creator blends the two and so makes the world.
Bharata is a swan in the lake of the solar race; by his birth he has parted virtue from fault.
ayodhya.232.cau4: Taking up the milk of virtue and leaving the water of fault, he has lit up the world with his fame.
